"DID you get the pair of trousers I sent you, Pat?" "No, yer honour; I only got wan." "WHY'S Faznoodle got a band on his hat?" " Oh. dontchyerknow ? He's so fond of music." WHEN a man is twenty-five he knows some- thing; when he is forty-five he wishes he knew

some-thing. GEORGI: : "Laura, will you be my better half?" Laura: "Oh, George, how can I, and you so good ? " IT was a Leeds girl, having heard a great deal of talk about the electric fluid, asked how much it sold for a quart. TEAcHER in mineralogy class: "Johnny, give me the name of the largest known diamond." Johnny: "The ace."

A YOUNG man should lay up something for a rainy day. He should consider what he is going to do when he cannot do anything. TEACHER (t 0 class in geography): "If I should dig a hole through the earth, where would I come out ? " Small boy: "Oat of the hole." JACK: "Have a cigar, Billy ? " Billy: "No. I've given up smoking.' Jack: "Well, tell me,all about her."

"Well, Colonel, I see that we're going to have cheaper sugar." "Won't make a particle of differ- ence to me. I never take sugar in mine." Jessie: "Mamma, what does pro and con mean?" Flossie: "Why, I'm s'prised at your ign'ance. It means man and wife; doesn't it, mamma ?" _ _ .

A.: "You are so modest I don't see how you ever came to propose to your wife." B.: "That was very simple. I said nothing, and she said nothing, and some word brought on another." "I AM growing up pretty fast, and soon I shall be raising a moustache," said Tommy Toddler. "You I are mistaken, my boy. When you raise a moustache ' you'll be growing down." SMITHSoN : "That's my latest 7.ust—cost me a hundred pounds." Levyson : "A 'uriderd pound, my dear! Why my latest 'bust' cost my creditors a 'and( rd thousand pound!" JUDGE: "How did you come to rob this man in broad daylight on a frequented thoroughfare 7" Highwayman: "I couldn't help it, Judge; I had an engagement for every night of that week." A SEmr-RELicaous weekly gives the following as "a true school story," which is "also now" :—Ques- tion "What is an improper framion ?" Answer: "A figure turned upside down." CENSUS enumerator: "Have you any children 2" Old plainsman "Yes, two." Census enumerator: "Sons or daughters 2" Old plainsman: Neither, confound 'era! They're both mashers." HE (after a tiff): "So you persist in breaking the engagement ?" Mature fiancee: "Certainly. What do you take me for ?" He: "About forty. Better think it over; it may be your,last chance." HOLLIS HOLWORTIdY (trying to grow a mous- tache): "I say, Tom, does it show at all 9" Tom Thayer (seriously): "Well, yes, a little • but never mind, I don't think any one will notice ft." TEACHER: "You should be more correct in your composition, Johnny. You say, love school.' Now, school cannot be loved. Can't you use a more correct expression ? " Johnny: "I hate school."

JACK : "So pretty, impecunious Sallie Jones, whom I used to flirt with, is the wife of a millionaire, you say? Bless me, how the wheel of fortune does turn!" Bill: "Yes, especially when a pair of pretty shoulders are put to it. A GREEN one, who had crossed the Atlantic, told a story of a storm, when the rain poured down in such torrents that the ocean rose Gin. "There's no mistake," said he, "because the captain kept a mark on the side of the vessel."

"A: "And what has become of your son, Jim- mie ?" B: " Jimmie's gone into journalism." A: "Why, he's only ten years old." B: "True; but, you know, ke sells forty newspapers a day. He's a smart boy, that Jimmie."

AN advocate before an English bench of magistrates lately said he had two witnesses in court in support of the cause of his client, and they would be sure to speak the truth, for he had had no opportunity of communicating with them. DAUGHTER: "Pa, Mr. S :in and I were discus- ing which was the prefere, He will go,' or he shall go.' What do you say?" Pa (looking at his watch): "As it is 11.30 o'clock, I should say he must go 'was the correct expression." SHE: "Now, John, I don't think you ought to go out to-night. This is the fourth night you have been out this week." He: "Business, you know, dear; and, besides, it will give you a chance to finish your magazine article on 'How to Keep a Husband at Home."

DOCTOR: "I am very sorry, sir, but I am obliged to tell you, In regard to the condition of your wife, that you have to be prepared for the worst." Husband (with a deep sigh) : "So you really think that she is convalescent."

BATCHELOR - FRIEND, to newly-married man: "Why this dejection, dear boy 7 Have you suffered a disappointment 7" "Yes, my wife can't sing." "Why, that should not distress you; I think you are to be congratulated.". " Ah, but she thinks she can r Bus' DRIVER (to director of van in front, which Is blocking the way): " J'yer, get on, get on I You've bin keepin' us waitin' five minutes." Van driver (turning round): "Five minutes Well, that ain't so long. You 'ad to wait five years once, 'adn't yell', " Wno was that gentleman I just saw you talking with so earnestly 7' "Oh, that was the exiled Nihilist, Mr. At-choo-at-chow-at-chee-at-chiski l" "Why, what a frightful cold you have 1" "Not at all; not at all. 1 was merely giving you the exact pronunciation of the gentleman's name. It's sneezy enough when you've learned how." "Ana you an Oddfellow?" "No, sir, I've been married a week." "I mean, do you belong to the Order of Oddfellows 7" "No, I belong to the Order of Married Men." "Dear mei how dull! Are you a Mason?" "No, I'm a carpenter." "Worse and worse. Are you a Son of Temperance?" "Con- found it, no! 1 am a son of Mr. John Gosling." The querist went his way. MEEK and lowly in bis tattered raiment, the tramp stood before the woman of the house and breathed forth the desire of his heart. "Fear not, gentle woman," said he, "it is not work that I seek, nor is it bread, but I strongly crave the companion- la shilling. Have foti it 7"

THE conversation had tamed on an old beau, who by the aid of cosmetics and other artifices seemed to grow a little younger every year. "Yon will see," said some one, "how he will succeed in hiding the ravages of time." "And finally die of extreme youth," added another speaker. "EVA," he said softly, as he strolled through the park, "let me call you Eve. It will make this place seem still more like the Garden of Eden." "Certainly, George," replied the bewitching maid, "but I can't call you Adam. You—yeu are not my first man, you know. Not by several, George." A MAN who boarded an open car found a woman occupying one end of the seat, while all the rest of It was empty. He stood for a moment waiting for her to "hitch," but as she made no move he quietly asked—" Madame, do you wish me to step on you 7" "If you dare to I" she promptly replied. "My husband tried it this morning and got left, and now I'm waiting for someone else." He went back to the last street. OVERHEARD at the Tralee lawn tennis meeting: —She—" Well, Mr. Flannagan, I bear Mr. Tawler pays his devours to you regularly." He—" Devours, Indeed! I should think he does. If he generally eats as much, I'd prefer to ask a travelling menagerie in to dinner, or give him a pound to go and pay for his devours elsewhere." And then she broke off the match with Mr. Tawler, who bad stated in his last letter that be could "scarcely eat for very love." A YOUNG woman, on becoming engaged for a second time, was somewhat astonished at receiving from number two the identical ring she had returned to her first love. "Why, Charles,' she said, "this Is the same ring I had when I was engaged to Harry." "I know it," replied the young man. "Harry is an old friend of mine, and when he heard of our engagement he came around to congratulate me, and offered to sell me the ring for half cost. He said you liked it very much and it fitted, 60 I took it. Good sch,nae, eh!" The young woman's sensations are not described. div.p: " CAPITAL" CHAT.
The Duke and Duchess of Westminster,who were at Newmarket last week for three days, have re- turned to Eaton Hall, Cheshire.
Tolstoi, the novelist, spent S:unday in Paris,at the. Hotel Mirabeau, and has now gone to Biarritz, where he intends remaining for some months. ,

The son of the Norwegian dramatist Ibsen, who is engaged to a daughter of the dramatist BjEirnsen, is not unknown in London. A few years ago he spent some months in London reading English law, and has inherited from his father a talent for writ- ing, which he has not always employed to his per- sonal advantage. He is not an lbsenite.

It is not generally known that Sir Charles Dalry- mple, M.P., for Ipswich, is a brother of Sir James Fergusson. The change of name was occasioned through succession to property. Other two brothers sit in the house under different cognomens. Mr. James Campbell, Conservative member for Glasgow University, is a broiler of Mr. Campbell-Bannerman, the Gladstonian.

While the Prince of Wales is rusticating at Cul- ford, his eldest son and heir is the guest of viscount Powerscourt, at his stately seat in county Wicklow. Prince Albert Victor's host is a rich man for an Irish peer, drawing considerable revenues from his land in Wexford and Wicklow. Powerscourt Castle,near Enniscorthy, has in its lovely deer park the highest waterfall in Ireland.

" There is no such doctrine in the Constitution," says that high authority on this sacred mystery, Mr. Bryce, "as that the House of Lords is entitled at its pleasure to compel a dissolution." Well, that is a good thing—for the Constitution. Most assuredly, if that sacred mystery allowed such powers to the House of Lords as Lord Salisbury or Mr. Goschen claim for it, the sacred mystery would have to be overhauled and licked into more intelligible shape.

The Dowager Lady Ailesbury,who died abroad last w,.:ek, was not,as some supposed,the famous "Maria, Marchioness," the favourite of Court circles. The latter lady, the widow of the first Marquis of Ailes- bury, shows no signs of age, though she was mar- ried in the days when William IV. was King. Her abundant light brown hair, her tall, youthful-look- ing figure, her observant eyes and witty tongue, will probably still adorn and enliven Court circles for many a day.

Lord Robert Cecil, Lord Salisbury's barrister son, has just transferred himself from the Northern Cir- cuit to the South-eastern, which is a remarkable move, considering how well he had beendoing, and how powerfully he was supported. Lord Robert is a very clever man,but he owes something of his suc- cess to his father's solicitor, Sir Richard Nicholson, who has been pushing him assiduously, and last session he gave him briefs in several important Parliamentary cases.

In a somewhat incoherent letter in the "Times " Lord Ebury, who is a nonagenarian, complains that the Liberals apply "the invidious appellation of Tory to the present Government." Tory, he says, is " a term of reproach." This is funny. Lord Salisbury frankly prefers the term Tory to Conser- vative. Lord Ebury does not provide us with a substitute, but a Tory by any other name would be just as objectionable to us. Your Tory cannot con- ceal his principles under another name any more than the Ethiopian can change his skin.

M. Henri Rochefort is engaged on the libretto of a grand opera founded on the well-worn subject of Mazeppa." The music will be composed by M. de Wenzel, the musical ditector of the Empire Theatre M. Rochefort seems to be returning to his early hobby. Before the versatile Frenchman entered into the regions of Socialism and Boulangism, he was considered as the rising author in the Parisian theatrical world, and no doubt would have become the W. S. Gilbert of France. Many of his (tharming early comedies, written a quarter of a century ago, have been "adapted for the English stage" with- out acknowledgement by J. S. Buckstone, Mark Lemon, and others.

"1 am the Dean of Christ Church, sir;. This is my wife—pray look at her, She is the Broad, I am the High, We are the University." These irreverent undergraduate lines (writes a cor- respondent) at least point out the important posi- tion held in Oxford by Dean Liddell, whose resig- nation of the deanery of Christ Church was announced yesterday, and his wife. Dean Liddell, a scion of the Ravensworth family, was second or third rate as a don, but an excellent courtier— second in that rle, however, to Mrs. Dean. The great fact about him to bear in mind is that he was once a chaplain to the Prince Consort.

It is not generally known that Lord de Tabley,. who is now lying seriously ill at his place in Cheshire, is a poet of no inconsidei able powers, He published between 1864 and 1873 no less than seven volumes of verse, besides two novels, a guide to the study of book plates, and a large amount of work on numismatic subjects. His metrical drama of " Philoctetes,"' published in 1865, created a gteat stir, an.l made men wonder if a new poet was arising. But in 1873 he broke away from litera- ture, and has not published a verse since. In 1866 Lord de Tabley contested Mid-Cheshire as a Lib- eral, but was unsuccessful. He was born in 1835, so that he is still in the prime of life. Most of his literary work was done under the nom de plume of Win. Lancaster.

A great African traveller arrived in London on Sunday. He did not blow his own trumpet, nor did others trumpet his arrival. He arrived quietly and unobserved. He wai Mr. Joseph Thomson,a young, modest, but intrepid traveller who has made we believe five if not six visits to Africa, and is not yet 30. Like Stanley, Mr. Thomson '-as been in the service of the British East Africa Company, and has been exploring in the neighbourhood of Lake Nyassa, and has travelled southwards through 'Mashonaland. Mr. Thomson in his travels saw the tree on which Livingstone's men carved the record of the great traveller's death. Mr. Thomson does not travel with a gang of retainers and reporters behind him, but this does not seem to incapacitate him from doing good work.

Lady Mildred Jessup, oue of Earl Strathmore's daughters, who were thrown out of a trap near Glamis Castle, was the first Englishwoman of rank to marry an American. Her husband is a wealthy banker of New York, but since his marriage he has lived chiefly at Lucerne. The Earl of Strathmore was rescued from comparative poverty by the death of Mr. Bowes, of Streatlam Costle, from whom immense estates in Durham and Yorkshire- passed to him in strict settlement six years ago, The pride of the family is still the ancient castle of Glamis, with its vaulted stone hall, huge baronial, kitchen, and secret rooms, cut out of the thick walls. There is one room in the castle known only to the Earl, his heir,and his factor, although many have tried to discover its position.

A pretty little matrimonial story was told on Saturday at Worship-st. police court by Emma Fielder, wife of John Fielder. Emma is now 1T years and 10 months old. She married John on, the 10th August last. She is able to fix the date exactly, because the wedding-ring was pawned the next day to provide dinner, and the ticket is dated 11th Aug. On the oth Sept., Mr. John Fielder, who is "appar- ently about 22," gave up housekeeping and returned to the maternal roof. Ile has been residing with his mother ever since, and refuses to support his wife. He has now been ordered to pay the latter 10a. a week. If is is really necessary that a boy and girl united in this way should be indissoluoly tied together for the rest of their mortal life, surely it would be well to put a few more difficulties in the way of their getting united in the first instance.

Little Billy Riddick, aged 11, has found out hlw to escape the doom. which the poet predicts for him who steals what mixt his'n. Billy was sent by a friend of his mother to change a sovereign. He not. only went to change the sovereign, but he went on to change the change, and made merry with the proceeds. When the confiding friend of his mother discovered Master William again, with the aid of a detective sergeant, the sovereign was chan'ked into nothing at all. One would think that Billy had stolen it, but Mr. Rose, the youngest metropolitan magistrate, is a smart lawyer, and knows better than that. Billy did not steal the money, because he was told to change it, and did so. He didn't steal the change, because the owner never had possession of it, and he did not commit embezzle- ment because embezzlement can only be committed by a paid servant. Who can feel much respect for the law when a child of 11 can make it look so foolish?

div.head: EXAMINER, SATURDAY, OCTOBER 24, 1891. A VOYAGE TO AUSTRALIA.
div.p: THE EXAMINER, SATURDAY, OCTOBER 24, 1891. A VOYAGE TO AUSTRALIA.

land. We had a good look round and visited some of the most important places, Houses of Parlia- ment, the Governor's house, and Botanical Gardens. Of course, its chief feature is the Table Mountain, with its table top from which it takes its name. I was asked by one old English gentleman what I thought about it (the mountain). I told him it looked very grand, but that we had as fine scenery in England in the lake districts. He laughed and said—" Well, there is nothing like having a good opinion of your own country." But, Mr. Editor, there are very few Englishmen—comparatively , speaking---who know the beauty of our Lake Dis- trict. There are sights there that thousands of peo- ple have travelled hundreds of miles to see, and yet those in its immediate neighbourhood,den't trouble themselves to become acquainted with them. But to return to the Cape: The impression of some Eng- lishmen that I spoke to, was that there was plenty of money to be made there if they could get rid of the Dutch. They seem to have a little respect for the coloured people who walk about with a jaunty air, which would convince you that they consider them- selves as good as you. One of my children on see- ing a coloured woman said rather loudly " 011,look at that nigger," when a man who was passing by turned round and said" You a nigger! " and not very pleasantly either. I cautioned them not to be so very pronounced in their opinions or they might get into trouble—although I must confess a black man looked rather comical in a tall white hat with a broad brim! To talk about these people revolting against the British looks almost comical; but this journey has taught me one lesson, and that is that the British public, as a rule, are very ignorant of what is going on in this part of the world. My im- pression of Cape Town people was, that they were contented with the British rule, and no comparison could be drawn between them and the people of , Las Palmas.
BY W
UNSWORTII.
The following is the continuation of Mr. Uns- worth's account of his voyage to Australia, to which reference was made in our last issue : Dear Mr. Editor,

I concluded my last letter just as we arrived at Las Palmas, the Capital of the Canary Isles. We put in with the intention of taking sufficient coal to carry us to Australia, and I took advantage of the few hours in looking round. It has a popula- tion of about °5,000; most of these people are wretchedly poor, living in huts built up of a kind of pumice stone, which is lying about in abundance, as the island seems to have been formed at some

time by volcanic disturbance. These huts are cov- ered by bamboo cane with a layer of long grass and mud on the top, and without windows, the only light being through the door. The people were very pleasant and invited me in—an invitation which I gladly accepted, as it was quite a novelty to me. Whilst looking at them, I could not help feeling sorry for them in their wretched condition, although they seemed quite contented. The child- ren were runing about almost naked, indeed some of them were quite so. All their cooking (which is very simple), is done on the floor—which is only the 'earth. Contrast these with the homes of the working classes of England, and for once I felt proud that I was an Englishman; and still with all this apparent wretchedness they could boast of such outside surroundings as are totally impossible in England. Plants which I saw growing wild here,l saw a short time ago at Kew Gardens, (London), in, glass-houses, and taken very great care of. Grapes .oranges, bananas, pineapples and all kinds of hot- house plants also grow here. The children seemed bright and cheerful, their time being spent in ram- bling about, School Boards being quite at a discount here. As we arrived nearer to the city—our landing place being about a mile out—the houses were more substantial, being built of gravel (found on the beach) mixed with cement, formed into blocks and dried in the sun, but even these had no windows, the light being admitted through open spaces in the day time, which were closed by shutters at night. Some of the shops had glass windows, and we were much amused at looking at one of the advertit ements over one of the doors to see " CROSFIELD'S PERFECTION SOAP."
(To be Concluded)

and felt a little proud of it, as it came from our native town. Although the majority of the people were very poor they could boast of a very tine Cath- edral—(Roman Catholic, the natives being of Span- ish descent)—which splendour one cannot help but look upon with something like contempt, seeing it is supported in the midst of poverty and ignor- ance, and more o when you learn as I did, that the bulk of workingmen earned from is. 6d. to 2s. per day, working from early morning till late at night; the women who work in the fields earned 'lid. per day. The food of the men, working at coaling the vessel consisted of Indian Meal mixed into a stiff paste with goat's milk, along with cheese and a banana or two. I asked one of them if he liked it, and he said pointing to some bread, " dis no good,!' and pointing to the Indian Meal mixture he drew up the muscle of his arm to show that there was more strength in it than bread. To. all appearance he was quite satisfied with his bill of fare; and that they are contented with their lot we had ample proof, as accidentally one of them felt asleep on the vessel and was carried out to sea with us. On awakening he made a dreadful noise wad wanted to be taken back; o! course this could not be done, he

had to go on with us. The captain found him a job at 2.95. per week and his food, with an offer of con- stant work to stay on the ship. but no,. on his arri- val at Melbourne ht said—" plenty ship,.go back to has Palmas." In a few days we sighted Chpe Verde, the extreme point on the West coast ot ...A.lfrica, and North of the Gulf of Guinea, and this we expected to be the last we should see of land for five weeks.
A DARING IMPOSTOR
THE STORY OF AN INNOCENT CONVICT.
BY ALFRED R. CALHOUN.
CHAPTER XIX.

THE BLOW FALLS. "You have denied me again and again. As a last favour I ask that you see me now, and let me hear from your own lips if it be your wish that we shall not meet again." The foregoing was the purport of a note which Mott Reybold sent up by a servant, with his card, to Irene Lefferts. _ _

Once Irene had felt, or imagined she felt, some- thing like love for this man. With more maturity of person and character there came indifference; an indifference that had in it something like contempt, as rumour or her own experience revealed to her more and more Reybold's true character. Irene Lefferts was incapable of hate, in the vicious meaning of the world, but ever since Rey- bold attempted what he called his "exposition of Allen Lee,' she actually hated him. Without being able to give a reason for her belief, she came to feel, as much as she did the fact of her own existence, that Mott Reybold was at the bottom of the persecution to which Allen had been so cruelly subjected. Gratitude for the heroism that preserved her own Life would have drawn her naturally to Allen Lee, even if he had been a less attractive man, intel- lectually and physically. But even if he had not been her rescuer, their association must have led to an attachment that aould have but one ending—love. Irene wanted to think that it was interest and not love that drew her to Allen Lee, and-she tried to reason herself into the belief that she regarded Florence with just the same feeling she had for the brother. But one cannot leng mistake the lightning's flash for the ingle's glow, nor be long deceived into thinking that love for the one in any way resembles the friendship that may be given to the many. Irene read Reybold's note, and decided to see him.

When she entered the parlour, where he awaited her, he rose and approached her with extende4 hand. She met his advance with a cold bow, waved him to a chair, and said, with a glance at the note which; she had brought with her,. "You see I have complied with your request." "I do not know whether I should express my pain at your past refusals to see me, or my thank- fulness that you have made an exception in the present instance," said Reyb6d, nervously twitching his moustache.
"You must have known + by my refusals," said Irene, calmly, but with a ring of unmistakeable reso- tution in her voice, "that if :11 had wished to see you I should have done so."

"Then I am to understand by this persistent rreatment that you wish me to consider our friend- ship at an end 2" he said, with' an angry glow in his ayes, though he tried to appear cool. "Yes; and the exception, in the present instance, is that I may tell you so." "You have a reason for this conduct?" "I try to have a reason for all my actions," she replied. "May I ask what your reasons are in this in- stance ? " "H you do not know, it woul& be a waste of time to tell you—" "But surely," lie broke in," "even the lowest 3riminal has the right to know the charges, and to hear the evidence on which he is convicted." "I neither condemn nor convict. If you are satisfied with your life, I can lee no reason why [should try to change it. Is it not sufficient that desire to hold no further intercourse with you 7" "Yes. Miss Lefferts, your wish should be law—it slways has been law with me. But your own sense A fairness should lead you to give me a reason for your change. If I cannot plead not guilty,' I can, A least, have the satisfaction of seeing myself as you do's "That would hardly be a satisfaction, / am think- :rig. But, let me ask you one question." "A dozen, if you wish, Miss Lefferts." "You remember the day I came so. near drowning A the Branch ?"

Florence admitted her, and it needed no second dance at the patient, beautiful face to prove that iome great calamity bad befallen the family. "What is it? What has hap .ened 1" cried Irene, as she caught Florence in her arms and kissed her again, as much to ease her own over-burdened heart as to express her sympathy. "The conspirators have Allen in their power again I" sobbed Florence; but no words could describe the agony in her voice. "Where is he ?"
"They have taken him to gaol. I have just come from seeing him. But I dare not stay away longer; for, as you know, mother is very low, and I fear this blow will kill her."

"What gaol is he in?" asked Irene, quickly. "In the Tombs." "When was he taken 2" "At daylight this morning...-. " And the charge?" "I do not understand them. They are many—". "And one is forgery?" interrupted Irene. " It is." "What name was forged?" "Your father's." "My father's!" "Yes."

"Then I see through it all. More than ever lam convinced that Allen Lee is the victim of a mon- strous conspiracy. He came to my rescue when my life was in danger, and he saved me. With God's help, I will save his name from infamy, and prove to the world that it has wronged and cruelly maligned him!" exclaimed Irene, with tragic/ force.
CHAPTER XX.
"COURAGE, AND I WILL SAVE YOU r
Kissing Florence again, and begging her to have faith and patience, Irene hurried out of the tene- ment house and half ran to Union-square, six blocks to the east.

Here she called a cab, and as the driver held the door open with one hand and touched his hat with the other, he asked: "Where to, lady?" "Do you know where the Tombs is r "Yes, lady; in Centre-street," said the driver. unable to conceal his surprise at her question. "Then take me there at once." "It will be a dollnr and a half, lady—" _

, "I did not ask what you would charge. The law regulates that. Take me to the Tombs at once," said Irene; and she sprang into the carriage and quickly shut the door_ "Well, that lady means business," said the driver, as he climbed into the front seat, on which an un. amployed companion was sitting. Keep noon," was the only explanation made by Irene to back nothing from me, for I must see my way the servant who spoke to her as she hurried out of clearly," she said, with such an expression of the house, , determination as he had never noticed in her before, Walking so fast as to attract the attention of ' Allen was still so much stunned by the blow, that , every one whom she met in the street, Irene hastened at once to the house in which Allen while he was sure of the source from which it came, i lica..lived.

div.head: NO W TO ZETERN TO THE SEA.
div.p: NO W TO ZETERN TO THE SEA.

If there is one thing I am disappointed in it is the scarcity of sea life. I should have thought, know- ing as we do that the-ocean abounds with life of one kind or another, that something would have turned up during each day, but it was quite the reverse you might travel tor clays without seeing the least signs of life, until we reached the equator. We then met with shoals of !Tying fish, at first rather small (abou( inches long). Some of these came on deck by night, attracted by the light , the sailors say. Later on they were much larger. I caught two of the finest seen during the voyage 22 inches long and 24 inches from tip to tip of the wing. If if could have preserved them Itwould have sent them 'home. They might have filled scone corner of the Mcseum, but I had to content myself with the wings, which I spread out on a board, and when dry they remained opened and made a splendid picture. , The body is something like a mackerel in al:pear-1 ance ; but the flavour is delicious. There is another kind of life pecular to this part of the world.. (and only seen at night) ; something like a jelly fish and called "The sailors' lantern." They are the shape of a sausage (excuse the comparison) only hollow and with w rough outside. lam able to give you this outline of them as we had a few of them on deck, and you may be sure they were pretty plenti- ful, when we could drops) bucket attached to arope over the side and bring, them on board while the ship was going at full speed. The peculiarity of those fish Was that they gave off a light on,sea, something like a glowworm on land, only, being so much larger, the light' was more brilliant. This power of illumination was evidently within itself, for,.on touching it, it would light up for about a minute and die out, or if the water was agitated it would become one mass et light, hence the name— "Sailors' lantern." I should think we passed through them for half-an-hour and it was a brilliant light while it lasted. This was the only time we saw them ;we kept one in a glass all night, but in the morning it had shrunk to, a mere nothing. On. the 9th July

div.head: WI4I CROMMI) THE LINE
div.p: WI4I CROMMI) THE LINE

and. tile saiibrs went through the performanceof ducking those of their mates who had not crossed the equator before ; andipoor beggars, they did catch it.. Insteadtof putting them over the side,.as used to be the custom, a sail, was fitted up on deck and filed with water. Father Neptune was raised on a platform last over the sail—and each one was brought to him and wae lathered and shavked, with. au occasional lather in the mouth, "and then mid-, , denly pushed into the-water and ducked anditossed. about by Fhther Neptune's assistants. Some had stowed away, and a search party was sent out for• them; those who went the quietest seemed to get on tl.e best.. To finish up, there was a. procession, round the vessel (the sailors, I forgot to say, were dressed up in all sorts of costumes). Three cheers. , for the captain were given, and they concluded with ' getting "lolly." Altogether it was a "rummy " sort. of business, and so the time goes; anything to.' create a little life. Occasionally we would sight a vessel—most of them being 5 or 6: miles away- one only coming l close enough for us to signal.. The sea was not rough—only what the sailors call. choppy, with a strong opposite currant all the war from Las Palraa.s. It became evident we, should have to call at the Cape, as we should not have, sufficient coal to carry us to Australia—having lost so much time owing to the opposite currents. This we were all glad of being anxious to.have

div.head: SIGHT OF CAPETOWN.
div.p: A SIGHT OF CAPETOWN.

and once more to put our foot on land. Had I I known a little sooner I should have posted a por- tion of this letter. On the 2Pst July,. we arrived at Capetown. Ido not know its population, but ' to look at it from the vessel, t seems a good-sized town and very beautiful as we viewed it from Table Bay, nestling at the. Doot of Table Mountain. The bulk of the houses skirt the bay, as the moun- tain runs almost perpendicular about a mile from the shore. I could not help but feel somewhat amused, and thought "And this is the great Cape- town, the metropolis of Cape Colony, that some- times talks (as the papers say) about revolting against the British rule, when they don't get all their own way." Why, Mr. Editor, half-a-dozen men-of-war would in so many hours blow the place out of existence. lam sure the people must feel highly flattered when they read the reports from home, as one half of them are Dutch Kaffirs, Hottentots,..tc. I called,with one of my daughters, in one of the schools we passed. The schoolmaster (Dutch) was very nice when he knew we came from the "old country," and gave the first class a dictation lesson, which they did very well, but the discipline was very poor. My daughter, who was taught at People's College, said to me "This would not do for Mr. Twiss," and I thought so too. They teach English in the morning and Dutch in the afternoon. The language. spoken is English, and although a nice place in itself, I cannct say I was much struck with it as a business place. My im- pression was that if Melbourne was anything like Capetown I should take the next boat back again. The goods we saw marked in the shop windows were as cheap, or perhaps cheaper, than in Bug-

div.head: LEARNT IN A BATH.
div.p: LEARNT IN A BATH.

(From "Little Folks.") Evoryone knows the word " Eureka " nowadays, but 1 wonder whether any of you know the meaning of that word, and the cause ot its being so famous? Eureka means simply I have found it. and it was made humus in this way. There was once a Tyrant or ruler of Syracuse whose name was hero. One day he gave some gold to a man, and ordered him to make a crown of it. When the crown was sent home, Hiero looked at it, and was quite sure from its lightness that all the gold had not been used. He thought, in fact. that the workman had cheated him by taking away some gold and putting some other metal to it to make up the etuie required. hero sent at once for Archimebes,. who was a very clever man, and asked him to help him find out what had been done. Of couvse this would be easy enough now, for we have proper means of testing whether a thing is made of pure metal or not; but in Those days, about two hundred years before Christ oame into the world, the only plan they knew of was to 'melt it down, which hero did not wish to dnt.

The king knew exactly what was the weight of the gold he halgiven tc,the workmanybut he knew too that a pound of silver would be larger in size than a pound of gold, and it would be easy for any dishonest person; to put silver instead a gold, and yet make the crown as big as had been ordered. Archimedes and: Hiero put their heads together, but it was no good.:. they could not think of arty plan for finding out the workman's trick, and Archimedes was at last obliged to own him-a-elf beaten.

There is an old saying that if you want to find something you have. lost, you ought to. begin By looking in the most unlilely places; and Avelq- eledesfound out this problem in the most unlikely place of all, I should:say. He was just' stepping into his bath one day when he noticed that as tirkt. bath wau very full, the water ran over the top. make room for his tedy. " Eureka !" he exclaimed. "I have found in. Supposing anything the sane size as my body were put in the bath, the same quantity of water would) runaver, even if the substance were onlyhalf'the *eight. It is size not, weight, that will.' send tha water over."

_ Ile jumped out at occe, and went home to try. experiments, still exclaiming " Eureka.!!' in hi - delight. -- lie took a lump of gcrld. and a lump of silver,efteh. weighing exactly the same as a crown, and having: filled'a vessel carefully with water, he put the sil- ver ins. and noticed exactly how much water fl6weg,q) overt Filling the vessel; up again, he plunged in, in thegold, and found that less water • ran overt Thew he took the crown o itself, and pnt it in the - brimming bath. Less water ran over than wheni the pure silver lump wont in, but more water thaw when the gold was immersed. So<by thinking this cut, you will see that the workman had made the crown not of pure gold now of pure silver, but of a mixture of the two.,. Hiero, was so pleased with Archimedea-for finding., this out that he said he should believe-whatever. he teld him after that.

He in a great rage went inland got a gun and shot the dog.. Yager immediately went and• summoned Alberts-rand when the-aaee was called the magis- trate- said "Mr. Alberts, you are charged with, shooting Mr. Yager's dog!' Alberts, a, perky 'Atte Dutchman, ejaculated" Rh?" "Did you, or didl yon,not, shoot the dog.??" "Oh, I shooted the dog right; enough," said Alberts, "At the same tinel make•him prove it." After the laughter had sub* sided the magistrate 'bolting towards Yager, said,. "What did you value yourdog at Mr. Tager ? Tager a ponderous old Germanreplied," Oh, I did not.value the dog at one farthin,.but I make him pay every shilling." Shrieks oblaughter followed thia-con, fession. Then, saidthe magistrate to Alberts,." .I suppose the dog flevrfat you, Mr. taberts, andiyou, shot him in self-defence ? LORD R CHURCHILL LION-ILIIIVILNCI

The " Star " says.—Lord Randolph Churchill is a lion who has gone through a good deal of hunting in his day. He has. now turned the tallies,. and come out as a lion hunter. His last "Daldly" '..fraphic" letter ccntains a thrilling narratireof Ms experiences in thieline, and it ia highly interesting to study his lordship's feeling in his new char- acter. They first. came upon one lion' and, as he was walking off, the Nimrod oi South Faddington "was at once going to dismount and take aim:" for, he tells us, "I we not frightened at the. idea of firing at a retreating lion." Nobody whoramembers Lord Randolph's.history will loubt that>.Bresently, I however, six more lions were discovered.. Still, he I 'writes, "I do not admit that Iwas at all frightened." He would not admit it either at the time,.so he and his companiontwent after the lions, and for a time it seems to have been rather an open question whether there would not be a vacancy in South 'Paddington.. As told by Lord Randolph. the adven- ture reads very fine and stirring, but—Ur.. Balfour is to be the. leader of tale House of COmmons. Apart from the lions, there is something very sickening in the incidental pictures of wanton butchery which fill in Lord Randolph' narrative. Lions of coarse are vermin, which anyone may put bullets into with an easy conscience ;. but after two or three lions have been peppered to. the point at which they become dangerous, Lord Randolph and his companion (the companion does all the lion- shooting, by the way),. decide to make tracks. Just then six Koodoo cows come galloping along. A bullet is at once put into one of them. The pair then gallop off. Further on theydiscover a herd of roan antelope. Lord Randolph dismounts and fires at one ("with what effect I do not know."), His companion brings clown one, and two more "stagger away badly wonnded." A moment after. Lord Randolph hits a quagga, which his companion finishes off, and after another gallop another ante- lope is "wounded severely,' and a quagga's hind leg broken by tnrd Randolph. If this is sport, so is sticking pins into cockchafers or pulling legs off flies.

He told her all about his meeting with Mingo. Pete, and how, through Dr. Putnam, he had secured the ex-convict a position as night watchman for the large jewellery firm of Edgefield Sc Phipps.

- Knowing the prejudice of employers against et- convicts, from his own bitter experience, he had kept from the doctor the story of Mingo l'ete's life. He explained the desire of Florence and himseli to help this man, and the fact that he had long kept a valise, supposed to contain clothing and to which he had access whenever he chose, with them.

"This morning, as I was about to go to work, two officers arrested me, on the charge of robbing the store of Edgefield and Phipps. They searched the house, and in the valise left by Mingo Pete, they found a large quantity of the stolen jewellery. It was useless for me to plead innocence, and so I was brought here—" "Does Mott Reybold know this Mingo Pets "1". asked Irene, nervously stroking her forehead. "That I do not know."

"But the eharge of forgery: What of that?" "When I reached here with the officers, I found other detectives with another warrant for my arrest. It appears that during the past month there has. been put in circulation a large quantity of skilfully forged paper. Among the business men, whose. names have been freely used, is that of your father. I, of course, anew nothing about this. The police - started out to find the guilty parties. Tllky investi- gated my antecedents, and found, as you know, that I had been convicted of the crime of forgery and served a long term in the penitentiary. Oh the curse that follows one charged with crime! It was natural that these men should susLect me, and here I am," he cried, with an anguish that shook him.
Irene Lefferts rose and, layja. g a hand on each boulder, said:
"Courage,. Allen Lee! Courage, and I will. save you, f"

THE LANCASHIRE PEOPLE'S BISHOP.

Mr. John Heywood, litanchester. has just pub- lished in form of a fourpenny pamphlet a new and concise biographical sketch of the late Bishop of Manchester, which is sure to have a good sale. It is dedicated to the 188,192 persons whom Bishop Fraser confirmed during his tenure of the See of Manchester, and on the title page appears the following apt quotation: "1 don't know how it is, but I never feel more at home, nor more sure that I am uselay employed, than when I am among these kindly natured, intelligent working-men." It does not appear on the face of it, but it is nevertheless the fact, that the little work is written by the Rev. S. F. Harris, B.C.L, M.A., Vicar of Walton-le-Dale, and formerly of Blackburn. We quote below an original anecdote which Mr. Harris gives. The frontispiece to the pamphlet is a life-like portrait, and there are five other illustrations-. -

There was one thing with regard to the working classes says the author—that Bishop Fraser could not do, that was--stand aloof from them. Anything.f like " starchiness" was utterly foreign to his nature, lie was willing to talk to anybody, at the same time being a patient listener; there was no keeping even the humblest at an arm's length. The following incident is one specimen of his. everyday life. The old apparitor of-a well-known church creserines the first occasion on which he ever • spoke to. the Bishop. He was sent, down by the • vicar to meet Bishop Fraser with a cab at the • station, as it was a pouring wet day; " Bishop came up the steps smiling brightly and saying, 'Thank. ye, my -man, for bringing me this cab;' and then I was getting on the box. But all at once his lord-- ship put out his head and said, qpite sharp like,. 'what are you about, man?' I scrambled down, and said it was such pouring rain that I thought I might have a lift into the town. Why,' said the bishop,, , do yo a think I shall let you sit out there in the wet waen I am sitting comfortable,here in the dry. Get in with me, my man, and we will go together into the town.' And then we rode together, and he talked so koindly like that I felt that he was c,own indeedi Aye, we shall never look on his like again But he's only gone before we 'aye, and we'll all try and live so that we may meethim again in a better worl dL

Thz Sporting Chronicle says • That good Irian,. Mr. Brunner, M.P., has been dispensing wisdom on the sub- ject of the unemployed. He says that the best way of relieving the unemployed is not by establishino,nranici- pal workshops, as suggested by the Trades Union Con- gress, but by giving the people technical eduaation. Smart man, Mr. Brunner. Knows lots of things, does Mn. Brunner. Very few men have made more money outs of other people's work. But still he doesn't under- stand everything. For instance, he doesn't understand the question of the unemployed, and he is,quite mis- taken in fancying that technical . education will fill the hungry mouths and stomachs of the unfortunates who are clamouring because they have nothing to eat. Technical education may make better workmen in the future. It can't keep those from starving who are un- employed to-day." , Mr. Brunner replies :—" Druid's Cross,. Wavertree, Liverpool, October 17, 1891. Dear Sir,—fOur comment on my speecbat Nelson is good-humoured; and I have Ino fault to find fault with it. Still I•should like you to make the aequaintance of the Winnington Park Rea reation Club,and see the quoiting grouncis„the bowling greens, the tennis court, the cricket ground, the foot- ball ground,. the racing track. If you do,. I think you will ask yourself whether there is any gentlemen's club, the members of which get better fun for their money. If you have any minutes to spare you might inspect the free schools, with workshop attached„ the cookery, laundry, warsing and evening classes,, the co-operative stores, have a chat with the leader of, the instrumentat band, and the Chairman of the Debating Society, and might call at the office for the last balance sheet of the. savings bank and the nick club, not forgetting to note, the splendid subscription-which the men send every year, to the local infirmary.. If you see all these and reflect that they are mostly provided by the Company of which. I havnthe honour to be Chairman, for the benefit of the workpeople employed, you will come to the conclusion that whether I know% anything or not about the unero-. ployed,l do know a thing or two.—Yours, &c., Jot 4. T, Britzwart. The Editor of the Sport*/ Chronicle."

WARRINGTON BOARD OF GUARDIANS.

The fortnightly meeting of this Board was held at the Workhouse on Wednesday morning, Mr. Balharry presided, and there were also present Messrs. Ratcliffe, Heaton, Davies, Diggle, Hood- Wright, Warburton, Humphreys, John Houghton, Turton, Clarke, W. Houghton,Dignum, Dobson,Rev. E. C. E. Carleton, Mr. Jolley ; and Mr. J. C. Sutton (derky. THE FORTRESS'S SALARY.—CONDITION OF TILE WORKHOUSE. The House Committee recommended that the salary of the portress be raised from £23 a year to £25 At a special meeting of the Committee held on the 16th Oct. a general inspection and examination of the workhouse and the hospital was made. The Committee found ample space, the number of inmates for the reception of which the workhouse is certified for by the Local Government Board being 425, while the present number of inmates is 262, and for several years the average has been little over that number,. The Committee con- sidered the suggestion of the medical officer in respect of want of ventilation and the best means of providing the same where necessary, and, as the alterations and improvements desired by the medical officer and officials and also suggested by the Committee were of a minor* character, they resolved that the medical officer and master be authorised to see to the same being effectually earried out forthwith, and to report to the Committee.—Mr. Ratcliffe moved adoption of 'the minutes, and remarked that when some small defects were remedied, the hospital would do for years to come, and if it should get overcrowded, they had plenty of spare room to meet the deficiency.—Mr. HEATON seconded, and said it seemed a pity that little matters of that description were not mentioned to the Committee in the first instance. The whale thing would be done under a £5 note, but it would appear from the way it got into the papers that they had a very bad sort of a house, whereas he was glad to say they had a very good house indeed.—The minutes were adopted.

div.head: GIFT OF TOBACCO.
div.p: A GIFT OF TOBACCO.
It was mentioned that a parcel of tobacco had been sent for the inmates by Mr. Sampson, of the Norton Arms Hotel.
AN ABSCONDING LUNATIC ATTENDANT.

The Workhouse Master reported that in the case of a lunatic being brought to the house, he had no attendant to look after him.—Mr. HEATON remarked that the late lunatic attendant had run away .with the Board's uni- form, and it had been decided to prosecute him if he was found.—Mr. W. HOUGHTON said it was quite evi- dent that, a; soon as the Committee increased his salary he could not stand his keep.—The CLERK suggested that a competent man should be appointed to the poet, as there was no inmate capabla of properly undertaking the work.—The matter was referred to the House Com- mittee.

div.head: MR. DIGOLE. THE REFORMER.
div.p: MR. DIGOLE. THE REFORMER.

-- • Mr. DIGGLE said it was his intention to bring under the notice of the Board at the next meeting the state or thefirewood manufactory at the Workhouse. The room was about 17 feet long, 12 feet wide, and seven feet high, and when he was there there were eighteen per- sons in it and he was told there had been as many as 25 in at one time. There was neither fire-grate nor stove, and the place was in no way ventilated.—Mr. HEATON, interrupting, said it,would be better .if Mr. Diggle would bring this betore the House Committee.— Mr. JOLLEY : He wants it in the papers.—Mr. DIGOLE, continuing, said there were very few of the guardians who attended the House Committee. In the second place he found the parade ground, both for the inmates and the convalescent people, in a most deplorable state. He had visited it that morning and found it filled with , lakes. Two convalescent people were walking about on sticks, but could not get along without going into these lakes of water. He thought that should be remedied. Last Friday he spoke to the chairman of the Commit tee (Mr. Ratcliffe) upon it and he simply replied, " Oh, you want to lay out another £1000." The inmates liad no other place to exercise in, as they were not allowed to go into the garden. It seemed abominable to thim that they were not to be allowed tosee the flowers.—Mr. DAVIES said it was hardly worth while replying to Mr. Diggle, but he was prepared to meet him on that matter.—Mr. DIGGLE :' lam very glad of opposition.—Mr. Re'reta-FTE said that when Mr. Diggle mentioned the matter to him, he told him to bring it before the Committee.—Mr. DIGGLE :You named p4oo3.—Mr. HEaToN hoped that feeling of one contra- dicting another would not increase. Their friend Mr. Diggle was an inquisitive sort of man—(Mr. Diggle: Hear, hear)—and sometimes he was right and sometimes he was wrong. The place referred to was never intended to chop wood in, and with regard to the yards he ad- mitted they were getting out of order. He was sure, however, that the Committee would not hesitate to spend ' any money they considered necessary for making the inmates comfortable.—The matter then dropped.

THE EDUCATION ACT. In ,reply to a question, the CLERK said that the Edu- cation Act made no difference in the law so far as they wiffe,concerned. Where school fees were charged the Guardians would still have to allow them in certain cases. It was mentioned, however% that there had been a great reduction in the number of application for fees. —Mr.NIIATcLIFFm considered that the ratepayers should have had more benefit from the Act than they had received, but the Clerk pointed out various ways in whichthe amount of relief granted by the Board was reducedby the abolition or lessening of schootfees. This.was all the business of public interest.

Mr. Aaron said: that a fortnight- ago the balance sheet of the Cheshire County Council was issued.and he should %like to ask a few.guestions upon it.. How much more ,had the county business cost since the :county council was formed than it did under the magistrates ?--abo clerk (Mr. J. Ashton) replied that for the three years end- ine the 29th September, 1888, the average cost was ,09,608155. 9d.., and the cost of thecounty,council for the year ending March of this year Was £183,316 17s. 10d.—Mr. Aaron,: So that the cost has.been £54,000 more than the magistrates managed tord—The Clerk: The council took over the main roads, which is a very goo item.—Mr. Aaron said the main roads had made no difference, as the rates of the local highway boards had,not been reduced at all. The council jumped their surveyor's salary from f,500 to £9OO with travelling ex- pense.s, and had four road surveyors at £2OO each. What. had tile council spent over the Slater Lewis-O'Donnell inquiry P—The Clerk.: -..9..573 7s. 3d.—Mr. Aaron : And what benefit kave the ratepayers of the county de- rived fr9m that expensive inquiry ?—The Clerk: That I cannot answer. (Laughter.)—Mr. Aaron: I think it is high time that all the boards of guardians in Cheshire combined and petitioned the ,Local Government Board to dispense•with the County Council when their time was up next March—(loud laugher)—for their extravagant waste of money.—Mr. Baxter.: It will be for the elec- tors to elect more economical men.—Mr. Whitlow said if they elected new men they would be experimenting with their money the same as the present members had done, and they would be worse off than ever. They had better return the old men and hope they would do better.—Mr. 'Stokes said the highway call for Clifton was £56 a year, which was .equal to the amount required before the County Council was formed and this in a township where there was not a highway at all,and had to repair its own roads.—Mr. Aaron said some use bad been made of the fact that the County Council repaid the Runcorn Union about £l,BOO a year. Well, that was not included in the Council estimates . it came from the Imperial Ex- chequer from taxes.—The Clerk said the Council re- ceived £BO,OOO from the Exchequer, and then distri- buted it amongst the various unions. The discussion then .ceased.

NEW CASUAL WARDS. The Rev. J. W. N. Tanner, as Chairman of the Visit- ing Committee, moved the adoption of plans proposed by Mr. H. Coward of Runcorn, for providing ten new casual wards.—Mr. Taylor seconded and pointed out that the Local Government Board considered the present accom- modation for vagrants insufficient.—Mr. Weir proposed that the plans be not passed until there was a place shown for breaking stones. If they had had such a place be- fore they would not have needed these new wards. After discussion the plans were passed unanimously, it being understood that Mr. Weir would bring forward his pro- position at some future time.

Two men named Hodgson and Stephenson went out in a boat at south Shields on Wednesday, and Stephen- son returned alone. He said that he went to sleep for a time, and on awaking Hodgson had disappeared. At the London bankruptcy Court on Thursday, the creditors of Messrs. Alexander and Co., corn merchants, Threadneedle-street, who failed recently for nearly £2,000,000, agreed to accept a composition of 7s. 6d. In the £.

A violent storm prevailed on Thursday, at Sandgate, Deal, and other Channel ports. Heavy rains have further increased the floods in the Thames valley thousands of acres being under water and many houses entirely isolated.

div.head: FXAMINER, SATURDAY, OCTOBER 24, 1891.
div.p: THE FXAMINER, SATURDAY, OCTOBER 24, 1891.

LIBERAL DEMONSTRATION AT RUNCORN. SPEECH BY MR. J. T. BRUNNER, M.P., &c. Mr. J. T. Brunner, M.P., for the Northwich Divi- sion, paid a visit to Runcorn, on Tuesday, in order to give what may be called his annual account of his stewardship. Accompanied by Mrs. Brunner and Mr. T. E. Ellis, M.P., he arrived in town during the afternoon, and by appointment met a deputa- tion front the publicans of the neighbourhood, who wished for a more full awl explicit explanation of his views on the licensing question than could be obtained in public meeting assembled. By desire of the interviewers the proceedings were private, but the full and free conversation tkat took place elucidated some points of difference, and will be generally helpful. RECEPTION. In the evening at .six o'clock, Mr. W. Ockleston, the president of the Liberal Club, held a reception in the Club Premises in High-st. The guests in- vited consisted of the local members of the Com- mittee of the Division Association, and a very large number availed themselves of the opportunity of meeting Mr. and Mrs. Brunner in a social way. Refreshments were provided, and dispersed by Miss Nellie and Miss C. Handley, Miss E. Riley, and Miss E. Wright, and a very pleasant hour and a half was Spent. Before the party separated Mr. Ockleston thanked the ladies for their kind assistance and Mr. Brunner, discanted at some length on the benefit of such gatherings. He expressed the indebtedness of all concerned to Mr. Ockleston for the pleasure he had afforded them, and their deep regret that the state of his health and the doctor's decision would prevent him being present with them at the public meeting. THE PUBLIC MEETING. At eight o'clock a public meeting was held in the Public Hall. The body of the building was well filled and the gallery contained a considerable number of electors, and the proceedings were char- acterised by intelligent interest and sustained en- thusiasm. In the absence of Mr. Ockleston, Mr. Alfred Norman presided and he was supported on the platform by Mr. J. Brunner M.P., Mr. H. Broad- hurst M.P., Mr. T. E. Ellis M.P., Revs. J. Simpson, R. G. Hughes, (Widnes), and C. Finc.h ; Messrs. S. Taylor, T. Clegg, W. Carroll, J. Bridgewater. F. Hartland, (Widnes), G. Bellamy, B. Kniveton, T. Handley, W. Handley, J. Lea, W. Betney, A. Riley, T. Dean, W. Jepsen, W. Wright, J. Clerk, T. Lea, T. Pickering, H. Wright, J. E. Poole, J. Bate, &c. The Rev. C. Finch moved the following resolution : "That this meeting of the electors of the Runcorn Pol- ling District thanks Mr. Brunner for his especially valu- able services as member of the Northwich Division, and his fidelity to the Liberal party and also for his great in- terest and active assistance in helping forward the social and educational movements which lie at the foundation of the happiness and prosperity of the peo- ple." (Applause.) Mr. Brunner, said the speaker was an intelligent Liberal who believed in Home Rule for Ireland, in Local or Popular Veto; he also took con- siderable interest in matters that related to the social welfare of the people and he (Mr. Finch) would be safe in saying that when the time came, as come it would, when the disestablishment of the Episcopal Church would be considered Mr. Brunner would be found on , the right aide. (Applause.) Mr. Brunner had done good I work in the House of Commcns and he had given a mar- vellous stimulus to Technical Education. (Applause.) Mr. W. Jepson seconded the motion and described Mr. Brunner as a" back boned "Radical, and one who be- lieved in equality for all. They would not exchange him for the Chancellor of Birmingham nor for that young , man who was shooting lions in Mashonaland. (Laughter and applause.) The resolution was carried by enthusiastic applause. Mr. Brunner, who was loudly applauded on rising, said he did not know how to find words which should be fitting for such a resolution as they had passed, but he could only ask them to believe that in working for them in London and in Cheshire he was doing that which gave him the greatest possible pleasure in life. Like me Finch he was a teacher of the Gospel of Work. It was the teaching of his father that it was the absolute duty of every strong and healthy man to give up to public work as much of his time as he could afford. Bearing that teaching in mind he had all his life been striving to attain to the position in which he found himself able to devote a very large part of his time to work which was mot selfish for his own pocket. (Applause.) He men- tioned this that he might once again—for he had done it before—place their mutual relations on a thoroughly sound and straightforward footing. In constituting him 'their servant they were making him a very happy and proud man. (Applause.) He expressed regret atthe cause which had compelled Mr. Ockleston to leave Run-• ,corn before the meeting, and after a complimentary , reference to the Chairman ; Mr. Brunner referred to THE LATE MR. W. H. SMITH, who, he said, had set them in the House of Commons an example of gentleness, of fair mindedness and of courtesy towards opponents which he trusted would long live in the memories of the members, and be:remembered as an example worthy to follow. (Applause.) As to Mr. Parnell, who had made such a gallant fight for his country, let them forget those unhappy differences of the last nine •months and remember alone the devotedness of his work and the ardency of his patriotism from 1874 to 1890. (Applause.) No country in the world, no people whose record was written in history, ever owed more to a leader than the Irish people owed to CHARLES STEWART PARNELL and he (Mr. Brunner) had had no harsh word to say of the men who had stood by him. They had been ani- mated by a feeling of gratitude towards :him, but they were making a mistake in trying to estrange their ,countrymen from the English nation. (Hear, hear.) Their Ipresent course would bring disaster upon their cGuntry. (Hear, hear.) After a brief allusion to his efforts in obtaining compensation for subsidence through pumping brine, Mr. Brunner dealt with
THE RIVER WEAVER TRUST,

which he desired should come to an end as soon as might be, and in place of the self-elected body, the only close corporation of its kind now left in the country, there should be elected a popular trust by the dwellers in the Valley of the Weaver, and by the owners of property there ; and that this trust should manage the Weaver for the benefit of those mentioned and for the benefit of the trades upon the river. (Applause.) He foresaw the time when the Weaver would be made a free highway and would be crowded with traffic' which would bring prosper- ity not only to Winsford and Northwich but to Runcorn in whose prosperity they were so deeply interested. (Ap- plause.) Would they help him to bring this close cor- poration to an end and replace it by a body on the prin- ciple of the Mersey Docks and Habour Board, whose sole duty it, should be to promote the prosperity of the people who lived iu the neighbourhood, and should not be used, as it had been, to save the estates of the trustees 2d. in the £ per annum. (Applause.) Alluding to his action on the Local Government Bill of 1868,141 r. Brunner pointed out that

div.head: "WHAT HAD WROUGHT THE WONDER-
div.p: "WHAT HAD WROUGHT THE WONDER-
FUL CHANGE?"
"I, Harvey Askew, of 2, Buck Timber Place, Ellerby Lane, Leeds, do solemnly and sincerely declare ,as fol- lows:

"Up to February, 1890, I was a strong healthy man. In the early part of this month I was suddenly seized with dizziness and pain in the head and a strange feeling came over me. I was feverish and shivered all over, and did not know what was the matter with me-. I went to our doctor, who said I was suffering from the English Influenza, and ordered me to bed. After being in bed a few days the fever left me, but my breath be- came very foul I had a bad taste in my mouth Lnd my tongue was thickly coated like a piece of brown leather. My skin was sallow and the whites of my eyes were of a yellow colour. My appetite left me and after every morsel of food I had great pain at the chest and side, and palpitation of the heart. I felt low, tired, languid, and weak., and had a sinking feeling at the pit of the stomach, as if I had no inside, and a gnawing, craving feeling which nothing relieved. I was unable to take any- thing but liquid food, and got so weak that I had barely strength to walk, and was afraid that every step I took I should fall down. Getting weaker and weaker the pain at my heart became so bad" that as I sat in my chair I could hear my heart thumping as if somgone was striking my back.' I got very little sleep at night and would lie awake for hours together tossing about the bed. I gradually got worse and worse and went almost to skin and bone. I lost over two stone weight, and was only a shadow of my former self. My cheeks had sunk until they were almost drawn together, and everyone who saw me shook their heads and said that I would not be long in this world. I had every confidence in the doctor who attended me, and kept on taking his medicine month after month, but got worse instead of better. I took some forty or fifty bottles of medicine, but from first to last I did not derive an atom of benefit. The doctor sounded my lungs and asked me if my father and mother were living, and if any of our family had died of consumption. He said my heart was swollen and that the palpitation was caused by dyspepsia. After being under his treatment nine months he recommended me to take further advice, say- ing that he could do nothing more for me. I had now given up all hopes of getting better, and all my friends and shop mates told me that I could not recover_ Weaker and weaker I continued in this state, and was fast sinking until December of last year, 1890, when one day a book was left at my house telling of a medi- cine called Mother SeigePs Curative Syrup, and I read of a case like mine having been cured by it. I determined to give it a trial, and got a bottle from Mr. Kirkman, chemist, in Ellerby-lane. After taking the first bottle I felt a little better, and by the time I had taken the second bottle I began to eat solid food, and it agreed with me. After thisa never looked behind me, but so reduced had I become that my recovery was the work of time. I kept on with the Syrup and soon got back to my work strong and healthy, and have never ailed any- thing since. "When I went back to the works the foreman and others gathered 'round me and asked what had wrought the wonderful change in me and brought me back to life. II told them all that Mother Seigel's Syrup had saved my life, and but for it I should be in my grave. When I told them that I wished to start work, they said I must be examined by a doctor. On going to the doctor he stated that my heart was sound and there was nothing wrong with it, and that pas fit for work. I went to work the next morning,and have never lost a minute since. I wish others to know what Mother Seigel's Syrup has done for me; and I am willing for the Proprietors to publish this statement,and I will gladly answer any inquiries. lam a cloth presser by trade, and have wOrked at Messrs. Hepworth and Sons, Clay Pit Lane, for four years, and I make this solemn Declaration conscientiously believing the Same to be true. By virtue of the Provisions of the Statutory Declaration Act, 1835 (5 and 6 William IV. c. 62.) (Signed" "HARVEY ASKEW." "BOROUGH OF LEEDS IN THE COUNTY OF YORK. "TO ALL TO WHOM THESE_ PRESENTS SHALL COME.

" I, ALr COOKS. Esq., May4or of the Borough of Leeds, in the County of York, in that part of the United King- dom of Great Britain and Ireland called England, in pur- suance of the Laws in that behalf, do hereby certify that

the signature HARVEY AsKxw written on the annexed paper writing is of the proper handwriting of Harvey Askew, of No. "2 Buck Timber Place, Ellerby Lane, Leeds, named therein, being a person well-known and worthy of good credit. And that the said document was signed by him in my presence at the town Hall, in Leeds, afore- said.

"IN FAITH AND TESTIMONY where- of I, the said Mayor, have caused my Seal of Office to be hereunto put and affixed, and the said paper writing to be hereunto annexed. Dated at Leeds, aforesaid, the 28th day of April, One thousand eight hundred and ninety-one. (Signed) ." ALF COOKE, _Mayor of Leeds."
