Mr. John Redmond, M.P., accompanied by some members of the Parnellite party, arrived at Cork, on Wednesday nightyand was met by a crowd of people with bands. On arriving at histotel he addressed the people, and met with an enthusiastic reception. Speak- ing from the window of his hotel, he said he did so as leader of the Parnellite party. STRAND.

A largely attended meeting in stspport of the candida- ture of Mr. F. Smith was held on Wednesday night. Mr. Smith said he would do his best to follow the example of his late father. He Was a very warm supporter of the present Government. In furtherance of the candidature of Dr. Gutteridge, a Liberal meeting was held in St. Martin's-st., Leicester-square. Muth activity continues .to prevail amongst the workers on both sides.

William Ewart Lloyd., a lad who received severe in- juries in the Vine Inn, Ystalyfera, through the mad freak of a miner named Ifusker in throwing a flask of blasting powder on thetre, has succumbed to his in- juries. Another lad named Benjamin Llewellyn is in a critical condition.

div.head: • SHIP CANAL.
div.p: THE • SHIP CANAL.

would impound the filthy waters of the Irwell which wotild lie stagnant and rot through many miles of Cheshire, and if the river Irwell was not purified this would bring disease and death to a terrible extent. Now through a very small amendment which he put in the Local Grcvernment Bill of HU there was a chance of this danger being averted. That amendment provided that the County Councils and the Councils of Boroughs

concerned in any river might form a joint committee to carry out the obligations of the Rivers Pollution Act passed in 1876. A Committee had been formed consist- ing of delegates from the County Councils of Lancashire, Cheshire, and Derbyshire and the Councils of Manches- ter, Salford, Bolton, Rochdale, and Bury, and this Com- mittee would meet periodically for the purpose of taking care that the rivers Mersey and Irwell shall be kept as pure as they possibly can be, so that they would qave the benefit in Cheshire of having not only a rnagmficie.nt waterway, which, he trusted, would carry upon its bosom millions of tons of merchandise to and fro—(ap- plause)—but that the ships should sail %mon water which should be pleasant to sight and to sense and not spread pestilence in our midst. (Applause.) He had opposed several measures and one of them was called The Sum- mary Jurisdiction of youthful offenders. This Bill en- acted that magistrates should have the power of order- ing

div.head: FLOGGING OF CHILDREN
div.p: THE FLOGGING OF CHILDREN

no matter how small their offence against the law. If boys were to be flogged, let them be flogged by the hands of these who loved them. (Applause.) The Bis- hop of Chester recently said, "No birch no boy. No cane no character." He very much doubted whether the bishop said that at his breakfast table. it VMS all very well when they were other people's children—poor people's children—but he did not think the bishop would recommend the flogging of rich people's children. (Ap- plause.) "No birch no boy, no cane no character !" No bishop no buckle! (Loud applause.) Referring to the report on the licensed houses in Cheshire, presented to Quarter Sessions, on his motion, Mr. Brunner said he found that in Runcorn there were 82 licensed houses, of which the police described 67 as "tied," and 15 as free, but he had been told that these 15 were only free nominally ; that if they did not belong to brewers they belonged to men who insisted that the occupiers should get their beer from certain houses, that owners should make a profit upon the beer before it got into the hands of the occupiers. (Laughter and applause.)

TIED HOUSES were unfair to the customers, and unfair to the occu- piers, and a fraud upon the magistrates. (Loud ap- plause.) It was unfair to the occupier because it was almost impossible for him to make an honest living. (Applause.) They were told by Captain Congreve who for 20 years was Chief Constable of Staffordshire that practically the occupants of tied houses broke the law every day simply because they were driven to it by the brewers who owned the houses. The system was unfair to the customers and for this reason. In Northwich they ould get no beer but Greenall's. (Laughter.)He believed that in Runcorn they had the choice of three beers—and he did not know which was the best off. (Laughter.) When three brewers had a monopoly in Runcorn did they not think they would make as good beer if the houses were free. (" Not they," and applause.) The tenants of tied houses could be removed on the very shortest notice, and whenever a conviction occurred,the iicense was quickly transferred which was an evasion of the law. Whenever he got a chance as their representa- tive of voting in such a way as would bring this system to an end, he should embrace it with gladness and with gratitude. (Applause.) In the meantime he urged temperance reformers to use their present powers of

OBJECTING TO ILL CONDUCTED OR UNNECESSARY HOUSES. And every publican knew there were too many now. —(laughter)—and the magistrates were absolutely bound by law to listen to them. They might derive en- couragement from the fact that no less than the re- newal of 245 licenses had been refused by the magis- trates at the recent Brewster Sessions. (Hear, hear,and applause.) In conclusion he thanked them in Runcorn for having for a good many years taxed themselves to maintain a

FREE PUBLIC LIBRARY. He would that it were open every day and as long as the public-houses were open—(applause \ —and he trusted that those amongst them that could afford to give would extend the subscription list of the Library. It did not take the secretary very long to write it out now. (Laughter.) There was only one name on it now, but there were a great many people in Runcorn who could afford 105. or 20s. a year in order that the Library should be open every day and every evening and he hoped these who could afford it would send to Mr. Jones some- thing every year, if it were only a shilling. But not- withstanding this he had to thank them for their self- denial for the sake of those who otherwise would not be able to get good books. He had also to thank them for adopting through their Board of Commissioners the TECHNICAL INSTRUCTION ACT, 1889.

He trusted that they would go on in the good work and that ere long they would have in their midst a build- ing which would educate by its beauty, and which by its appliances inside and the teachers devoted to the noble work should so help the people of Runcorn that their happiness and prosperity might be greater and greater all the days that they and he had to look forward to. (Loud applause.) Mr. Broadhurst then delivered a speech in which he commenced with complimentary references to Mr. Bruuner's personal character and services to the Liberal party, and alluding to the appointment of Mr. Palfour to the leadership of the House of Commons, the speaker said he was no doubt very clever and learned but that he had succeeded in his Irish policy they all doubted and some denied, and they could not agree with the choice of him as the representative of the House of Commons before the nation and the world. (Hear, hear.) What Mr. Goschen and his poor deluded friends the Liberal Union- ists thought of it he was unable to say and he cared very little. (Laughter.) It was a remarkable thing that in 1891, with household suffrage and voting by ballot that we had the government of this great empire absolutely in the hands of the family of one great autocrat and landowner. tHear, hear.) Because it was evident to all that the members of the Cabinet and the Government were the mere hired servants of this great peer. (Laughter and applause.) It was an- nounced that day that the Under Secretary of State for India, Sir John Gorst, was about to visit Wolverhampton, Liverpool, and Halifax to discuss subjects of great interest to working people Was he sent out as a kite in order that the Government might show which way the wind blew. (Hear, hear.) There was not a single subject mentioned in this pro- gramme that was in any way new, and which had not been advocated by the Radical party for a great many years. The speaker urged that several limitations in the Employers' Liability Act should be removed, and re- ferring to the Factory and Workshops Act, strongly ani- madverted on the Tory Government having fixed the age for half-timers at ten years in spite of all opposi- tion. He hoped that next time the Liberal party dealt with education they would make the age 12 or 14 years rather than 10 years of age. (Applause.) In conclusion, Mr. Broadhurst bore testimony to the wise choice North- wich Division had made, and he wished that the House of Commons had a score more Brunners in it. (Ap- plause.) Mr. T. E. Ellis also spoke, and paid a tribute to Mr. Parnell's parliamentary career. The Coercion Act was now practically a dead title in Ireland and next sessi on the Government were going to pass the Local Govern- ment Bill for Ireland. The Tories thought the Liberal party were going to oppose that Bill but they were not. They would give it the same sort of welcome that they gave to the Free Education Bill. They would accept whatever the Tories were ready to give and then in an- other twelve months they would be able to get from the Democracy a mandate to go back and finish the work which these Tories and the House of Lords had left in- complete—to finish the Free Education Bill by making the schools really free and popularly governed—(ap- plause)—and by giving to Ireland that great Council of the Irish nation which should unite the two countries despite the bitterness and division that had been fostered by their enemies in the past, and should bring every blessing to that distracted country. (Applause.)

Mr. E. Wynne Humphries moved a resolution thank ing Mr. Broadhurst and Mr. Ellis for their stirring and stimulating addresses, and reaffirming the confidence of the electors in the Liberal party and its speedy re- turn to power,and in their revered leader the Right Hon. W. E. Gladstone. (Applause,) Whenever the general election arrived Mr. Humphreys said they were not only ready but willing for the fight. They had a winning cause a popular-cindidate and a perfect register—as perfect as an able agent could make it—(hear, hear)—and they were only anxious for the opportunity to record their judgment. (Applause.) Mr.Kniveton seconded the motion which was supported by Mr. T. Clegg, and carried by acclamation.—Mr. Ellis in replying proposed a vote of thanks to the Chairman, which was heartily accorded, and the meeting con- cluded.

div.head: SHOCKING TREATMENT_ OF A WIFE AT
div.p: SHOCKING TREATMENT_ OF A WIFE AT
RUNCORN.

George Holt was summoned before Mr. Brundrit and Mr. Thomas at Runcorn Petty Sessions, on Monday, to answer a charge of assaulting his wife Alice.—Mr. Burton appeared for the complainant. Defendant pleaded guilty.—Mrs. Holt said she had been married to the defendant for 18 sears, and there were six children, the eldest being 18 and the youngest eleven months. During the whole of that time, the defendant had ill-treated her, and she had continually forgiven him on promising to be better, but he got worse. He was a driver of a stationary engine at a Widnes Chemisal Works, and he earned s• good money" but he had not worked for the past eleven months. He was living upon what he had saved, and he had a good bit left yet, but he kept the bankbook secret. He had not given her a farthing during the eleven months and she had had to go out washing to maintain herself and children while he was drinking. On several occasions she had had to leave the house in the middle of the night to escape his violence, and he threatened to throw a lighted lamp at her. On Thursday, the 13th inst, he came home drunk and asked her to get his tea ready,and she set about doing so,when he said that if it could not be got ready with comfort, he had better go. She then put the tea things back into the cupboard, and he commenced to quarrel. He pulled out a knife, and, calling her foul names, threatened that if she uttered another word he would run it through her. She was afraid he would do her bodily harm, and went to her sister-in-law's house, and had not since been home.—The defendant denied all that his wife had said. He was merely cutting tobacco with his knife, when she came and scratched his face and then went out of the house.—Mary Ann Holt, wife of the defendant's brother, said the complainant had come to her house at two o'clock in the morning in her night dress. She had fre- quently seen her with black eyes.—Mr. Brundrit charac- terised the defendant's conduct as disgraceful and granted the separation order that Mr. Burton asked for. Defendant was fined 10s. and costs £1 us. 6d., and was also ordered to contribute 15s. per week towards the maintenance of his wife and three younger children of which she was given the custody.

div.head: LECTURE ON "THE ZULU WAR"
div.p: LECTURE ON "THE ZULU WAR"

The members of the Earlesto wn Baptist Improve- ment Class opened their session on Wednesday evening,by a lecture which wasgiven in the chapel, by the Rev. J. W. Varley, of Latchford. The subject of the lecture was "The Zulu War," and as the lecturer had taken part as a volunteer :in the war, the recital of the various incidents connected with it, rendered it doubly interesting. The Rev. J. Cottam presided, and there was a fairly numerous audience. The Chairman said that he could pro- mise them that the lecturer would tell them some- thing that would be highly gratifying to them. The Baptists were honoured by having some fighting men in their ranks,amongst others being Sir Henry Havelock, of Lucknow fame. (Applause.) The Rev. J. W.Varley proceeding with his lecture,said his task :was not a very difficult one, because he had simply to relate very largely what he had seen, and that through which he had passed. Perhaps it would be as well for him to say why he was in the Zulu War. He had been in South Africa for several months, and that awful battle of Isandula had been fought, in which we lost over 1,000 white men, and some hundreds of blacks who were fighting for us. The result of that battle was to leave a large tract of country entirely open to the mercies of the Zulu nation. The cry in Natal was for every man to go up there and try and defend the hamlets and small towns, and by any means and all means keep back the I Zulu Army from entering the territory. As they all knew, the Zulu Army received a great check at Rorke's drift, and in consequence of that, men entered upon English teritory. The cry from Natal for men led to a 'large number of Englishmen considering seriously whether they should not go to help their comrades who were in such great danger. Like other Englishmen, he joined Baker's horse, a volunteer corps, better known in England as Yeomanry. Some 700 or 800 men, compris- ing Baker's horse, set sail for Cape Town and Delagoa Bay for Natal. On arriving there they were joined to one of the two main bodies of the British troops, as scouts. It might perhaps be wise for them to consider why the British nation entered upon this war. If they , did not remember, it was nevertheless a fact that some 30,000 men were congregated in Zululand, ready at any time to wash their spears in lolood. The Zulus under King Cetewayo were not allowed to be married, except by the command of the king, and occasionally he took a freak and would order 1.000 men to be married straight away. But as a rule, the warriors were expected to demonstrate their powers by engaging in some war, generally against some of the people immediately ad- joining Zululand. It turned out, however, that instead of there being 30,000 there were 60,000 men, and a large portion of this body :were ready for any pretext to wash their spears in blood. Very naturally Sir Bartle Frere considered this large body of men, as a standing menace to Natal. That was one reason. Another reason was, a brother of King Cetewayo had several wives, and one of them took a fancy to a younger man, and ran away with him into British territory. One miming the kraal, where this man and woman were, was surrounded by a body of warriors, who demanded that this woman, and another woman who was with her should be given up to them. The men in the kraal were entirely unarmed,and unable to cope with the vast body of warriors, the result being that these two women had to be given up. The women were taken across the river, and in the sight of the men, were speared to death. That was regarded as a thing which could not be allowed, because these persons having reached British territory, they were regarded as being under the protection of the British nation, that was if they had not done anything particularly wrong. Cetewayo was askedto give up the murderers of those two women, but he refused, because adultery among the native tribes was always punished with death. These among others were con- sidered sufficient reasons for entering upon the Zulu war. Thereupon the British Army was divided into three parties, and started in different directions with the in- tention of meeting at a certain point,and makinga sudden sweep upon the capital of the country, and subdue Cete- wayo. The body which started via the coast reached tableland and were practically made prisoners for several months. He then gave a very graphic account of the battle of Isandula and of the massacre which took place there. After that event Baker's horse was sent to join Colonel Wood's column, which they reached, being al- lotted scout duty. When ordered out they never knew where they were going, the orders to the Captain being always sealed. One morning they were told off to bring in 5,000 head of cattle which spies had said were on a particular mountain. On reaching the mountain, all with the exception of about 50 men, scaled it, and on getting to the top, found the cattle, and after a little skirmishing with the men in charge, they took them. They were ordered to off-saddle, upon the mountain top, and prepared their mid-day meal. They had just got it over in, shots were heard, and an outlying picket dashed white as a sheet, saying that the path by which they had come, was filled with in army of Zulus. It turned out there were 25,000t0 30,000 Zulus, while the British numbered 600 or 700. What was to be done 2 80 m tried and two succeeded in getting through. The remainder of the 700 descended the mountain as best they could, but only 400 reached the bottom in safsty. 300 were lost with the cattle. The news • quickly spread and preparations were made at the camp for giving the Zulus a Warn recv.tion, Next morn- ing at 8 o'clock, the left arm7of the Zulu Army seen coming, and then the right. A battle was ' fought and over 2,500 Zulus were killed, whilst the British lost about 80 men. The next event he referred to was the death of :the Prince Imperial, at the finding of whose body he was present. He then passed on to the concluding battle, and the capture of Cetewayo. War, he said had its glories, but it had its horrors. .agaTihn.e man who had been in war never wanted to g He was afraid the Zulu war would remain a stain upon our British name for years to come. He was sorry to find that while we had taken possession of Zululand, and had parcelled out the country to suit ourselves, our white people had taken their worst civilising influences into the country andhe was told upon the authority of a man who was there to-day that our drink was being taken there, and was debasing the morals of the people. Send out more missionaries, but do not send barrels of rum with them. (Applause.) Mr. B. Harrison in moving a vote of thanks to the lecturer said they had had a very graphic description of Zulu war, not only by an eye witness but by one who took part in it. Mr. Hughes ( Ear les,town) ex-Baptist minister, Bacup, seconded the motion, which was heart- ily passed.
'The lecturer duly acknowledged the vote, and the gathering dispersed.

Two butchers excavating for gravel on Monday, in their garden, Wilham-road, Clapton, found about seven feet below the surface a large tin box containing £2,000 in sovereigns, the coins being all of the reign of Queen Elizabeth.

_ A tram from Liverpool-street Sation, London, left the metals at Bishop's Stortford, on Monday, and several of the passengers received a shaking, the train being de- layed about an hour. A breakdown occurred on Mon- day on the Waterford Railway at Dungarvan, owing to the heavy:rains having swept the ballast from beneath the rails.

MERE are few members of Paella- Mr. Benner ment, either Liberal or Conserva- at Runcorn. tive, who. devote themselves so completelyto the interests of their, constituents as the member for the .Northwich Division of Cheshire. lUs speeches, from the moment he appeared as..a candidate, showed that ho understood the wants.and wishes of the demo- cracy; but his opponents were ready with the re- , marktthat itrwasell so much bird-lime, and that, once returned to Parliament/ he would find it con- venient to forget his professions. That, however, 'las not been so ;on the contrary, .he, has done niece than Was:exppeted of him ; and renders a real service to electors by coming before them at least once in each year to give an account .of his .stewardship.. What ,a,contrast to the condact of the Tory members of Parliament in this pprt of the country, and , especially of the member for 'Warrington ! It newer was within .the power, of !Sir GILBZILT GREENALL to discuss, ,politics intelli-. gently, and: for many years he has treated his constituents as if it was absurd to •expect that he ahould say,anything to them beyond aaking , for, their vcateset a General Eleetion. lvlr. Bsurnsmit. on Tuesday evening addressed a large meeting in the Public .11itll, Runccen ; and met with a reception which was ample testimony to the hold' which he has 'non the eleetors of this portion ot the rfiktision. The resolution which was adopted, tendered thaulea for his "especially valuable ser- vices as -member for the Aorthwich Division, ,and. his fidelity to ,the Libera)2 party, and also for his, great interest. and activo,fassistance ,in helping.fee-_ ward the social and eduaational movements which lio,at, the feundation of the happiness,and. parity of of the people." In the, courso of hiss ad- dress,,Mr., BRUNNER. rferrecl to the action he,had, taken in,seeking to ?rovide for,. compensation, to sufferers, from brine, pumping. Se.believes,. and ;rightly,- believes, that the Act whidfi has. been -placed' upon the Statute Book bethe-mokans of remedymg a great amoua of inipatice, .Another valuable service rendered by him,was in getting a clau . inserted in the becal, Government Bill I.of 18.88, which provides, for County. Councils acting in conjunction, with the, objecit of carrying out the Rivers, Pollution, A,et., It is, in conse- quence of this important provision, that a Joint, Committee has been florfned,, and. is now setting about the task of purifying tho Mersey and its tributaries. The labours of Hercules are as no-. , thing to this formidable inadertakhag but its sue- ' cessful aceomplishment is absolutely necessary, to the suceess of the. ahip, Canal. If the great waterway be supplied from a foul source, it is, obvious that it will soon, became a huge sewer of the very worst kind, Mr. BRUNNER. prOCßeded next to explain, the grounds of his opposition to the power which it was proposed to take to flog children for breaches of the law. tie is not, like the Bishop, of Chester, an advocate of flogging as a means of discipline. His motto is—" o flogg- ing of children except at the hands of those who love them," Coming to the licensing question, he did not hesitate to characterise the tied-house system as a fraud upon the public, and gave it as his opinion, after careful inquiry, that there is not a really free house in the Runcorn polling district. ' There are certainly very few in Warrington ; the member for Warrington thrives upon tied - houses, and there are interested supporters of his

who seek to trade upon the gullibility of the electors by professing to regard him as a benefac— tor to the borough! The eyes of the blind are, however, being opened by such men as Mr. BRUNNER. Parliament is being gradually weedea of brewers as a noxious element. They have had their day as legislators and will spon cease to be, thanks to the growth of an enlightened public opinion,and to the persistent and unselfish labours of such whole-hearted publicans as the member for the Northwich Division.
SCIENCE has assailed poetry, and now it threatens kissing. There is a

"scientific gentleman "—a German of course—who, we are told, has "employed him- self with analysing the dangers that lurk in a kiss. Re has classified the bacteria which lodge in the human mouth into some twenty-two distinct species, His conclusion would appear to be that persons who cannot altogether abstain from so deleterious a habit should indulge in it through the medium of respirators.' Kissing through the medium of a respirator! Try to fancy Romeo and Juliet doing that; it takes all the romance out of lovers young dream. Pyramus and Thisb6 did endeavour to kiss each other when there was a wall between them;. but a respirator That would never do. What an ineult it would be to—

Lips ruby as a rosebud cut in twain, Which seem to say—" Kiss love and come again." And how ridiculous under such circumstances to, speak (If "Kisses whose fire clasps the failing heart in knguishment," or say with Shakespeare— So.sweet a kiss the golden sun gives not To those fresh morning drop& upon the rose. Byron, who may be regard iad a& an. authority upon the subject,, describes— A long, long kiss, a kiss of youth, and love And beauty,, all concentrating their rays Into one focus kindled f COM above; Such kisses as belong to early days— When heart and soul and lips inconcert move, And the blood's lava and. the pulse ablaze.

But "through the medium, of a respirator!" Never! "The scientific gentleman" may be vary learned and very clever—" one,'.' to quote Words- worth, "that would peep ma botanise upon his mother's grave;" but he doestirt know a half penny- worth of that which, Shelley, describes as the 'essence of " love's, philosophy." He has ,no con- ception whateVer of the divine- flavour of that which the Irish poet compared to— " dish,of ripe strawberries smothered in cream; and deserves to, besmotheredi not in kisees but in treacle, as his highest. conception: of the sweetest thing in the world.. Bother the bacteria I Who cares for 'era? Ifortwo pins—or two guizaeas—we would engage to find ". a scientific gentleman " who would demonstrate to.alL the world, and his
wife, that, firstly,, as-bet ween. lovers, tha bacteria
have an affinity for each other which is absolutely harmless; that, secondlypwhen there i 3 no lave

in the case,. the bacteria seize upon, and des- tray each othen-;- and, thindly, that a respirator becomes_a lodginghouse-ofbcteria ef the most pestilentialkind..As for the German who has dared to utter heresy at Love's holy shrine, " Seize on him, furies!' Take him toyour torments! and let Romeepand Juliet sttill continue to take— " Ten kisses short as one, one long as twenty."

It has been decided to have a loan exhibition of works of art and curios in the early spring, in Victoria Park, St. Helens. The effect cannot be other than pod, for the inhabitants need a stimu- lus in this direction. Besides, "Art is long and time is fleeting."

The War:ington Co-operative Society are about to take into consideration the advisability of pro- viding scholarships for the children of members. An exceptional oppm tunity is afforded by the es- tablishment of the Technical Institute. It will be money well spoilt, and may be the means o 2 deve- loping the talent of some bright boy, or girl, who stands in need of this lift on the way.

The I:Parisians have voted funds for a Chair of :Labour; and why not? The best way of dealing with a difficult problem is, first of all, to make sure that wo thoroughly understand all it 3 factors. The choice of Professor has fallen upon Mr. Andre Revile. He means to commence on right lines. His programme is the naked truth, and he intends neither to point a moral nor to draw a conclusion.

There is a plentir.ul lack of Volunteer officers, for it is officially stated that, as many as 1,615 are required to complete the service. How is it ? Is the Volunteer officer played out Or is it that he has been so shabbily treated by successive Gov- ernments that he has turned his back upon the force in disgust? The 'alter most likely ; and in that case the remedy is easy. It means more public and less private expenditure.

Everybody says that the Queen has datie a very graceful thing in conferring a peerage upon the widow of the late Mr. NV. H. Smith; and what everybody says must be right. What is it, bye- the-bye, that Burns says ? A prince can make a belted knight, A marquis, duke and a' that; But an honest man's aboon his might— Guid faith, he maunna fa' that.

Mr. Smith seems to have well deserved the title honest; and yet he commenced his career as a politician by an act which must be described as ques- tionable, to say the least of it. When he was re- jected as a member of the Reform Club, it is now stated, that, within a few weeks he joined the opposite camp and became a member of the Carl- ton. It was certainly not a good beginning, for he was, in this particular instance, actuated by pique rather than principle.

"Tommy Burns" is cectainly a most daring diver, and he will "keep on doing it," we suppose, until he dives once too often. The crowd cheered lustily when he mointed the roadway of the new bridge at Walton, on Tuesday; but when it was seen that he was going --like Shelley's skylark— "higher still and higher," in order to dive from the top of the girders, the cheering was of the rantic kind. The greater the danger the more they cheered; but to what end? That is the question.

Mr. Chamberlain is still on the down grade. Speaking at Sunderland, on Wednesday evening, he said :—" If he considered only the interests of the party to which he belonged, he would ask nothing better than that Mr. Gladstone should be allowed to show once more what an awful mess he could make of our affairs." Considering that Mr. Chamberlain was a member of:Mr. Gladstone's last two cabinets, it is obvious that in condemning the ex-Premier he is condemning himself; and "it's a dirty bird that fouls its own nest."

The two principal dishes in the Government bill of fare for next year are a District Councils Bill, and an Irish Local Government Bill. There will be little difficulty about the former, unless the Government act on their favourite plan of taking back with oqe hand what they give with the other. They will probably try the same method with the Irish Bill; but, do what they will, they cannot fail to offend their Irish supporters, and at the same time pave the way to Home Rule. They would do nothing at all if, it were not that they are" deeply sworn," and have the constituencies to face.

Of corn fields and potato fields we hear often; but what is this about "a jewel field ?" It is stated that— " Great sensation has been created in Montana owing to the secret of the existence there of im- mense quantities of sapphires having leaked out. The fact that precious stones could be found has for some time been known to a few experts, and to them only. The sapphires are of great beauty, and in practically unlimited supply. The district also yields rubies and gold, and it is affirmed that Mon- tana will be found to possess the greatest and most lucrative jewel fields in the world?'

Montana is a territory of the United States, and the story is a very,very pretty one; but—au! these "buts"—perhaps it is only a story. Watches in Montana may be " jewelled " in many "holes " ; but it is quite certain that there are holes in Mon- tana which are not jewelled. The description of the jewel mine is good, but not so good as that of Shakespeare's, who makes Clarence dream of— Wedges of gold, great anchors, heaps of pearl, Inestimable stones, unvalued jewels, All scattered in the bottom of the sea. Well, well, one dream is as good as another, and, as Pat would say, a great deal better.

div.head: SUDDEN DEATH AT WIDNES.
div.p: SUDDEN DEATH AT WIDNES.

Edward Bibby, aged '25 years, assistant to Mr. William Palin, grocer, Anne-st., died suddenly on Monday. Immediately after he had finished a hearty dinner and before he had risen from the table he fell forward in his chair and expired. Dr. O'Neil was called in, and the Coroner deemed an in- quest unnecessary. SUDDEN DEATH OF MR. STEAD, OF FARNWORTII.

Mr. G. Stead, chemist and druggist,cf Church-st. Farnworth, died suddenly on Tuesday morning,and• much sympathy is expressed for the bereaved family. He had been in business in the neighbour- hood for 31 years. The funeral took place at Farn- worth Church, yesterday.

div.head: WIDNES COUNTY COURT.
div.p: WIDNES COUNTY COURT.

His Honour, Judge Shand, held a sitting of this court, yesterday,when the list comprised 139 plaints, and 79 judgment summonses.—Hugh O'Donnell, grocer, Widnes-road, Simms Cross, sued John Craik for £4 2s. 6d., for groceries and provisions supplied from 1882.—After hearing evidence, His Honour gave judgment. for the defendant.

RUNCORN FREE PUBLIC 'LIBRARY COMMITTEE. The monthly meeting was held on Wednesday under the presidency of Mr. T. Riley. The Librarian's report showed that 1892 books had been issued. Several gifts of books had been received. It was decided to ask the Board of Commissioners for an instalment of .£5O on account of the rate. Accounts amounting to £26 lls. Ild, were passed for pay- ment.

div.head: WIDNES PUBLIC DEBATING SOCIETY.
div.p: WIDNES PUBLIC DEBATING SOCIETY.

In connection with the Irish National League, a debating society has been formed and the first meet- ing was held on Wednesday evening, under the presidency of Dr. O'Keeffe. A discussion took place on the question "Would it he beneficial or other- wise to the people of Widnes to have a bridge from Runcorn to Widnes for car and passenger traffic ?" The debate Was adjourned without a decision being arrived at. THEFT OF A HORSE AND TRAP AT WIDNES.

At Widnes Petty Sessions, on Thursday, Henry Oldham, of no fixed abode, a well-known character, was charged with stealing a horse and trap con- taining a number of fowls, the property of Mr. Naylor, farmer, Halewood, valued altogether at £32. On Saturday last Mr. Naylor left the horse and trap in the lane near the football field for a tew minutes, and when he returned they were gone. Informa- tion was given to the police, who traced the prisoner to Whiston, *here he sold the fowls, and then he proceeded to Liverpool, where he was apprended in a state of drunkenness. He was committed to the Quarter Sessions for trial.

div.head: WESLEYAN FOREIGN MISSIONS AT WIDNES.
div.p: WESLEYAN FOREIGN MISSIONS AT WIDNES.

Special sermons in aid of these missions were preached in Moss Bank Chapel, on Sunday, in the morning by Mr. J. Balmer, and in the evening by Mr. J. R. Routledge. Collections were made. On Tuesday evening, a public meeting was held under the presidency of Mr. T. Robinson. The Rev. G. S. Meek read the report, showing Moss Bank had cont ibuteci 9s. 6d. more than last year. Miss Clegg, returned missionary from Ceylon, gave a de- scription of the work of the missionary in that land, and addresses were also delivered by the Rev. G. S. Meek, Messrs. B. Brown, F. Lacrowson, T. Robinson, and 11. Johnson. The collection realised £6 4s. 2d., an increase of £3. In connection with the same missions, the Rev. W. H. Picken. mission- ary from Bangalore, preached two sermons to large congregations in Hartland Chapel, Widnes, on Sunday. The collections realised a good sum.

div.head: lIYEcIRNB OR" How TO KEEP WELL."
div.p: lIYEcIRNB OR" How TO KEEP WELL."

The introductory lecture on the above subject was given in the Greenway-rd., Board Schools, Runcorn' on Monday evening by Miss E. Stuart Evans. The lecturer pointed out that Hygiene, or, in other words, the "Science which treats of the health of the body "was not in reality a new thing but dated back as far as the Mosaic Law. Of late years much had been done in England to bring about a better stats of things, and the London death-rate which 200 years ago was 80 per 1000 was row less than 20 per 1001 There was, however, still room for improvement and it had been calcul- ated that one-third of the deaths and a proportion- ate amount of sickness in this country are due to Preventible auses. The yearly victims demanded by consumption, typhoid or typhus fever, small- pox, diptheria, scarlet fever, cholera, and other diseases indicated in an awful manner how great is the need for instruction in, and observance of, elementary sanitary rules.

div.p: CIiESUIRE AGRICULTURAL SOCIETY.

Exhibitions of £lO have been gained by Minnie J. Smethurst,pupil teacher at Hamilton-st. schools, Warrington, and by Catherine Roberts, pupil teacher at the Higher Grade School, Hunter-st., Chester, for having gained the first place in the Government and religious examinations, respec- tively, among those who sat at this college. An exhibition of £5 has been awarded to Annie Parks, pupil teacher at St. Peter's school, Newton-in- Maker-field, for having gained the second place at the Government examination among those who sat at Warrington. Miss Smethurst, mentioned above, is the daughter of Mr. James Smethurst. The ex- hibition she has won entitles her to a scholarship at the Training College. A LUNATIC IN A POLICE COURT.

On Tuesday, at the St. Helens Police Court, Geo. Owen, of Chapel-st., Cowley Hill, a respectably dressed young man, was charged as a lunatic. It was stated that he was labouring under the delu- sion that he was a detective, and that Dr. M‘Nicoll, the borough medical officer, and Mr. Stuart, reliev- ing officer,were anxious to strangle him. Immedi- ately his name was mentioned, and he was asked to stand forward in court he wildly shouted—" No. I am supposed to be insane. They will strangle me, and lam not insane." Dr. M•Nicoll certified that the man was not in his right mind, and the bench made an order for his removal to Rainhill Asylum.
UMBRELLAS IiECOVERED.—J. and W. DUTTON, Saßli'ey-St., Warrington.—Ar'vt.
THE WEAVED, WATEIMEN'S DISPUTE.

A private meeting of the members of the Water- men's Association was held on Saturday evening, at Northwich, when the following proposal from the Salt Union was laid before them : "After dis- charging in Liverpool during the day and leaving by night's tide for the salt wort s to load next day, the second night, the men will not be forced to work at the works, or to start for any tide flowing before ten o'clock the next morning at Liverpool." It was decided to accept the above, providing that the Salt Union will agree to the adoption of a num- ber of details. What the dt ,ails are we cannot state, as a resolution of secrecy was adopted ; but it is now stated that the dispute is at an end. Although an amicable tettlement has thus been effected in regard to the. watermen, nothing has been done to reinstate the 70 men thrown out of work, and it is stated that there is no prospect of their re-engage- ment unless trade speedily improves. SKINNING DUCKS ALIVE AT WIDNES.

Four boys named Joseph Hopkins (8), Joseph Welsh (8), Robert Addy Plant (12), and Mark O'Brien (8), were brought up at Widnes Petty Ses- sions, on Thursday, charged with unlawfully stoning and skinning alive two ducks.—The evidence showed that on the 10th inst. the boys were chas- ing and stoning the ducks and that Plant seized one by the neck, swung it round his head, and threw it into a pit.—lnspector Dowty, R.S.P.C.A.,said he had examined one of the ducks and found that it was skinned from the wings to the head which caused the crop to tall out. The duck was alive, but he afterwards killed it. The other duck had a wing and a leg broken. On that day there were 20 ducks injured on the same land,which was off Milton-road, and the defendants admitted having broken the back of one duck and the breast of another duck. When charged Hopkins said " I held the duck." Welsh: "I skinned the duck," and Plant and O'Brien replied that they stoned the ducks.—The Bench committed the boys to an industrial schopl until they are 16 years of age,

THE LANCASHIRE WATCH COMPANY AND THEIR WORKMEN.

At Prescot Petty Sessions, on Tuesday, Samuel Nelson, of Liverpool, and Edwin Fisher, William Baker, Walter Watts, and Charles Wood, of Coven- try, were summoned, under the Employers and Workmen Act, by the Lancashire Watch Company, for leaving their work without notice. In each case the company claimed El as eompensation. Mr. H. P. Walker, from the office of Mr. W. Tyrer, pro- secuted. It appeared that the defendants were pivot-makers, and according to the evidence of Mr. Stephen Farren, of Coventry, an agent of the Lan- cashire Watch Company, the defendants were en- gaged by him to work for the firm. They each signed the usual contract of work, and all turned up at the watch factory. Wood and Watts promised to commence on the day following their atte adance, but they had never been seen there since. The other defendants had worked several days and then left. All the defendants, with the exception of Nelson, admitted their liability and promised to pay the amounts demanded. Nelson denied having signed any contract to work, but the agreement was produced in court.—The bench intimated that the defendants were bound to fulfil their contracts or pay the penalty. They ordered each defendant to pay the amount claimed, with costs. UMBRELLA. 3 RECOVERED.—J. and W. DUTTON, Sankey-et., Warrington.—Adv.

div.head: WIDNES SCHOOL BOARD.
div.p: WIDNES SCHOOL BOARD.

The monthly meeting was held on Tuesday. Mr. T. S. Timmis presided and there were present Dean Finegan, Father Clarke, Major Wareing, Mr. B. Brown., and Mr. G. H. Denby, (clerk.)—The Finance Committee recommended various sums for payment. The committee further reported that during the month £1,467 6s. sd. had been paid into the bank. The report was adopted.—Various committees were subsequently appointed for the ensuing year. The Committees elected were as follows :—General Pur- poses Committee: The Chairmen of the various Corn- mittees.—Distriet Education Committee : Rev. Father Clarke, Messrs. H. W. Deacon and S. Quinn.—School Management Committee: Dean Finegan, Messrs. C. E. Barlow, and B. Brown.—Sites and _Building Committee: Messrs. T. S. Timmis, R. ST. JOHN'S AMBULANCE ASSOCIA.TION RUNCORN BRANCH.

In c.onnection with the ladies' branch of this As- sociation a tea party and concert wera held in Bethesda Lecture Hall, on Wedn3sday evening. There was a large attendance at tea, and the tables were in .charge of Mesdames T. Norman, Kay, Bankes, Littler, Le Couteur,Guest, Imison,W. Jones, Moore, Holden, and Large; Misses A. Large,Wright, Smith, Preston, and Kilburn. Afterwards the con- cert was held, and the room was crowded to excess. The Rev. Dr. Preston presided, and in his opening speech said since the formation of the classes, first aid had been rendered as follows :--Restoring appar- ently drowned persons 4; fits 6 ; broken limbs and dislocations 12; hemorrhage 7; and concussion of the brain 1 ; total 30. A report prepared by Super- intendent Large, the hon. treasurer, showed how the classes had been started at the suggestion of the Chief Constable. and that of the above thirty cases, the police had attended to fourteen. During an interval in the programme Mr. J. Brun- drit, the president, distributed the certificates to the successful ladies, and in the course of his Speech said two years ago he had the pleasure of distributing the certificates to the first class held in Runcorn. which was for males only, when only three failed, and last year the whole class passed. These results were highly satisfactory, and the students had since rendered valuable first aid to the injured, and he knew ot two cases where life had been saved by their prompt assistance. (Ap- plause.) That night they had to deal with the ladies, who according to the old adage never failed to do a thing when they set their heads that way, and in this instance 56 were examined and 56 passed. In conclusion Mr. Brundrit attributed the success of the Association to the energy and attention and enthusiasm of their lecturer Dr. McDougall.— Mrs. W. B. Kay, on behalf of the lady members of the Association, now presented Dr. McDougall with a valu.able pair of gold-rimmed eye-glasses and gold chain, for the kindness and consideration he had shown towards them.—Dr. McDougall was deeply thankful for the present. He congratulated the ladies upon their intelligence, and the attention they had paid, and eulogised the work of the association generally. A capital programme of music was gone through. The opening song was" Good company," sang with good taste by Mr. C. Pownall. Miss Pierpoint con- tributed "The cry of the little ones," and" Tears," in a pleasing manner,and Mrs.Ains/ey gave "Golden love," in good style; "Golden dreams," was accept- ably rendered by Miss Taylor. Mr. J. Nicksou gave a capital vocalisation of "The mighty deep," and Mr' T. Fox was heard to advantage in "Life's a river." Mr. James Woods performed the cornet solo "Rose softly blooming" with the skill and harmony which have won him more than a local reputation, and Mr. J. J. F. Ainsley, F.S. Sc., (London), exe- cuted a pianoforte solo in a manner which showed a thorough mastery over the instrument. The comic element was supplied by Mr. A.E. Hallam, of Man- chester. who convulsed the audience by his powers of mimicry and humorous song. The quartette party (Messrs. Edwards, Pilgrim, Fox, and Nickson) sang two pieces with tunefulaess and harmony. The accompanists were Mrs. W. B. Bay and Mr. Ainsley.

WARRINGTON MUNICIPAL ELECTIONS.
AN ALL ROUND CONTEST.

Candidates representative of both political par- ties have now been selected for every ward in "kr- rington, and there are signs on every hand of a vigorous all-round contest. As the Ist of November is a Sunday, the polling will take place on Monday, week, the 2nd of November. To-day (Satur- day) is the last day for receiving nominations, but. as will be seen below, most of the nominations have already been placed in the hands of the Town Clerk. Through the Liberals having been occupied with the bazaar that was held the other week, the' Tories have got a considerable start in the matter of canvassing and organisation generally, and in some wards they are making good use of their ad- vantage. Still, the Liberals have not been idle dur- ing the past week, and the preliminary work on all sides may now be said to be in full swing. It would • seem that in each ward, except in Howley district, the struggle will be left to the representatives, pure and simple, of each political party, one Liberal and one Conservative being pitted against each other. In Howley Ware however, Mr. niggle is again thrusting himself up- on the electors, who have again and again shown that they have not the remotest idea of selecting him as their representative, Liberal electors can- not too clearly understand that, whatever his inten- tion may be, he is simply playing into the hands of the Tories, and they would do well,therefore, to re- serve their votes for the Libel al candidate. Below, in connection with each ward, we give a summary of the addresses which will be found in our adver- tising columns. QUESTIONS TO CANDIDATES.

At a meeting of the members of the Warrington Temperance Federation, held on Wednesday even- ing,it was unanimously resolved that the following questions be forwarded to all candidates for muni- cipal honours at the forthcoming elections. Question you, if elected, vote against any rierson connecteal with the Liquor Trade having a seat upon the Watch Committee? Question 2.—Are you in favour of the Chief Con- stable being instructed to systematically enforce the Licensing Laws with a view to reducing the drunkenness which prevails in Warrington? It was further resolved that another meeting of the Federation should be held this (Saturday) even- ing, to consider the replies received, and to decide what action shall be taken in the matter. THE TRADES' COUNCIL'S QUESTIONS.

The Warrington Trades' Council has sent out the fol- lowing questions to the different candidates, viz. : (1.1 Will you (if elected), promise to vote for all Cor- poration work and contracts being given only to those employers who pay the standard rate of wages; and for all such work and contracts being given (as far as prac- ticable), to Warrington persons, firms, or companies? (2.) The better paid servants of the Corporation are allowed holidays and are paid for the same. Will you vote that the poorer paid servants should also have holi- days and be paid their wages for the same? (3.) The members of the Warrington Trades' and Labour Council are of opinion that by the insertion of the Fair Wage Clause in all public contracts, it would be one great step towards abolishing that cruel evil known as the "sweating system." Would you (if elected) vote for such clause being inserted?
TOWN HALL WARD.
Polling Place: Drill Shed; No of voters, 1,044.

In thii-Ward Mr. W. Pierpoint is the reth:ing Councillor and Mr. James Smethurst, who represents the Conserva- tives, is his opponent. Mr. Smethurst has not previously been in the Council, and it is hardly likely that he will be selected on this occasion, as Mr. Pierpoint is recognised by both political parties as one of the most straightfor- ward and ablest members of the Warrington Town Council.

Mr.W. Pierpoint, in his address, says that the freeing of the Library, the purchase of the Waterworks, and the establishment of classes for technical education have had his cordial support, and trust they have the approval of his constituents. As a business man he claims to know something of the requirements of the town, and will do all in his power in the future, as in the past, to further its improvement. Mr. James Smethurst, the Conservative candidate who Opposes Mr. W. Pierpoint in Town Hall Ward, in hise address to the burgesses remarks that he has for many years taken an active part in all movements for the benefit of the people,and whether or not they return him to the Council his servic:!s in all matters, where their welfare is concerned, will be at their disposal. Reis in favour of the abolition of meter rents at the earliest possible moment, and of a reduction in the price of gas. He has no sell-interest to serve by being a member of the Town Council, and if elected shall feel himself free at all times to bring forward and support measures necessary for the comfort and convenieace of the burgesses of the Town Hall Ward. -

div.head: LYMAI.
div.p: LYMAI.

THE PRIMITIVE METHODIST CHAPEL.—A special chil- dren's service was held in the Primitive Methodist Chapel on Sunday afternoon, at which Mr. G. L. Wei- ford gave an address. The same gentleman also preached in the evening, taking his subject from Pro- verbs iv. 20-21. There were large congregations. WESLEYAN MUTUAL IMPROVEMENT SociETv.—A meet- ing of this society was held on Monday evening, Mr. F. 0. Moston in the chair. The sabject was "The Resur- rection," the essayist being Mr. E. Moston. Mr. Brown and Mr. Allen replied, and the•meeting was adjourned until Monday, when the subject will be reconsidered.
LIBERALISM AT ST. HELENS.

Mr. W. R. Kennedy, the Liberal candidate for St. Helens, has made good use of his week's visit to the town. On Thursday week he descended the shaft at the Whitecross Colliery, at Peasley Cross, and thoroughly examined the workings, and watched the miners following their employment. On Saturday forenoon he went down the shalt and examined the workings of the Ashtons Green Col- liery. On Saturday afternoon he was present at the football match played on the St. lielens ground Knowsley-road, between St. Helens and ' Elland, and on Monday forenoon he went through Messrs. Cannington, Shaw and Co.'s Glass Bottle Works, and watched all the interesting processes of bottle- making. On Monday evening he addressed a well attended private meeting in the. St. Thomas' school- room, when Mr. S, Taylor, of Eccleston Hall, was also present and delivered an address. Mr. W. R. Kennedy, Q.C.. the Liberal candidate con- cluded his week's visit to the town on Wednesday night, when an enthusiastic meeting of Liberals was held in the Town Hall. During his stay Mr. Kennedy and the local leaders of his party attended the series of ward meetings throughout the borough, where the display of enthusiasm among the rank and file of the workers was most encouraging, and a good augu:y for the future oti local Liberalism. At Wednesday night's gathering there was a crowded attendance. Ihe chair was occupied by Councillor John Foister, chairman of the executive of the Liberal Association, and he was supported by Mr. W. R. Kennedy, Q.C. ; Councillors H. Martin, J. P. Mearns, J. B. Leach, J. Jones, W. Morris ; Messrs. J. Prest, W. Seath, M. Phillips, W. Bate, W. Woodward,W. Farthman, J. Lindon, and others. The Chairman announced that Mr. Channing, M.P., had written regretting his inability to attend through illness, but promising to visit St. Helens on the first occasion that he appeared in public in the north of Eng- land. In regard to general politics the Tories seemed to be awaiting the death of Mr. Gladstone, and their hope seemed to be that before the present Government left office Mr. Gladstone might , have passed beyond the realms where politics were discussed, and where his enormous weight could influence the masses of this coun- try. Such a policy was very discreditanle, and especi- ally to the Tory party, who were trying to wear out the life of an old man who had spent all his life and all the best hours of his day in the service of his Queen and his country. The very fact that they were doing that was a mark of their weakness, and was evidence that they an- ticipated a defeat all along the line at the next election. Mr. Gladstone was in touch and sympathy with the masses of the country, and it was to his return to power that they looked for the reform so greatly needed. (Cheers.) Councillor Leach urged that St. Helens in the past had been dependent uooli Liberalism for its progress and for its great commercial importance. If they con- trasted the past histories of Liberalism and Toryism, they would be forced to the conclusion that if they wished to further their own interests they must do their utmost to return Mr. Kennedy at the next election. (Cheers.) Councillor H. Martin said the meetings held by Mr. Kennedy during the week had shown to him that there was a very large true Liberal spirit existing among the working-men of St. Helens. (Cheers.) He asked them to assist in returning to Parliament a supporter of Mr. Gladstone, who in his closing hours was anxious to bring about peace and contentment between two nations so , that they might work hand in hand and heart to heart, and feel that they were brothers indeed to do full ser- vice together for their Queen and their country. (Cheers.) Mr. W. R. Kennedy, Q.C., received a mostenthusiastic welcome. He claimed their support on behalf of the greatest statesman of his country, and asked them to assist in helping. Mr. Gladstone to do something still more for the people whom he had loved and served. Referring to the Liberal programme, he submitted that the measures offered by the Liberal leaders satisfied the test of being in accordance with the application of Christian principles to public policy, and were truly and really in the interests of the many, and those interests were not sacrificed to the prejudices or to the wishes of the few. (Cheers.) He urged that the passing of Home Rule for Ireland would result in good, not only to that country, which was of itself sufficient why it should be given, providing it was not hostile to the maintenance of a great and undivided empire, Which it was not, but it would be a good thing for this country. (Applause.). The Liberal party were pledged to give Ireland that for which her people were patiently waiting, and to which they were by every right entitled. (Applause.) RI regard to the question of the disestablishment of the. Church in Wales, he was a loyal member of the Church of England, and he believed that the good work of the Church would not be hindered by such a measure of ' disendowment as the sober, good sense of Liberalism ' would bring forward and carry. He was in favonr- of the one man one vote policy, under conditions which which would do away with many of the difficulties of the present registration system, and in regard to. the question of temperance reform, he thought the Liberal party, without an exception, were prepared to give to the people precisely the same measure of right as was at present enjoyed by large landholders of say- ing whether there should be any public-houses or what number in a given area. (Cheers.) He believed that popular control would be temperately and wisely exer- cised, and they must, of course, be reasonable and statesmanlike in carrying out the policy. Dealing with the /and question, he said he wanted land to be as productive as possible, and legislation should be directed to so amennding the laws relating to land that the exodus of the agricuttural classes into their alreadyover-crowded cities and towns would, to some extent, be prevented. (Cheers.) In concluding he dealt with labour questions, and said he did not think that the working classes had any desire to do anything which would injure the trade of the country or to fetter the freedom of their fellow workmen. If there wasto be a legislation it should not be of a wholesale character. It should be legislation founded upon the consideration of each trade and occupation on its own merits. (Cheers.) Councillor J. P.Mearns urged the Liberals of the town to be prepared for the approaching elections, and help to,further the cause they had at heart whenever the time might come. (Applause.) Councillor Jones moved a vote of thanks to Mr. Ken- nedy for his attendance and address, and Councillor Morris seconded the motion, which was supported by Mr. W. Seath, and passed with acclamation. A similar compliment to the Chairman concluded the meeting.
The Qti.een has conferred -;, peerage upon Mrs. W. H. Smith.

div.head: WHITECROSS WARD.
div.p: WHITECROSS WARD.

Polling Place: St. Barnabas ISchool ; No. of voters 891, There was a contest in this ward no later than June when Councillor Plumpten, who is again before the electors, was returned by a large majority. Mr. Alfred Woods,who was then his opponent,has not thought fit to take the field again, leaving the struggle on behalf of the Conservatives to Mr. W. Bellian, who poses in his ad- dress as an employer of labour, although, it is stated, he has only one man working for him besides the members of his own family. He was formerly a Liberal, and it is being said on his behalf that he is a Liberal still, but it Is to be hoped that the Liberal electors of the ward will take care not to be misled by such a transparent subter- fuge. Canvassing on both sides has been vigorously proceeded with, and there is every reason to believe that Mr. Plumpton will again have a large majority. Mr. Plimpton, in his address to the electors of White- cross Ward, points out that since he was honoured with the confidence of the electors in June last, when he was returned by a large majority, he has redeemed the promises he made by speaking and voting in favour of a public inquiry as to the Longford Works and the inter- cepting depots, and in favour of fair-wage clauses being inserted in Corporation contracts. He has spoken and voted, too, in support of new public baths. A great deal, however, remains to be done in the direction of improving streets, yards, and back passages, and if again returned he should make it his duty to urge the matter upon the attention of the Town Council. Mr. Plurnpton regrets that the electors are again, within so short a period, put to the turmoil and expense of a municipal contest, for, as he reasonably points out, after the recent decisive struggles. the Conservatives cannot pretend to say that they are in any doubt as to the opinion of the ward. Mr. Rellian, the Conservative candidate, in his address to the electors says that, having been a resident in the ward for upwards of 36 years, he may fairly claire to be thoroughly conversant with the real wants and require- ments of his fellow townsmen. The paving, lighting and sewerage of a large portion of the ward have been much neglected in the past and demand immediate at- tention. Any improvement in that direction would have his active support. As a. working-man and an employer of labour, he thought the whole of his past action was a sufficient guarantee that he believed in a "Fair day's pay for a fair day's work," and there was no necessity for him to alter his principles in that respect at the pre- sent moment simply to gain their votes. As will be seen from our advertising columns, there will be a meeting of Mr. Plumpton's supporters in St. Barnabas school on Friday night next, commencing at 8 o'clock.

Thornton, Jun. , MEETING IN WHITECROSS WARD LAST NIGHT.

Last everting a meeting of the supporters of Mr. W. &Can was held in St. Barnabas schoolroom. Mr. A. Woods presided, and there was a full attendance. The CPIAIFtMAN said he hoped that next Monday week the working-men of the Whitecross ward would show that they were thoroughly independent in every sense of the word, and that they had a perfect right to support any one they thought to be the proper man to represent them in the Town Council. (Hear, hear.) . They had the secresy of the ballot, and Mr. Bellian asked them to use their right to vote manfully and rightfully, indepen- dent of any screw or any other influence there might be an inclination to use—he did not say there was an in- clination to use those influenkeli. laqt there might be. (Rear, hear, and applaiug.e.),
Mr. JAMES Birrnnm, proposed a resolution pledging the meeting to use all la.vful efforts to secure the return of Mr. Bellian. Mr. MASON seconded the r•.solution. .

Counncillor Muss, in an adtlress, said they knew the cause of the Radical victories at the last elections, and they were determined to remekly those causes. He alleged that their opponents had got; their man in at the last election by terrorism.—(No, no.) He bad never come across so many evidences of terrorism—(question)—as in that ward on the last occasion and the previous occa- sion. There was a perfect reign of terror. (Interrup- tion and cries of" prove it.") Forty or fifty people had told him themselves that they dare not go out of their houses for fear of being suspected. (Much interruption, amidst which the Chairman appealed to the meeting to give Councillor Muir a hearing.) In concluding, Mr. Muir said he' only knew Mr. Bellies' as a good singer, but a good singer was always a good man. (Laughter and applause.) The resolution was then put to the meeting and car- ried, though several hands were held up against it. Mr. BELLIAN, in his speech, spoke of the need of im- proving the condition of the streets in the ward, and also said he was in favour of abolishing gas meter rents. He referred to two questions which had been sent to him by the Temperance Federation. The first was as to whether he was opposed to brewers and publicans having a seat on the Watch Committee, and to this he replied that if a man was returned by the burgesses of a ward,it showed that they were convinced that he would vote for their benefit and not for his own interests. (Hear, hear.) The second, question was as to whether he was in favour of the Chief Constable being instructed to systematically enforce the licensing laws with a view to reducing the drunkenness which prevailed in War- rington. To this he replied that he did not think the Chief Constable needed to be bothered with any new- fangled questions which those so-called teetotallers wanted to bring up. (Laughter and hear, hear.) No. of voters, 772

div.head: BEWSEY WARD.
div.p: BEWSEY WARD.

Mr. W. J. Shaw has taken the field on behalf of the Tories in opposition to Councillor T. Flood, who was re- turned three years ago as a workingman's representa- tive' and who will, in all probability, be returned again. Mr. Flood is supported by working class electors gener- ally, and by the members of the Trades Council in par- ticular, that Council having publicly thanked him for the services he has rendered in bringing before the Town Council the questions in which tney are specially inter- ested. Mr. Shaw, who is himself a beerseller, offers to use his influence to get another full licensed house in this ward. An attempt has been made to damage Coun- cillor Flood's candidature by saying that he was a party to a reduction of the wages of the stone-masons employed on the Shin Canal. The very reverse of this, however, is the fact, as Mr. Flood was instrumental in securing for the masons on the Canal a halfpenny per hour more than the masons in the town were obtaining, and this advantage they enjoyed until the wages of the town masons were similarly increased over fifteen months afterwards.

In his address to the electors of Bewsey Ward, the suffrages of whom he again seeks, Mr. T. Flood remarks that he had taken part in every educational movement that had from time to time come before the Council, and he had contributed in every way he could to securing a free library, which will be a bless,ng to the present and future generations. He has devoted special attention to the paving and sewering of the streets of the ward, and in that direction he has secured an improved state of things compared with what existed previous to his entering the Council. During his term c‘f office the ratepayers have become the owners of the Waterwork3, and with regard to this he takes some little credit for early efforts in promoting the agitation which led to this valuable acquisition. As many of Ulm know, he Las, for nearly 30 years, been an active trades unionist, and only the other week he had the satisfaction of receiving a unanimeus vote of thanks from the Warrington Trades Council for the successful efforts he made to induce the Town Council to pass a motion in favour of fair wage clauses being inserted in Corporation contracts. Mr. Shaw promises, if returned, to give his attention to sanitary matters, and will have regard to the im- provement of streets and passages. He thinks that men of Bewsey are being unfairly treated, and will do his utmest to promote the granting of a fully licensed house in Bewsey-road. He claims to be a Trades Unionist of 20 years standing, and an advocate of workingmen's rights.

div.head: ORFORD WARD..
div.p: ORFORD WARD..

Polling place : Silver-street schools ;,no.. of voters, 688. Councillor Jenkins is the retiring representative of this Ward. He succeeded in being returned as an Inde- pendent before the division of the old North-sast Ward when there was a split amongst the Liberals of the ward. He is not so well-known in the Orford district, as Mr. John Bonnell, his present Liberal opponent, who has so far prosecuted an active canvass. I. Bonnell is being heartily supported by a considerable body of volunteer workers, and, as he is highly esteemed as an ernployer of labour in the district, his supporters are sanguine that , he will head the poll. ' Addressing himself to the burgesses of Orford ward, Mr. John Bonnell, the Liberal candidate, says he may describe himself as a friend and neighbour—in fact, one of themselves—because it has been his good fortune to live in the ward, and also to be an employer of labour in their midst, for upwards of thirty years. He is, therefore, personally known to a great number of the electors, and shall, if elected, do his utmost to improve the condition of their streets, and,,if possible, secure better homes for the working classes. It will be known to some of them, Mr. Bonnell adds,, that many years ago he was the means of introducing and establishing in Warrington the "Saturday afternoon holiday" for working-men ; and throughout his business career he had always been an advocate of "- A Fair Day's Wage for a Fair Day's work." He will endeavour to promote every measure which aims at malting life happier, brighter, and better tor the deserving poor, and to seek to remove some of the burdens which are so oppressive, to the working classes. Addressing the electors, Councillor Jenkins says that during the past three years he hag- attended about 180 meetings of committees and 33 meetings of the Council, and if again returned will devote the same attention to their interests as in the past, and support all measures which are for the general benefit of the community, and especially such as are likely to improve the working of the sanitary arrangements of the borough.

div.p: ST. JOHN'S WARD.

Joseph Dobson, who has found his way as a candidate into the ward from the neighbourhood of Lumb-brook in Cheshire. As Councillor Garner is a retired tradesman and has prenty of tine on his hands, and as he is highly esteemed' by his neighbours, he has every reason to suppose he wifl obtain a majOrity of votes. Mr. Dobson's address sets forth the fact that he was brought up in the ward',, and urges that that he is a large ratepayer. He engages to both speak and act, if returned, on &Very question of interest to the ward. He regard's the depots as incapable of remedy, and thinks they should toe "done away with as soon as possible." We gave a summary last week of Mr. Garner's address which, will be again found in our advertising columns.

div.head: FAIRFIELD WARD,
div.p: FAIRFIELD WARD,

Polling place : Brick-street school ; no. of voters, 7921 . Councillor Hutchinson is the Conservative member in. possession of Fairfield Ward, but his position is being vigorously assailed by Mr. Walker, architect, who has the advantage of being a resident of the ward; and being perFonally popular with a large number of electors, Conservative as well as Liberal, he will certainly make a stout fight, and, if his supporters work hard enough, they will have a good chance of returning him. Mr. T. Hutchinson, the retiring Conservative COUR- cillor for Fairfield Ward, in his address to the burgesses refers to his nine years service in the Council,and to the fact that he has attended nearly 100 meetings of the Council and the various Committees of which he was a member, il i 4 a native of the borough, and during the

Ifirst 24 years of his life resided in the ward. He has been a manufacturer and employer of labour in Warring- ton for over 30 years, and is a large ratepayer, conse- quently it would always be his desire to keep down the rates as low as possible consistent with their necossitiev.pavingThe proper lighting, paving and sewetrage' of the streets shall have his earmat and constant attention. He con- siders that the intercepting depots are on their trial, and it they could not be worked so as not ter be ogensive, he should vote for their ent:re removal.

div.head: HOWLEY WARD
div.p: HOWLEY WARD

Polling place: National Silrouls: --no. of voters, '993. In Howley Ward there is a strong feel in., against Conn-- cillor Bolton as a brewer and publican who seems to re-- gard it as his special mission to represent the liquor trade. It is felt to be unfair to the police that he should have a seat on the Ward Committee, and Mr. Joseph Mounfield,- - junior, has come forward as the representative of the• tenaperance party to contest the seat. As a joiner and t builder Mr. Mounfield has acquired a large amount of practical experience which will make him a useful mem- ber of the Corporation, and it is to be hoped the electors- will do themselves credit by returning him. Mr. Joseph Mounfield, who contests Howley ward as - a Liberal, against Mr. W. Bolton, in his address refers- to his thirty years residence in the ward, which gives - him a claim to know something of the district. If elected as their representative, he will do what he can in helping to get rid of the nuisance of the intercepting depots. It is time, too, he considers, that something was done to ensure that there shall be no further sacrifice of life at Hoscley Brook and that the lower parts of the ward shall be safeguarded from the flooding of the river. As a joiner and builder, he believes he can be of some service in considering how to remedy these defects, and in helping the working classes of the ward to healthier and more comfortable homes by providing them with well-paved streets, yards, and back passages. Councillor Bolton, in his address, refers to his nine years' service, and promises to continue to oppose the planting of depots, and other experiments, of a like nature, in their midst. He calls himself a working-men's representative, and intends to do what he can to fur- ther their interests.

div.head: LATCHFORD WARD.
div.p: LATCHFORD WARD.

Polling place : St. James's School; no. of voters, 890. There has been a shuffling of the cards in Latchford Ward, Councillor James Fairclough, who at present holds the seat there having, as a candidate been trans- ferred to St. Austin's ward to make room for Mr. W. Tinsley, who formerly represented Latchford. Mr. S. B. Stringer, who made a gallant fight on behalf of the Liberals last year, has again come forward to do, battle on their behalf. He knows that Latchford is the strong- hold of the Tory party, but believes it may in the-end be ' stormed and carried if the Liberal workers will rally round him, as he trusts they will, and give him all the help they can until the day of election. Mr. S. B. Stringer again takes the field in Latchford Ward as the Liberal candidate, and in his address he I says that although since he last addressed the electors Iseveral of the important measures he then advocated had been passed, many desirable improvements still remained to be effected before the laws of health could thoroughly be complied with in the borough. In- many parts of the town there were "Black spots" demanding thoughtful cansideration before the rate of mortality could he brought down to its lowest possible point. Be was still of opinion that it is contrary to the highest interests of the inhabitants that the liquor trade•should be so- strongly represented on the Watch Committee. Mr. Tinsley, in consenting to stand, reminds the- elec- tors that he has previously represented the ward: in the Council fer over six years, and he plulges himself, if returned, to support all measures calculated to- secure the convenience of the burgesses of the Latchford‘ Ward.

In this ward, the Liberals have an excellent candidate in Mr. Charles Jacks6n Holmes, who, as a business matt in the centre of the town, may be said to be specially qualified to represent this essentially business ward. The Tories have a strong candidate in Councillor James Fairclough, but as the firm with which he is connected are at odds with the Corporation at the present moment it" the matter of an important right of way at Rank Quay, it would perhaps be no worse for the town if Mr. Fairclough were left to watch his interests in this matter outside rather than inside the Corporation. Mr. C. Jackson Holmes, who fights the Liberal battle lin St. Austin's Ward, in his address promises, if re- turned,to do all in his power to assist in the efficient and economical government of the borough. He is well known to most of the electors, having been born in the ward and actively engaged in business in the town for a considerable number of years. Mr. James Fairclough, the Conservative candidate for. St. Austin's Ward, in his address, mentions that he has- now been in the Town Council for two years, and if again returned, he will do his utmost, as benstofore, to consider impartially all schemes that may be brought forward for the health and comfort of the inhabitants. of the town..
