div.head: BEFORE THE MAGISTRATES.
div.p: BEFORE THE MAGISTRATES.
THEFT OF MEAT AND COLLARS

Before the Warrington borough magistrates on Mon- day morning Mary Coakley, of Tilley-st., wife of a brewers' labourer, was charged with stealing on Satur- day night, from the house of George Corbett, 28 Bridge- it., 51b. of meat and half-a-dszen men's collars. The complainant got up in the morning and was intending to fry some of the meat for breakfast when he missed it, and then the collars also. Suspicion fell on the prisoner who had been in the previous night to buy a bottle of herb beer.—lnspector Bowen was informed, and went to the prisoner's house and there found in a cupboard the meat, of which the family had had a meal. She said she had bought it,but had got drunk and did not know where she got it; but her little girl brought it in. She denied knowledge of the collars, but afterwards produced them. At the police station she admitted stealing them and the meat, but said she was willing to pay for them.—She was fined 20s. and costs, £1 19s. in all; in default a month's imprisonment.

div.head: MINOR CASES.
div.p: MINOR CASES.
WARRINGTON BOROUGH POLICE COURT.

MONDAY.—Before the Mayor (Alderman R. W. Fran- comb) and Aldermen Harrison and Wright. DRUNK.—Thomas Kelly, in Buttermarket-street on Eaturday night, ss. and costs. DRUNK AND DISORDERLY.—DanieI Hennessey, drunk and disorderly on Cropper's Brow, Buttermarket-st., on Saturday night. Inspector Spinks and P.C.'s Amson, and Ward gave evidence against him. His face was bleeding and he was creating a great disturbance.—The defendant's wife and another female witness said the defendant only acted in self-defence on being struck by a navvy.—P.C. 44 said he heard the defendant threaten the navvy for pushing his wife.—The Mayer told the defendant he had better have kept his temper,and had the navvy locked up.—P.C. 44 said the defendant attempted, to kick him. The defendant was discharged with a caution. John and Elizabeth Kearns, husband and wife, were charged with being drunk and disorderly in School Brow on Saturday night, in Back Crossley-st. P.C. 6 said the woman was almost destitute of clothing and creating a great disturbance. He got her into the house, and afterwards found both her and her husband behaving in a very disorderly manner. The female was striking her husband's stepfather with a poker.—She stated that it was because he struck her husband. They were fined ss. and costs each.—James Holden,drunk and disorderly in Buttermarket-street, on the Wednesday night prev- ious, ss. and costs. Two WANDERING WAlFS.—George Giffen, from Earles- town, and James Grahame, of Stockport, were charged with being found, on Saturday night, concealed under a Stall in the Market Place with intent to commit felony. They denied the charge, and it appeared from their statements that they had got under the stall for shelter. Grahame said he was an orphan, and Giffen that his mother had turned him out because what he earned, 12s. a week, would not keep him. Grahame was discharged with a caution, and said he would go back to Stockport. Griffen was sent to the Workhouse. CKIIANEY ON FlRE.—Aleck Chadwick, for having his chimney on fire on the 14th inst., was fined is. TVESDAY.—Before Alderman Platt (chairman), and Mr. R. Garnett.

OBSTREPEROUS CASUALS. —George Heywood and Alfred Jones were charged by Mr. Curry, porter at the War- rington Union, with refusing to do the work set them by him, also with damaging a door at the workhouse. The porter said the prisoners were requested by him to break a quantity of stones on Saturday morning in re- turn for a night's lodging' and they broke some before breakfast, but afterwards refused to break any or to pick any oakum. He put them into the cells and they smashed the door open, doing damage to the amount of Ig.—They were sent to jail for seven days each on the first charge, and for the same period on the second. CHARGE OF ASSAULT.—Thomas Glynn was charged with assaulting Ellen Hardy on the night of the 17th Inst. at Pinner's Brow. The complainant appeared with a black eye, and said it had been caused by the defen- dant. The defence was that the blow was struck in self- defence. Fined ss. and costs.

Dimwit AND DISORDERLY.—James Wood, in Butter- market-st.„ on Monday afternoon, ss. including costs. SCHOOL CASES.—Mr. G. Riley, school attendance officer, prosecuted in the following cases :—Henry Bate, forge labourer, Alder-st., 2s.—Leah Briars, William-st., ss.—Peter Carey, forgeman, Dallam-lane, ss.—Michael Dunn, labourer, 19, Clare-st., was also charged as to his two boys, to one of whom, the only one present, the Bench talked about using the birch rod to him, the Chairman asking the father it he would consent to the lad being birched if brought up again. The father replied that he would, and the Chairman told the boy that in case he came again he woul3. probably be birched. Fined 2s.—Wm. Evans, butcher, New-road, ss. including costs. —George Freeth, 27, Orford-lane, 2s. 6d.—Edward Murray, two children, who had paid £6 15s. fines in school cases. Fined ss. for one child,and the other case dismissed.—Henry Palmer, coalman, 16, Alice-st.,2s. 6d. —Mary Towey, 38, Oliver-st.,ss.—James Ward,labourer, 16, Stanley-st., ss.
WEDNESDAY.—Before Alderman Holmes and Mr. John

Fairclough. DRUNK AND DISORDERLY.—Mary Smith, in Buttermar- ket-st., the previous night, was fined ss. and costs. VAGRANCY.—Joshua Pollitt and Joseph Jones were charged with being found sleeping that morning on the enclosed premises of the Cheshire Lines Committee. Pollitt was found in a van at the Waggon Works and Jones under the girder on the railway bridge there. The window of a weighing machine house 15 yards from the prisoner was newly broken, and a screw inside W2S loose. They were both sent to prison for a week. THIIESDAY.—Before Major Pickmere (chairman) and _
Councillor -James Fairclouin.
DRUNK. Pelina Oultram charied with being drunk in Horsemarket-street, the previous afternoon, and whom P.C. 40 had had to bring to the police station in a band cart, was fined ss. and costs.

FRlDAY.—Before Alderman Harrison (chairman) and Alderman Wright. DRUNK AND DISORDERLY.—John Shiels was charged with being drunk and disorderly, in Wilderspool-road, the previous night, also with assaultino. P.C. Bell on the same occasion. The constable said the defendant was in company of a woman of loose character, and a young gentleman as he passed them blew with his mouth whether at the defendant or not witness did not know. The defendant went up to him and struck him. Witness separated them. Later on he saw the defendant mis- conducting himself with the female in Wilderspool-road, and took hold of her, when the defendant struck him three times, and they struggled together 20 minutes, when Henry Ashton, son of the landlord of the Bridge Inn, came to witness's assistance. P.C.'s 16 and 24 gave corroborative evidence and P.C. 18 said the defendant assaulted him in the police station.—lnspector Spinks said the man was so disorderly in the cells all night that he had to get out of bed several times to him.—He was sent to prison for a month.—Sarah Bowman, a m arried woman, the woman who was in company with the last defendant was charged with being drunk and disorderly in Wilderspool-road, on Thursday night. P.C. Bell said she tried to rescue her companion from him. On her promising to leave Warrington within an hour she was disckarged.

NON-CONTRIBUTION FOR EDUCATION.—Patrick Lennady was summoned by Inspector James for non-contribution for the support of his son in St. Anne's industrial school. He was ordered to pay is. per week. CHARGE OF NON-MAINTENANCE OF A WlFE.—Robert Worsley, puddler, Flaydock-street, was summoned for non-maintenance of his wife, Mary Worsley. The defendant, it will be remembered, was recently charged with attempting suicide, and on the same occasion his wife summoned him on a charge of non-maintenance, when the case was adjourned a month.—She did not appear and it was now dismissed. WORKING HORSES IN AN UNFIT STATE. —Joseph Stafford 75, Chorley-street, was charged by Inspector Dowty, with working a horse while in an unfit state in Wilders- pool-road, on the 14th inst., and Samuel Stokes, 17, Cambria Place, was charged with causing the same to be so worked. Mr. Dowty said he saw Stafford in charge of three horses and a lurry. The leader was very uneasy, and he stopped the horses, and found that in a poor and weak condition and suffering from wounds on the shoulders. Stokes was stableman for Mr. Pilkington to whom the horse belonged, and witness called upon hint and he admitted sending the horse out in the state discribed. Stafford was fined 6s. costs and Stokes 10s. and costs. .

ASSAULT.—Joseph Hewitt was charged with assault- ing James Woods, a shoemaker, on the 14th inst. The defence was that the complainant struck first. The de- fendant was bound over in his own recognisances of £5 to keep the peace for six months. ABSENCE FROM SCHOOL.—Patrick Lennardy, of War- burton-st., was charged under a warrant with not send- ing his two children regularly to school, and fined ss.

div.head: WARRINGTON COUNTY SESSIONS.
div.p: WARRINGTON COUNTY SESSIONS.

WEDNESDAY.—Before Major Yickmere and Mr. P. Stubs. POACHING.—Sydney Phillips, of Cadishead, canal worker, was charged with being found in possession of a gun coming from land in the occupation of Captain Parr at Howcroft on the 17th inst.—P.S. Barnes deposed to hearing a shot fired on the land and seeing the defend- ant come with other men from the land. He found the defendant in possession of a loaded gun and ten cart- ridges. He admitted he had been in the cover shooting rabbits.—He now pleaded guilty.—He was fined 20s. and costs.—James Shaw, collier, was charged with being found in Cow-lane, Burtonwood, on the 30th ult., with a live rabbit in his pocket, and a loaded gun in his posses- sion, he being supposed to be coming from land where he had been in pursuit of game.—P.S. Devlin gave evidence against the defendant.—Thomas Jones was found in his company with a wet netin his pocket.—Shaw said he had a right to shoot on Mr. Joshua Xenwright's land, but this was three miles away. —Mr. Riley,of St. Helens, appeared for the defence. He said under existing legislation a large section of game belonged now as much to the ten- ant and those whom he chose to invite on to his premises as to the owner of the freehold and those who had the shooting of the higher kind of game. There was nothing illegal in a man being found on the Queen's highway in possession of a gun. The name of the Hon. Leopold Powis appeared on the information, but he was not re- presented as he ought to have been, and he (Mr. Riley) contended the police ought not to undertake these prose- cutions, which were essentially civil in their nature. This case was a matter of an absolute question of title, and the taking up of these cases by the police was exercising the most vexatious powers they could have in their ands ; and which the magistrates ought not to encourage them in using. Becausesome martinette of a country sergeant chose to, suspect a man who had lived in the neighbourhood a dozen years with a good charac- ter, should their worships assume on that ground that he had thrown all his character to the winds? The defen- dant was coming from Mr. Kenwright's land where he had permission to shoot, and had the gun license.—He was fined 20s. and costs.
DRUNK.—John Moss, drunk on the highway at Pen- keth, ss. and costs. ASLEEP IN A CART.—Joseph Ellison, for being asleep while in charge of a horse and cart, was fined is. and costs.

div.head: WARRINGTON YOUNG MEN'S CHRIS-
div.p: WARRINGTON YOUNG MEN'S CHRIS-
TIAN ASSOCIATION. RECITAL BY MISS DUTTON.

On Wednesday evening, at the new premises of the Young Men's Christian Association, there was an entertainment, presided over by Mr. W. Owen, the principal feature of which consisted of a series of elocutionary performances by Miss B. Dutton, of Moore. The entertainment was opened by a per- formance on the piano by Miss N. Pigot, after which Miss Dutton gave a reading from Lawrence Sterne's "Tristram Shandy."—The Chairman appealed to the audience, which was large, for contributions to a collection to be made that night. He said he was told that at the entertainments on Wednesday even- ings those present were occasionally asked to put their hands into their pockets. The reason for this was that the Association was not yet self-support- ing. There was accommodation for something like 400 members, and at present there were only 170, so that there was a large margin to be covered in other ways than by subscriptions. They had a capital read- ing room, well-lighted and comfortable, and plenty of papers. They had a pleasant room called a drawing room,he believed—but drawing rooms were going out of fashion—and he should call it a living room, where they could have conversation and pass a pleasant evening. Then they had a class room, and a room where draughts could be played or light refreshment partaken of. There was a shorthand class, a Bible class, and a debating society. Besides that, they had something on the mus- cular side of Christianity, a bicycle club, a cricket club, and they would have next year a tennis club, for they had ample room on their own ground for the game. A rambling club would also be instituted; and possibly there might be some other classes. They had plenty to do, and all they wanted was money. On Sunday evenings there would be inaugurated classes to meet after the service were over in the churches and chapels, for men who likedto come in between 8 and 9 on Sunday night. —A song followed by Miss Pigot,after which Miss Dutton gave a Scotch reading in which the full flavour of the pawky Caledonian humour was well brought out by her delivery. Messrs. Sudlow and Wright succeeded with a piano duet, and then, after a ten minutes interval, Miss Dutton read Macauley's " Virginius," her audience throughout being enchained in silent attention.—Mr. Thomas Morris proposed a vote of thanks to the Chairman and artistes. The latter, he said, had done very well indeed, and Miss Dutton was most excellent ; he did not know whether to admire most the matter she had given or the way she had given it.—The Chairman responded for himself and the artistes. Another song by Miss Pigot followed, after which Miss Dutton gave in very good style, from memory, a lengthy recital descriptive of the sorrows of an Italian organ grinder in London. Another duet by Messrs. Sudlow and Wright succeeded, after which Mr. Wylie thanked the audience on behalf of the Committee for their attendance, and the singing of part of the National Anthem closed the proceedings.

div.head: EXAMINER, SATURDAY, OCTOBER 24, 1891.
div.p: THE EXAMINER, SATURDAY, OCTOBER 24, 1891.

Widnes continued to press, and Rochdale were com- pelled to touch down in self defence. Whelan and Gordon dribbled well, and Emery charged the fullbacks' kick down, the ball going dead. Widnes were now having all the best of the game and from a free kick St. Clement's pressed. Drummond ran splendidly, and most unselfishly passed to Brennan, but there was no one to take his pass, and the chaaca was lost. Shortly after- wards Wright scored, but Brennan failed at the goal. Half-time score :—Widnes, 1 goal and 1 try ; Rochdale, nil. Final score :—Widnes, 1 goal and 1 try ; Rochdale, nil.

FRODSHAII v. Sr. HELENS "A."—This match was played at Frodsham, on Saturday. The visitors won the toss, and Garner kicked off for Frodsham against the wind, a good return being made. Play was carried into the visitors' quarter, and from a pass Goddall got over, but lost possession of the ball, a minor only resulting. Shortly after Fred Darlington picked up smartly, and had passed all opposition, when he foolishly passed, and a certain try was thrown away. From now up to half time the play was more even. From the restart Frod- sham played up well, their forwards showing particu- larly good form. From some loose play T. Rogers secured, and making a splendid dodging run, scored a try. T. Darlington kicked a good goal from a difficult angle. The tome team showed very good form, their play all mound being superior to that of their opponents, and a very pleasant game ended In a win for them (Frod- sham) by 1 goal tl (St. Helens) nil, or five points to nil.

div.head: WARRINGTON v. ST. HELENS RECREATION.
div.p: WARRINGTON v. ST. HELENS RECREATION.

Wretched weather marked the fiust of the annual engagements between the above clubs, which took place at Wilderspool, on Saturday. The St. Helens combina- tion have now appeared on the Warrington card for the past three seasons, and the majority of victories in their favour up to Saturday was recorded as three to one. The interest in the match had not deteriorated in the least, as was evidenced in the attendance, as besides the usual attendance of the ordinary home enthusiasts, two special trains ran from the glass-blowing towns, convey- ing nearly 1,800 to the scene of action. Warrington placed the team as originally selected on the field, but Jackson was away from the visitors' side. I In threatening weather, Ashton losing the toss,started towards the pavilion goat The spectators and players were soon on their mettle, and a short reply being forth- coming, a loud shout from the Saints' supporters showed that Warrington were busy defending, owing to a mull Iby Webster. The oval had no sooner been scrimmagid I than Turton and Pilkington passed across the pack, for the latter to score a somewhat clever try in such an easy position that Pyke had little difficulty in augment- ing the point. This reverse staggered the home suppor- ters temporarily, but on Ashton's restart being followed by a spirited attack, led up by the home skipper and Nevins, an encouraging cheer was forthcoming. Rain now began to fall, and continued without intermission throughout the match. The adverse circumstances un- der which the game was played had not the least effect on the enthusiasm, for each individual piece of play was cheered to the echo. Following the slight attack on the Saints' goal came a forward rush, headed by Dolan and Pyke, but Warrington gave them a taste of their pass- ing capabilities,when the two Bates, Barnes, and Web- ster indulged in a series, only to find the latter putting in a short kick at the second attempt. Fine kicking by Seddon neutralized, but Boscow, who played a grand game throughout, met the oval in his usual cool style, and effected a prompt reply. Play was confined to neutral territory,and ultimately J. Bate passed to Barnes, who transferred to Webster, the movement terminating in the Recreation defending. Not to be denied, Warring- ton still attacked, and Bandies, Jolley, Berry, and Law- less were prominent with respective essays. Another flue run byJ. Bate from a pass by his companion half, found both Barnes and Webster slow in making head- way, but although Seddon partially relieved, Boscow, Fair. Turner, and James Bate, with fine kicking once more had the oval in close proximity to the pavilion goal- It•was now the Recs' turn to attack, and follow- ing a fine peace of play by Ellison, Turton narrowly missed a score. Jolley and Berry were foremost in bringing relief ,and Briers was on one occasion passed ,but an anxiety to get possession instead of dribbling on spoiled a certain try. However, James Bate made no mistake in the chance afforded him a minute later, for, out- witting his hitherto too attentive rival half back, he finally cleared Seddon, Ellison, and Briers, scoring a clever try, which Webster failed to augment. Inspired by this success, Warrington kept up the pressure, and chiefly by the aid of Boscow and Barnes they were able ,to maintain their position. Ellison obliged with another fine run and kick, but the home custodian never allowed St. Helens a semblance of a chance, and a free kick be- ing granted Seddon, Fair Turner's huge kicking was of immense value, by the latter means Warrington having the agreeable task of invading. A return was forth- coming from Briers, and then Dolan was almast in from a miskick. The oval was promptly rushed out, Donohue and Holmes being at the head of affairs, and James Bate and Ashton kicking judiciously, play was taken to the half-way flag. A penalty kick to St. Helens was met by Lawless, who was promptly floored, and Warrington had rather an anxious time of it. Barnes kicked well and another mark by Seddon was this time met by Bandies with success. A display by the Bates, Barnes, and Webster had a futile ending, and the score at the inter- val read—St. Helens Recreation, a goal; Warrington, a , try. By this time the players and spectators presented a sorry spectacle, the heavy rain giving one an idea that they had been indulging in the art of natation. They bravely stood the elements, and the initial movements of this half were cheered by the rival enthusiasts. The Recs, almost scored direct from the kick-off, Nevins failing to catch the restart. An infringement gave War- rington an opportunity of relieving, and Webster being also to the fore, Seddon eventually, by a long drop, com- pelled a minor. A fine kick by J. T. Bate was instru- mental in Warrington changing the oval to the opposing end, and after Dolan had got away, Nevins floored his man in fine style. A permanent attack was here set up by the homesters, and for fully a quarter of an hour the game settled down to a series of scrimmages on the rail- way goal line. Twice J. T. Bate claimed to have scored, whilst Jolley also appealed for a major point, the result of a scramble. It was not Warrington's day out, ap- parently, for all were disallowed, and aft:lough the oval was got away, Boscow replied, and a minor was all that was credited. The home custodian was in fine form, and another fine effort aided his side in attacking. Once the Recreation got away to the home 25, but they were easily repulsed, and had to rely on the defensive. This they did with credit to themselves, and Warrington be- ing weak in their final essays, failed to utilize chances, and in the end were defeated by a goal and two minors to a try and four minors. Teams :—Warrington: Boscow, back ; Webster, Barnes, and Lawless, three-quarter backs ; James Bate and John Bate, half backs; Ashton, Fair Turner, Randles, Jolley, Nevins, Holmes, Davies, Berry, and Donohue, forwards. St. Helens Recreation: Briers, back; Gerrard, Seddon, and Ellison, threequarter backs; Pilkington and Turton, half backs; Pike, Dolan, Fildes, Dean, Mousdale, Reynolds, Winstanley, Briers, and Collins, forwards. WARRINGTON" A "v. ST. HELENS RECREATION "A."— Heavy rain which descended throughout the game be- tween these teams at St. Helens, was entirely against football, greatly militating against passing, and numer- ous mistakes were made in consequence. The " Recs." started the leather-chasing, and the kick-off was well returned by Barnes. The forwards were quickly in evi- dence, and some spills amongst the visitors' backs were taken full advantage of by the homesters a couple of minors following in quick succession. A dodgy run by Faren was nullified by Antrobus and Barnes getting away with a dribble' and a rush, in which Bailey, Moly- neux, Knowles and Rowlands were notable, forced the ball into the" Rees' " 25. Here Newey looked like scor- ing after a strong run, but Goolden frustrated the effort, and a flying kick removed the danger. Then followed a strong rush by the " Recs." forwards, Potts coming to the timely rescue by a long punt, only to see Mees re- turn and a minor issue. Play still hovered around the Warrington quarters, but after Hampson, Russell, Row- lands, and Edwards had transferred the game to near the centre, a magnificent dodgy run by Heesom was only pulled up wider the goal—hard lines indeed. The home forwards were playing up, and bested the Warring- ton front rank, several of whom had a strong tendency to "wing it," but eventually a long kick by Hamblett found play at the Saints' line. The attack was repulsed and the leather sent to Hamblett,who replied splendidly. Hampson, Molyneux, Barnes and Knowles threatened the downfall of the home goal, but Mees spoiled the endeavour, and a kick being charged by the "Roes." at mid-field, a fine chance was afforded to the Saints, but it was lost, and Molyneux transferred to the home territory by a kick. This gave Warrington a foothold they / had been longing for, and Antrobus passing quickly to Lally, the latter ran to the line and re-passed to Antrobus, who was almost over. Directly afterwards, the same tactics ensued, and this time Lally dodged over, Sampson making a fine bid for goal. Potts replied to the drop-out, but Little dribbled rapidly to mid-field, and again the home team assumed an attack- ing position. Knowles, Bailey, and Barnes temporarily relieved, but Warrington had to concede another minor. Following this, Hampson, Russell, and Rowlands rushed down, but Mees saved splendidly, and half-time arrived with Warrington 1 try to 4 minors. Resuming, some bad mistakes by Warrington let in their opponents, but Barnes, Russell, and Lally responded, and cleared any danger to their lines. A dashing piece of loose play by Hampson found the Saints concedinga minor. Scrambl- ing play was the order for some time, and after Sampson had saved a couple of rushes, Knowles, Newey, Bailey, and Molyneaux got to the half-way, where Lally got possession and ran finely to the line, but was overtaken. After Heesom had shown up, the leather was quickly transferred to the other end and a minor given; a couple of kicks followed shortly after. Unfortunately at this stage one of the home team was hurt and had to retire. Warrington then quickly rushed the ball to their antagonists' quarters,a bad pass allowing the home team to reach the half-way. Bailey, Rowlands, Russell, and Edwards in the loose harassed the backs of the "Recs.," and two minors were conceded. Nothing of interest occurred after this except a splendid boa of , passing near the close between Lally, Antrobus, Samp- son, Heesom, and Potts, but nothing came of it, and a scambling game ended—Warrington, I try 4 minors to 71 minors.

WIDNHS V. ROCHDALE ST. CLEMENT'S.—Before 3,000 spectators, on Saturday, at Rochdale. The homesters had the best of the opening exchanges, but Widnes got together, and Farmer scored a try. Brennan was entrusted with the kick, and landed a neat goal.

div.head: RUNCORN v. BURTON.
div.p: RUNCORN v. BURTON.

This match was played at Runcorn, on Saturday, but owing to a misunderstanding with the railway company a late start was effected. Faulkner kicked off for Run- corn against wind and rain. Play was fairly even for some time, until a rush by the Burton forwards, led by Evershed, forced the home team to defend. Some pas- sing between the Burton backs lost ground, and lot in the home forwards, who took the ball dangerously near the Burton line, Lowe making a good save again. The Burtonians broke away, Houghton kicking grandly to touch. A moment later P. Riley was conspicuous with a tine dribble, Ward having to touch down. Smart pas- between Evans, Abrahams, and Davies, gave the latter a chance, but Ward held him safely. Faulkner at last got a chance, and, throwing wide to Davies, the latter sprinted grandly over, the kick failing. Kicking out, Burton paid a visit to the home lines, but Houghton was playing finely at half-time, when the score was— Runcorn, 1 try, 2 minors; Burton, nil. The second half was very evenly contested, neither side being able to score. At the close of the game Runcorn were declared winners by 1 try and 2 minors to Burton nil.

div.head: ASSOCIATION.
div.p: ASSOCIATION.

WIDNES PARISH CHURCH V. WESTON.—This Association game was played at Widnes on Saturday,in wet weather. Weston kicked off against the wind, but were first to press. Williams had to handle the ball, and several goal kicks were the result of the attack. The homesters then played up, and after a series of futile attacks, Clibborn got one past the visitors' custodian. From the centre kick, Watson again pressed, and put the ball through the uprights, but the whistle had just previously gone off-side play. Final result :—Widnes Parish Church, 1 goal ; Weston, nil.

div.head: NOTES ON GAMES AND
div.p: NOTES ON GAMES AND
ATHLETICS.
FOOTBALL.

Several of the half-dozen League matches that were decided on Saturday proved great attractions. There were upwards of 10,000 persons at Bolton, where the Wanderers defeated the champions by a goal to none. The latter were not fully represented, and they were deprived of the services of Jardine, their goalkeeper, owing to an accident before the interval. The Wan- derers are now well established at the top of the table, and as they play their next two fixtures at Pike's Lane they are not likely to be replaced for some time to come. The visit of the Blackburn Rovers to Darwen furnished a very exciting contest, in which the cup holders scored five goals to throe. At one stage they had only nine men on the field, and Forbes permanently retired owing to an injured leg in the first half. Burnley had the best of the luck in their match with Aston Villa, the last-named being handicapped ow- ing to their goal-keeper being seriously hurt. Burnley won by four goals to one. A draw of two goals each was the finish of the game between Derby County and Stoke, this being a good performance on tilt part of the Pottery representatives. Notts had to put up with a defeat at Wolverhampton, as had the Albion at West Bromwich, their victors being Sunderland. At the in- terval the visitors were behind by a goal, but they sub- sequently played admirable football.

The question as to whether there is more danger to players in the Rugby than in the Association game' or vice versa, is sometimes debated in a lively fashion. On the face of it the natural conclusion would seem to be that the Rugby style of play was the rougher of the two, but as a matter of fact there seem to be at least as many, and probably more, cases of injury to players in Association games. The note given above, for instance, shows that in the principal Association contests on Satur- day the players were knocked about like nine pins, and in several instances thop ho.a. to leave the field. After all,in a vigorous sport like football accidents wur uepene far more largely on the character of the players, and the policy of the governing body, than on the differences in the code. Perhaps professionalism does not tend to ameliorate the Association game. There is a money value in victory to the professional, and skilful play is not the only way of winning a victory.
ArilOpenst s, and tb-

The refusal of the county committee to sanction the transfer of a player from the Littleborough to the Roch- dale Hornets' Club will, at any rate, make it plain that the executive are fully alive to their duties. Anything that tends in the direction of professionalism should be nipped in the bud at once, and this lesson will not be thrown away. There is frequently a good deal more in the transfer of a player than meets the eye, but actual proof is difficult to get at.

Among the outside matches on Saturday that between Swinton and Swansea was of a good deal of interest. The Welsh team was a powerful one, including no fewer than seven members of last year's Welsh international fifteen. Their opponents had to turn out without Val- entine, whose knee was not quite recoverel. Despite the heavy nature of the ground there was some excel- lent football, the outcome of which was a win for the home side, the only point secured by the visitors being a beautifully dropped goal by Bancroft. The four three quarter back move adopted by Swinton was successful in counteracting the well-known style of play which the Welshmen have nude familar ; whilst the home for- wards were decidedly superior to those on the other side.

Salford have at last broken their spell of ill-luck and crediteo: themselves with their first victory. This was achieved over Broughton, who were beaten by four tries to one. That Miles was prominent for the victors, will be seen when it is pointed out that he himself crossed the line no fewer than three times. Despite the absence of Berry, their crack half back, Tyldesley, more than once held their own with Mamchester Rangers, winning by nine points to two, having had much the best of the proceedings. Oldham were again on the winning tack, Crompton being their victims, Gwynn and Hurst largely contributing to this result. Wigan managed to pull off their fixture at Leigh,but the difference was only a goal and a try to a try,a mistake by Cook proving expensive. Kendal had the assistance of ' Berry, the County half back, but they were still easily vanquished by Bradford. Berry played well. For a specimen of tall scoring the record piled up by West Leigh against Ringley will take some beating. Seven goals and four tries to a goal were overwhelming.

The question of a referee is often a sore point between two competing teams, the gentlemen who officiate being invariably looked upon with a:certain amount of ill-nlaced suspicion. This feeling has,to some extent,been removed by the establishment of the various societies of referees, by which the clubs have been relieved of the unpleasant task of finding officials. At the meeting of the London Rugby Union Society of Referees, last week, Mr. Row- land Hill made a strong appeal to old players to take up what many declared to be a melancholy and thankless office, " but what he always found to be a most enjoy- able duty." If gentlemen who are fully qualified by ex- perience and knowledge would respond to the appeal of the hon. sec. we should see better football than we some- times witness, where a strong man is badly wanted to take the game under his charge. Teams quickly dis- cover when they have a firm hand to deal with, and play accordingly.

Warrington had to put up with another reverse on Saturday, as they were beaten by St. Helens Recs. by a goal to a try. The encounters of these two teams had always been of the stiffest kind, and that of Saturday was certainly not an exception. The home team seemed rather taken by surprise at the dash and energy with which the Recs. opened the game, and before they had fairly grasped the situation Pilkington, with one of his dodgy runs, carried the leather behind the posts. From this easy position the goal which won the game was kicked. The local men pulled themselves together after that, and when Bate outwitted his opponents in his immitable style there was a chance of equalising accounts,but the goal did not comeoff. Towards the end of the game Warrington did the pressing, and once or twice they were over with what seemed fair tries, but they were ruled back.

Speaking critically of the game, the wirepullers did not show the all-round smartness that they displayed in the earlier matches of the season. The three-quarters either did not get the chances or they did not make the best use of them, and there were several occasions when a little clean accurate passing might have brought about the desired result.

There were two Warrington players taking part in the Lancashire county trial match on Wednesday, Jolley amongst the forwards, and "Smack "Bate at half-back, and both acquitted themselves so well that they have ueen selected to do duty in the team of " Possiblea "
against the " Probables " at Whalley Range next Wed- nesday. From the accounts Bate seems to have put in some very smart play at half-ba3k, and two of the tries scored were from his passes.

div.head: WARRINGTON CO-OPERATIVE SOCIETY.
div.p: WARRINGTON CO-OPERATIVE SOCIETY.
QUARTERLY MEETING.

A quarterly- meeting of the members of this Society was held in the Sankey-st. Co-operative Hall on Monday evening. The President (Mr. T. Birchall) presiued, and there was a large attendance ot members. The balance sheet submitted showed that the sales during the quarter had been £20,279 ss. 6d., and the Chairman commented upon the very satisfactory progress which the society continued to make. The balance sheet was adopted, as was also the recommendation of the Committee that a divi- dend of 3s. 2d. in the pound on members' purchases be declared. In the minutes of the Committee's meetings it was stated that a donation had been made to Wycliffe Schools, and, in answer to a question, the President replied that the Committee were, of course, prepared to consider the subject of donations to other schools as well, though the granting of the donation would depend upon the circumstances of each school. He also was of opinion that the question of providing, out of the edu- cational fund of the society, scholarships in connection with the elementary schools for children of members was well worth considering. (Hear, hear.) It was also mentioned that during the present quarter the new cheque system upon sales would come into force at the various shops. The system was explained to the meet- ing, and, after various questions had been asked and answered, it seemed to meet with the approval of those present. It is estimated that the cost of working the cheque system will be about 3s. in every £lOO of sales.

Weir, Lewis, Heywood, Aaron, Edwards, W. Ellison, W. Turner, J. Baguley, J. Whitlow; W. Whitlow, Brandreth, J. Hall, Moun- field, J. Stokes, J. W. Baguley, P. Hall, Baxter, J. Ashton (clerk), G. div.head: ALLEGED POLLUTION OF KECKWICK BROOK.
div.p: THE ALLEGED POLLUTION OF KECKWICK BROOK.

Mr. H. J. Longton, solicitor, Warrington' wrote on behalf of Mr. Earp with respect to Keckwick Brook, ask- ing for an opportunity of being heard against the pro- posed proceedings pursuant to section 6 of the Rivers Pollution Act.

div.head: ROAD SUBSIDENCE AT FRODSHAM.
div.p: ROAD SUBSIDENCE AT FRODSHAM.

Mr. W. Clark of Church-st., Frodsl7;t-m-,-;;rote stating that on the night of the 2nd inst., whilst his horse and cart were standing on the road at Netherton, near Mr. Ralph Bate's the roadway suddenly gave way causing the animal to fall down and severely injure both its knees— in fact it was ruined. A few months ago he refused 40 guineas for the cob, and he should be glad for directions as to the recovery of compensation for the damage sus- tained.—The Clerk said Mr. Farrington had inspected the spot and he reported that he failed to see that the Rural Sanitary Authority were in any way responsible for the accident. The subsidence he said had occurred througk the backing-up of the water of the road drain and not through the sewer of the Rural Sanitary Autho- rity.—The Clerk said he had written to Mr. Clark to that effect.—Mr. Edwards said the County Council also dis- claimed all responsibility, as they had handed all drains over to the Rural Sanitary Authority.—The Chairman : I don't see that at all. If it is not a sewage drain we have nothing to do with it.
FEVER OUTBREAKS.

The Medical Officer reported outbreaks of diptheria at Frodsham Bridgeand Antrobus. A case of typhoid fever had occurred at Helsby, four cases had occurred at Hatchmere Norley, and four at London Bridge, Stockton Heath. Scarlet fever had broken out at Manley, and there were three cases of the same disease at Halton. The usual precautions had been taken against the spread of the disease.
NUISANCE AT FIVE CROSSES.

Mr. Reynolds drew attention to the filthy state of a number of ccttages at Five Crosses, and stated that the water supply was bad. After the water had stood 24 hours in a can it became green on the surface.—Tht Clerk said this was a question for the Frodsham Lord- ship Parochial Committee.—Mr. Reynolis : I wondered whether this Board thought the Frodsham Committee capable of. deciding anything. (Laughter.)—Mr. Edwards: That is so.—The Nuisance Inspector said it was one of the worst blocks of property in the township.
THE PRODSHAM WATER SCHEME.

The consideration of the proposed scheme of water supply for Frodshain was resumed. Mr. Edwards an- nounced that at a meeting of the ratepayers of the town- ship, on Thursday night, the scheme was rejected by 21 votes to twelve.—ln reply to Mr. Reynolds,Mr. Heywood said there were about 50 people present at the meeting, but they did not all vote. The meeting was not held on a suitable night, as the harvest festival would prevent many ratepayers from attending.—Mr. Edwards said originally the meeting was called for the Friday night, but the-atant overseer altered the date on the repre- sentation ot arra, cx at- a abwayerer------rtniroverseers cave asked to change the day from the Thursday.—Mr. Rey- nolds asked if the engineer of the scheme was there, or was it all one-sided advocacy.—Mr. Edwards: The engineer was not there. I don't think he has the cour- age to support his own scheme. (Oh, oh). At the pre- vious meeting he was present and had nothing at all to say.—Mr. Heywood said Mr. Edwards was mistaken. Mr. Walter Timmins was not present.—Mr. Thomas The engineer is prepared to take the job at the price.—: Mr. Heywood said it had been suggested that this scheme would entail great expense and hardship upon several farmers, who would derive neither directly nor indirectly any benefit from the scheme. With regard to two forms he had it on good authority that it was very probable that the landlord would take the water rates from these farms.—Mr. Stokes: That is what all the landlords ought to do.—Mr. Edwards: Hear, hear.—Mr. Stokes : The providing of water is a landlord's ques- tion .altogether.—The Clerk said it did not follow that those farmers would be rated at all. Section. 10 of the public Health (Water) Act empowered any five persons rated to the relief of the poor in the township of which a past is supplied to require the Sanitary Author- ity to charge water rates or water rents in respect of all water supplied by them in such township. Section Bof the same Act empowered the Local Government Board on the application of the Sanitary Authority to fix by order a general scale of charges for the supply of water and if the cost of a supply to any house within the area specified in the order does not exceed such scale it shall be deemed to be reasonable. So that the tenant could attend before the Government Inspector and state his claim to be exempted from the water rate, and the Local Government Board would decide whether his claim was reasonable.—Mr. Edwards asked where Mr. Far- rington was a he wished to ask him a few questions.— A Member said he had observed Mr. Edwards looking at the clock, and he wished to talk the question out against time. Mr. Edwards had been in a minority of five .to one on one or two occasions, and it seemed to him, and he hoped it would seem to the Board that the whole of the opposition was coming from Mr. Edwards. He called upon the Chairman to put the motion.—Mr. Edwards :—What I say is that there is plenty of water from above.—Mr. Reynolds: There has plenty come down from above the last two or three weeks anyway. (Laughter.)—On the motion being put the scheme was approved by ten votes to one, only Mr. Edwards voting against. Several members abstained from voting.—Mr. Reynolds remarked that Mr. Edwards had had the courage of his opinions.•

EXTRAORDINARY SUCCESS IN THE TREATMENT OF ODE- SITY.-Our corpulent readers will be glad to learn how to positively lose two stone in abut a month with the greatest possible benefit in health, strength, and muscle by a comparatively new system. It is a singular para- dox that the patient, returning quickly to a healthy state with increased activity of brain digestive and other organs naturally requires more food than hitherto, yet notwithstanding this, he absolutely loses in weight one to two pounds daily, as the weighing machine will prove. Thus, there is no suggestion of starvation. It is an absolute success, and the author, who has devoted years of study to the subject, absolutely guarantees a noticeable reduction within 24 hours of commencing the treatment. This is different with other diseases, for the patient in some cases may go for weeks without be- ing able to test whether the Physician has rightly treated him, and may have derived no real or apparent improvement in health. Here, we repeat, the author guarantees it in 24 hours, the scale to be the unerring judge. The treatment aims at the actual root of the disease,so that the superfluous fat does not return when discontinuing the treatment. It is perfectly harmless. We advise our readers to call the attention of stout friends to this, because, sincerely, we think they ought to know. For the information we may say that a re- print of Press notices from some hundreds of Medical and other journals (British and foreign), and other in- teresting particulars, including the " recipe " can be had from a Mr. F. -A burslem minister, Mr. Cheshire, was on Saturday night found unconscious on the line at Stoke-on-Trent railway station, haying been knocked down by an en- gine while attemptmg to cross. He is progressing favourably.
" TOMMY " BURNS AT WAR- RINGTON. A "BIG DIVE" AT WALTON ARCHE

The public of Warrington have this week had an opportunity of witnessing one of the daring feats of diving from great heights into the water below which have made the name of Tommy Burns famous in the world of athletics. A few months ago there was a great deal of talk about Burns' dive from the lofty parapets of Runcorn Bridge into the Mersey, and there were people who professed to disbelieve thet any such thing ever took place, and they roundly asserted that the whole affair had been concocted as a kind of cheap advertisement. "See- ing is believing," however, and the large crowd of Warringtonians who witnessed the performance of this week will have come to the conclusion that "Tommy "does not stick at a trifle, and that he certainly does not lack courage to attempt anything in the way of big diving. The performance took place on Tuesday afternoon at Walton Arches,when Burns dived from the highest point of the new iron bridge there into the river. The announcement that this was to take place was not made in any very public manner, but in spite of this, a knowledge of it seemed to have spread all over the town and district, and long before half-past two, when the " dive "was to come off, there was a lot of people assembled at the Arches. Spectators in larger or smaller numbers seemed to be coining from all directions—trom Warrington, from Bank Quay, from Walton, and even from Moore. They assem- bled on both sides of the river and on the embank- ments and railways, and waited patiently for the advent of the hero of the 'moment. Punctual to time a small steamer was seen coming down the river, and amongst the numerous passengers the knowing ones soon recognised "Tommy," and they set up a cheer of welcome. Tommy doffed his cap in acknowledgment of the cheering, and when the boat had been brought alongside the little landing stage, be very quickly scrambled up the em- bankment, and was seen through the girders of the bridge in his swimming costume. Prior to this, however, " Professor " Boston, who seems to be Burns's inseparable friend and mentor, went round with the box, "Tommy Burns's box" he called it. A fair number of coins seemed to be dropped into it, but it was clear that a large pro- portion of the spectators had come to see and not to contribute, and the " Professor," judging from his remarks, did not appear to be fully satisfied with the donations. It was ex- pected that Burns would make his dire from the road level of the bridge, but when he had got up this did not appear to be high enough fcir him—al- though the bridge is of great hwght, and towers high above the adjacent Arches"—and a ladder having been brought he ascended to the top of the girders, some twenty or thirty feet higher than the road level, we should think. As soon as the crowd perceived the intentions of the daring diver, there was another outburst of cheering, but, as a moment later he was seen to be standing erect on the very topmost point of the structure, all noise was sud- denly hushed, and the crowd waited in almost breathless expectation for the grand leap. Burns himself took matters very coolly. There was an easy smile on his face as he looked round,as though it was a very ordinary feat that he was about to perform, and certainly there was not the least trace of timidity or hesitation. " Profes- sor" Boston, who had followed Burns part of the way up the ladder, shouted, " Are you ready?" Burns replied "Yes," and almost directly after brought his hands together in front of him, and plunged head first from the bridge. Al- though his descent must have been very rapid, he seemed to the spectators to be several seconds in the air. During part of the fall he shot down straight as an arrow, but the strong current of wind underneath the bridge then caught him, and, turn- ing part of a somersault, he fell into the water on his back or side. In an instant or two he was again seen above the water, swimming vigorously down the stream, and apparently not the least injured by his risky plunge. For about ten minutes he re- maiued in the water,performing several feats of fancy swimming, and then he was again taken on to the boat and conveyed back to Warrington. It is said that the distance from the surface to the part of the bridge where Burns leaped is 61 feet, and it cer- tainly looked this height. The river at the time was high with a receding tide, and apart from the dis- tance of the fall there was some danger to the diver from small pieces of floating timber that could occasionally be seen in the water. Fortun- ately Burns does not seem to have come in contact with any of these, although we are informed that there was to be noticed a slight mark or bruise on his back.

Barns had undertaken to make an even bigger dive from Litton's Mill at Bank Quay, oil Thursday afternoon, but tots, we are informed, he was pre- vented from doing by the police, on the ground that the crowd that would be drawn together might do some damage. Burns informs us that it is his intention to jump from the Tay Bridge in the course of about six weeks.
MARRIAGE OF MISS JACKSON AND MR.
TINSLEY.

At the Leeds Parish Church ,on Tuesday afternoon, the marriage took place, in the presence of a crowded congregation, of Miss Alice Tempest Jack- son, the eldest daughter of the Right Hon. W. L. Jackson, M.P. (Financial Secretary to the Treasury, and representative of the Leeds Northern Division in Parliament), of Allerton Hall, Leeds, to Mr. Harrison Tinsley, of the firm of Messrs. John and James Tinsley, tanners, of Mersey-street, Warring- ton, and of Grappenhall, Cheshire. Between 300 and 400 invitations had been sent out, and about 250 acceptances had been received, including the following ladies and gentlemen .—The Bishop of Ripon and Mrs, Boyd-Carpenter, 'Sir Edward and Lady Green, Colonel and the Misses Gunter, Sir James and Miss Kitson, Mr. and Mrs. Flemwell, Mr. and Mrs. Tinsley (the brother and sister-in-law of the bridegroom), Mr. James Tinsley (uncle of the bridegroom), Mr. J. J. Harrison, the Rev. Dr. and Mrs. Talbot (vicar of Leeds) Mr. and Mrs. Harry Greenall, Mr. E Beckett Faber, Sir George and Lady Morrison, Mr. aud Mrs. Arthur Lawson, Mr. and Mrs. Fred Law- son, Mr. and Mrs. Grosvenor Talbot, Mr. John Barran, M.P., and Mrs. Barren, Mrs. Gott, Mrs. and Mies Stansfeld, Mr. and Mrs. T. Marshall, Mr. and Miss Nelson, Mr. and Mrs. Arthur Greenwood, Mr. A. H. Meysey-Thompson, Mr. and Mrs. Carter, the Rev. N. Egerton Leigh, Mr. and Mrs. North. Mr. and Mrs. Bousefield, Mr. and Mrs. Reginald Wigram, Mr. and Miss Ryder, Mr. and Mrs. J. M. Sagar-Musgrave, the Rev. Canon and Mrs. Wood Major and Mrs. Walker, Mr. R. H. Braithwaite, and others. The church was crowded when the bride entered leaning on the arm of her father. She wore a dress of white satin, with a folded sash trimmed with old Irish guipure lace. The tulle veil was fastered with a diamond star, the gift of the mother of the bride, and she wore a small wreath of orange blossoms. The bride's ornaments, the gift of the bridegroom, were a diamond ring and a diamond brooch. She was attended by two train-bearers, Miss Dorothy O'Brien, her godchild, and Miss Olive Lawson, (laughter of Mr. A. T. Lawson. They wore white satin dresses with " smocked " bodices and pink sashes. The hats were large brown ones, trimmed with brown and pink feathers. The four sisters of the bride—Miss L. R. Jackson, Miss Annie Jackson, Miss E. Maud Jackson, and Miss Grace M. Jackson— were the bridesmaids. They wore white satin dresses made perfectly plain, with pink sashes and brown hats trimmed with pink and brown feathers. Toe bride- groom's gifts to the bridemaids consisted of pearl brooches, and the bride's gift to the bridegroom was a set of pearl studs.

At he commencement of the service the choir sang the well-known hymn, " The voice that breathed o'er Eden." The bride was given away by her father, the officiating clergy being the Bishop of Ripon, the Rev. Canon Dodd, of Stretton (formerly tutor of the bride- groom), and the Rev. J. P. Maude (of Chapel-Illerton.) The anthem was Wesley's setting of "Lead me Lord," and at the conclusion of the ceremony, as the wedding party was leaving the church, Dr. Creser, who presided at the organ, played the well-known" Wedding March." Later in the afternoon an " at home "was held at the house of the father of the bride, and subsequently the newly-married couple left for London.
, The wedding presents were extremely numerous and valuable.

CHESHIRE STANDING JOINT COMMITTEE. "NOTORIOUS RUNCORN."

Colonel C. H. France-Hayhurst presided at the quarterly meeting of this committee held at Chester Castle on Saturday. The chief constable s report showed that compared with 1886 (before the Ship Canal works were commenced), there had been an increase of 333 persons apprehended and of 532 per- - sons summoned, the former being caused mainly by cases of drunkenness, petty larceny, and sleep- ing out, while the latter increase was due to pro- ceedings under the Dog Muzzling Order and the Education and Highways Acts. Eight hundred and sixty males and 169 females had been proceeded against for drunkenness—an increase of 31 males and 25 females when compared with August quar- ter, 1890, and an increase of 221 males and 49 females when compared with the same period in 1886. Twenty-four licensed houses were proceeded against, 17 being convicted and seven dismissed,as against 33 proceeded against, 15 convicted, and 18 dismissed in August quarter 1890; and 19 proceeded agstilist, ten convicted, and nine dismissed in the corresponding quarter of 1886.

div.head: NON-PAYMBNT OF FINES.
div.p: NON-PAYMBNT OF FINES.

Mr. C. Lister (Lymm) asked what were the rules generally adopted with regard to imprisonment for non- payment of fines. The returns in the Chief Constable's report showed that on an average nearly a thousand people were sent to prison during the year for non- payment of fines.—The Chief Constable said they were generally of the labouring classes and tramps who were unable to pay fines.—Mr. Lister hoped the discretion as to sending them to prison rested with the magistrates and not the police.—The Chief Constable replied that it rested with the magistrates, only the police gave their opinion as to the ability of the persons to pay.—Mr. Lis- ter thought there ought to be instructions Oven throughout the county that bail should be accepted, ex- cept in cases where there would be no chance of the prisoners appearing after their liberation. It was the dictum of the judges and everybody that bail should be taken wherever possible.—The Chief Constable said this was the practice throughout the county, and the present case was the exception which he hoped proved the rule.

div.head: INCREASE OF DRUNKENNESS
div.p: INCREASE OF DRUNKENNESS

Mr. M. T. Graveson (Liscard) commented upon the fact that drunkenness was increasing quarter by quarter, and that it was now 40 per cent. more prevalent than it was four or five years ago. "Notorious Runcorn" headed the list with 156 persons fined for drunkennese and with 138 licensed houses. Northwich came next. He was satisfied that if the police kept a better oversight in those localities where there was an excess of drunken- ness, in time the amour* would be reduced. Those per- sons in the trade, when they felt that they would be well looked after, would be more careful, and thus without persecution the crime would be reduced very much. He therefore moved "That we recommend the head con- stable to watch with increased diligence the causes which lead to a continuous increase of drunkenness, and exer- cise a more guarded oversight over those districts where drunkenness is in greatest excess." Mr. Howard seconded. Sir Hpratio Lloyd suggested that certaie words in the resolution implied censure of the police;4 and with the omission of the words " increased " dili- gence and " more " guarded oversight it would be just as efficacious, and would meet with his support. Mr. Smith endorsed this suggestion, which was at once accepted by Mr. Howard and eventually by Mr. Graveson. Mr. Speakman and Mr. Brdndrit resented Mr. Graveson's remarks about Runcorn, and attributed the statistics of drunkenness to the population from the Manchester Ship Canal. Mr. Earp opposed the 'notion. There were plenty of teetotal societies, but soon there would be drinking societies to protect drinkers from these repeated attacks. (Laughter.) Beer had been * national beverage ever since the country was a countrf —for breakfast, dinner and sapper there was beer and coffee was the invention of list century, and it NOS only in recent years thas people had taken to denoune' ing the best beverage of the lot. (Laughter.) They might just as well speak against razors because ree.,l sometimes cut their throats with them, and let tbey. beards grow till they would do to wipe their feet O. (Laughter.) Mr. Graveson said he did not object to drieig but to the infringement of the law by drunkennest4 The Rev. C. Wolley-Dod said he had very great plea Sure in seconding the amendment, on the ground that he oir jected on principle to eliciting information from drunkell persons, and acting upon that information without of proof. That was what was suggested. Dr. Hodgeo° said they had had an interesting disquisition on core' parison between razors and beer—(laughter)—and noir die equally interesting scene of the only clergyman el that committee getting up to defend the publicans ail': their trade. (Hear, htar.) He had usually noticed Om their friend the Rev. Woolley-Dod managed soment, or other always to get up to defend the drink traffic. 12n did not know how it was, but supposed he felt a specity interest in it, and felt morally compelled to do 50. (Laughter.) He warmly supported the motion. TM altered motion was then put—" That the Chief Coir 5r...we be recommended to watch the causes leading tO. the continued drunkenness, and to exercise a guardea oversight in those districts where convictions are in the greatest excess." In this form it was carried by a largo majority.

div.head: JOHN SMITH.
div.p: JOHN SMITH.

By the Liverpool packet, a double letter, folded and sealed in a way which led to the belief that money was enclosed, and addressed to Mrs. John Smith, was received at our post-office. It had not long been deposited in its proper box before a short, fat, smirking little woman made her appear- ance at the window, and, in a broad Irish accent, inquired, "Have you iver a letter for Mrs. Smith 7" _ .
"Yes, here is one for Mrs. Smith—Airs. Catharine Smith—is that your name, good woman ?" "No, that's not it—my name is Bridget." "Ah, here is one. Pray, what is your husband's name ?"

"Out on the vagabone, his name is John." The clerk was about to give the letter to the woman, but his experience had taught him that John Smiths were as plenty as blackberries; and he held it back, while he asked a tew more ques- tions. "And where did you expect a letter from, Mrs. Smith 7"

"Oh, from Cincinnati or New Orleans, or there- abouts. The villain John Smith (that I should say so!) promised to write me these two months, and not the bit scrape of his ugly pen have I seen at all at all."
"Bat this letter is from Liverpobl, my good wo- man, and of course is not for you."
. _ "Liverpool, did you say! Oh, the ruffian, has.he then deserted me entirely, and gone back to the euld country ? " "Supposing he has, you would probably expect to receive money from him."

"Is it money you mane? Sure then you have put your fut in it. The saddle is on the tother horse. It would be asking for money, not sending me any, that John Smith would be after. No, no, sharp's the eye that ever sees the colour of John's money more nor himself, and the man where he buys his whiskey." "I fear, if that is the case," said the clerk, "that I shall not be able to give you this letter. It appears to contain a large sum of money, and must be for some other person of your name." The woman went away grumbling and scolding, and vowing "it was all a chate," and threatening, if there was law in the land, she would have her letter. In about an hour after, a tall, sallow- looking man, whose straight black hair, keen eye and Indian gait, denote him as one of that portion of our countrymen who style themselves 'half- horse, half-alligator, and a little touch of the snap- ping turtle," walked up to the place of letter deliv- ery. "I say, stranger, I want a letter for John Smith." 'There is none addressed to that name," said the clerk; "but here is one for Mrs. John Smith." " Ah, that's me, or what's the same thing, it's my woman; so shell it out here in a little less than no time."
"Stay a moment, my friend; where did you expect a letter from?"

"Whar from!" exclaimed the Kentuckian in sur- prise. "Look here, stranger, I reckon you want to poke fun at me. Now let me tell you, I'm a pretty considerable sort of a chap—l'm a ring-tail roarer, all the way from Salt River. So, none of your cock- Idtical °averting about me, or I'll be into you like a streak of lightning." "I merely wish to know where you expect a letter from, to avoid mistakes, as there are so many John Smiths. This letter contains money." "That's why I want it. And so you're gwaing [going] to keep the letter for the, sake of the shiners. Maybe you think I ar'nt worth no money. I tell you what stranger, my old man's a heavy dog, and thinks no more of a hundred dollars (State Bank, you see, and not the rale specie) than you do of a hundred cents. Why should he? Ar'nt he a director, and what account is money to him ?"

"But this letter is from England. Your father is not an Englishman, is he 7" "Look here, stranger; if you mean to insult me, jist step out here, and I'll lick you within an inch of your life. Englishman! I reckon if you had seen me at Orleans, with old Hickory, you would'nt a' thought there was much English blood in me, though there war a pretty considerable smart chance of it on to me. And my wife's rale Kentuck' to the backbone, too; none of your half-and-half Yankee thrash. If the letter's from England, she should'nt touch it, if it contained ever such a powerful heap of money." And so saying, the stranger turned indignantly from the office, satisfied that a letter from IGngland could not be intended for him or his.

The next applicant for a letter for John Smith Was a small dapper gentleman, with hair of a reddish cast, light eyes, and sandy complexion. The bosom of his vest was traversed in every direction with strings of silk braid and safety chains, and his collar was rolled back with great precision, so as to display to the best advan- tage a curiously plaited bosom to his linen, and a set of gilt-mounted studs, with which it was adorned. His upper lip was shaded with some dozen or twenty hairs, which, as the weaver said of the threads of his carpet, were not as neighbourly as they should be; but they glistened with bear's grease, and had been forced with infinite pains from their bristling to a supine position, so that they presented quite a smart apology for mcustachios. Our beau was highly indignant that a postoffice clerk should dare to question him, or withhold a letter addressed "to his lady "—but said it was no more than might be looked for under a rascally Jackson administration—told him with impressive earnestness that he was a gentleman—threw his card down with the look of an angry Cesar—and uttered mighty threats in a very weak and effeminate voice, which was not without a certain quaver, that seemed to denote that the speaker was not altogether sure whether the intermediate wall afforded a pro- tection to his exquisite person. The clerk, however, receiving no satisfactory answers to his inquiries, was not intimidated into giving the dandy the letter, and the disappointed applicant walked off in a most unbecoming passion. A long blue-eyed, red-cheeked, raw-boned, awk- ward-looking man, from "down east," was the next to ask for the much-claimed letter for Mrs. John Smith; he was succeeded by a chubby negro woman, and a thickset, heavy-looking Dutchntan followed her. None of them, however, gave satis- factory answers to the questions which the careful clerk thought it his duty to ask, and were obliged to go away as they came. At last a small pretty woman' with high cheek bones, rosy complexion, dressed in a neat close habit, a gipsy hat, having altogether a John Bull air, came to the post-office window, and modestly asked if there was a letter by the Liverpool packet for Mrs. John Smith. Noticing that the clerk felt some little hesitation at giving it to her, she authorised him to break the seal, telling him what amount of money it would probably be found to contain, and one or two other facts, which would establish her claim beyond doubt. The contents of the letter proved her right to it, and, much to the joy of the clerk, the trouble- some epistle passed out of his custody.

TWENTY years ago there roamed over the plains and mountains of the Far West nearly eight million buffaloes. To-day there are less than five hundred and fifty head of the animals in existence. There are but eighty-five head of' wild buffaloes, three hundred and four alive in captivity, and about two hundred under the protection of the Government in Yellowstone Park.

_ _ CHARITY is greater than justice? Yes, it la greater; it is the summit of justice—it is the tem- ple of wPich justice is the foundation. But you cannot 'Wive the top without the bottom; you can- not build upon charity. You must build upon justice, for this reason, that you have not at first charity to build with. It is the last reward of good work. Do justice to your brother (you can do that whether you love him or not), and you will come tc love him..—Ruskin.
