SOUTH LANCASHIRE NEEDLEWORK GUILD.

Sir,—My attention having been drawn to a paragraph in the" Queen and otner papers that the Lanca,hire Needlework Guild was broken up, allow me to state through your valuable columns, that my division estab- lished in 1888 of the South Lancashire Branch of Lady Wolverton's Needlework guild, founded in 1882, is in full working urder, and our distribution of clothing takes place at the Town Hall, here on Nov. 7th.—l am yours faithfully,
JOSE F. BOYSE, president S.L.N.G. Newton-le-Willows, Lancashire, Oct. 18tb, 1891.
EARLESTOWN AMBULANCE AND MEDICAL AID SOCIETIES.

We have in Earlestown two Societies, the Ambulance, also the Medical and Surgical Aid, both doing good work. As kn interested resident, it occurs to me that there is a 1033 of power and usefulness, also a greater expense than necessary,Ly these societies working apart. It would be, I think, more economical to unite their forces and work together. As a suggestion : Would it not be advisable, before the Ambulance Society com- mence to build, to ask the opinion of the district as to the necessity of forming a society and erecting a building suitable for an Ambulance,Medical Aid Stcres, mortuary, etc., and engage a qualified nurse (female) who with her husband could live on the premises, and her setvices be available for the sick of the district.
Trusting that you may be able to insert this in your next issue and that it may attract some attentiont—l am yours truly
"UNION IS STRENGTH."
DRAWING OR RAFFLING AT BAZAARS.

Sir,—We ad know that the goods made and given for political, or any other bazaars, or sales of work, are mostly given for the good of some organisation, church, school, or Infirmary. It is certain, that many articles would not be disposed of for the amount thus realised except by having them drawn for, and some assuredly would not be sold, unless they were drawn for. There- fore by this means, larger sums of money are realised for this kind of objects. This method of raising money from time to time is resorted to in almost every school of every religious creed or body, and is patronised by a very large number, if not the greatest number, of mem- bers of the Christian churches of the day, who attend and support bazaars, &c. The disinterested labours, and winning manners, of those engaged in such enterprises have never failed to commend themselves and their worthy objects to my heart and mind; and secure all the help it was in my power to render for any benevo- lent or worthy cause. Here is a person who has an article on her stall; she fears that unless it is disposed of by having it drawn for it will be left on her hands. It is more beautiful than useful. The poor cannot afford to buy it, and the rich don't appear to be inclined to do so. Therefore, to obtain the sale of the article and its value, not in order to further her own selfish ends, but the reverse of this—the love of some cause, far-reaching, or touchingly human ends, she, or say,:her sister or brother as the case may be, have spent hours yea days in patiently toiling at the article in order to obtain funds. She now takes the article in hand, goes about the room from person to person, in such a winning way ; her face wreadied with hopeful smiles, an index of her labour of love which no one fails to see and be impressed by. Up to this point not even the remotest motive of any- thing but love for the cause she so willingly and cheer- fully toils for, has caused either of you to take steps in the matter. At least, I most frankly confess, such was my own case, and I doubt not but that many others thus joined in the drawing. The love of gain was ab- sent from the motives and and actions of the seller and purchaser, while love for the cause was the central force of action. This being so, it differs widely from what I have always taken to be what constitutes "gambling," which takes its rise from an inner longing to over-mas- ter a competitor, and secure his rival's money or goods with whom one tests his skill, or strength as in card- playing, wrestling, &c. for stakes. Dr. Martineau soundly puts the matter thus—" The moment the simple excite- ment of competition of skill becomes insufficient without the money stakes, the taint of moral character, the con- tended gain at other's expense, has set in; and that the stake is 2d. instead of £2O makes no more moral differ- ence than there is between a theft of 2d. and a theft of £2O. The mischief, of course,increases enormously with high play. But the immorality does not wait to begin with the larger amount." In such as this love of gain is at the root, regardless of the loss inflicted on an antagonist. Notwithstanding the wide difference between yielding to the disinterested pleadings of those who labour from love at religious, humane, or political bazaars, for the welfare of such worthy objects, and the purely gambling object of the orginatorsi sellers, and buyers of such as race-horse tickets, and all those who play at any game for stakes—whose love of game is clearly the ruling force in the games, I would ask is it not wisest, and best to forego our liberty in assisting any Rind of humane, religious, or poli- tical ends, by ceasing to countenance drawings, rather than continue them, and thereby cause the ardent and thoughtless gambler to imagine that his selfish habits are no worse or more degrading than are the habits of any of those whom we think,we have shown, act mostly from love to others in yielding to buy tickets for goods not likely to be sold.

To some persons it may be hard, even painful, to thus give up their personal liberty in such matters for ex- ample's sake. But a little calmer and deeper reflection will, I trust, by the help of God, lead many others as well as the writer, from this time henceforth never to yield to auyone to c9uutenance drawings. This kind of

thing has obtained up to the preser: . amongst our own people, the Wesleyan Methodists. Mts., .01 this town, and also with others. We have though, ostly of the good aimed at, and too little of the that might arise therefrom, evil by countenancing .draw„ 1.4-----called by the Editor of this newspaper " Rail i t concure with you, sir, in seek- ingn., to put an ow to Stlth matters. The moral gain will by far outweigh in the long run all monetary loss. May that nobleness of mind operate which ;in many instances lead persons to give up their personal liberty in the use of the pipe and the pot„ and which led Paul out of pure love to others wisely to affirm "Wherefore, if meat make my brother to offend, I will eat no flesh while the world standeth, lest I make my brother to offend." (I Cot. Bc. 13v.)—Yours sincerely, DUTY.

Oct. 14th, 1891. P.S.—I could have wished that a plea for this matter had fallen into abler hands. But finding that my taking part in drawings has offended a number of our Methodist people, who never before complained about this kind of thing in our schoolrooms, &c., I feel that, with your kind permission, this expression of the rea- sons actuating me hitherto, and this sincere appeal to others, would help to clear the matter up, and, I hops do good.
MR. PEERS AS METAPHYSICIAN AND BIBLI- CAL CRITIC.

Sir,—ln reply to Mr. Peers I must say that no amour t of argument will convince me that an ignorant man is entitled to a position higher than or even equal to that ef one who is in the possession of knowledge. An ignorant man is an ignoramus, and is entitled to no respect what- ever until such time as he obtains knowledge, no matter whether he terms his ignorant " agoosticisal " or not. Still further am I at issue with him in his disastious attempt to shift the point in discussion. " Let us first settle the point at issue," says Mr. Peers, " that is the logical position of prayer." Now, the quest.ion at issue is not the logical position of prayer, but the legical position of the laws of nature, or what I prefer to term the scientific aspect of the laws of nature. This is the question which he raised in his former letter when he reflected on the serious consequences which would ensue if the" linked concatenation of nature's laws "were rudely broken in answer to prayer. This was the point which I answered, and in illustration of it I referred to the laws of gravitation and chemistry. If these do not represent the " linked concatenation of nature's laws," It would like to know what laws do so. And, in answer- ing this question, I would remind Mr. Peers that, in order to do so, he must become a gnostic, that is, as translated by himself, a "knowing one .;" not an agnos- tic, that is, an ignorant one. lea question of this kind Mr. Peers will find that ignorance or agnosticism will prove of little consequence. My efforts to discuss the question on purely scientific grounds Mr. Peers characterizes as " mazes of meta- physical divergencies." Now let us consider the position which Mr. Peers takes up, and which he puts forward as the stronghold of his argument. He says "surely if Infinite wisdom has decided that such a course or con- dition of things is best, the selfish pleadings of us poor mortals can but be regarded as an impious and i nper- tineut interference with His decrees:" But, in order to know the responsibilities which Infinite wisdcm im- poses on poor mortals, man, on the other hand, must know something of Infinite wisdom. This knowledge is still further involved in the differentiation which Mr. Peers draws between Infinite wisdom and the popular view of God as " fickle, inconstant, wavering, and for- getful." This at once raises the question ;—how can the finite mind of man know the Infinite? And in rais- ing this question Mr. Peers plunges into the deepest depths et metaphysics. It is also to be noted that Mr. Peers says nothing at present regarding the "linked concatenation of nature's laws ;" but raises the question as to the nature of prayer in the New Testament, and even heads his letter with a quotation from Matthew's Gospel. In order to answer this question with any satisfaction, one must be an authority on Biblical criticism. Such an authority I do not pretend to be, any more than a metaphysician. It is truly astonishing, however, to find Mr. Peers ignore the scientific aspect of the question, and betake himself to the" mazes" of metaphysics and Biblical criticism, where I cannot follow him. Such extraordinary conduct shows how readily Mr. Peers can become all things to all men—Biblical critic, metaphysician, even eschew science—provided he can deal an opponent a hard blow. Nor is the frankness with which he avows it less remark- able. He will "cross swords" with me after discussing the logical nature of prayer. But the very question which he raised was regarding the" linked concatena- tion of nature's laws.' This phrase was coined by him- self; it is the offspring of his own brain, which, scarcely a week old, he has left, like an unfortunate bantling, to look after itself, reminding one of the Hindoo leaving his helpless parent on the banks of the Ganges, there to be exposed to the tender mercies of the elements or to be swept away by the innundation of the river. Mr. Peers wishes to find a single instance of answer to prayer. Instead of doing that, I will produce an in- stance which more particularly illustrates the case in hand, simply because the prayer was not answered. I take the great pleading scene which occurs in the "Mer- chant of Venice." On the one side there is Portia, pleading earnestly for mercy; on the other, there is old Shylock-, the Jew, obdurate, relentless, and merciless, still exacting his pound of flesh to the uttermost. Now, the very questions which Mr. Peers puts in regard to Infinite wisdom might equally well be put in regard to this scene. Why does Portia pray for mercy when she knows that Shylock will not relent ' • and when he has actually told her he will not relent? The same ques- tions apply much more forcibly to Shakespeare himself. Why does he put this prayer for mercy in the mouth of Portia when he knows perfectly well that the old Jew will not relent ? Why does he not get Portia to " tap old Shylock on the shoulder" to remind him of some- thing else? Such questions would go a long way to prove that Shakespeare was not merely "fickle, incon- stant, wavering," but that he was a consummate fool, and his work a huge burlesque. Mr. Peers raises an objection to prayer which is rather peculiar, and shows what worthless arguments one makes use of at times when committed to a foregone conclusion. Should an alteration of weather take place in answer to prayer, "it would necessitate a corresponding alteration in the weather of the continent and consequently of the whole world." Now, such alterations d 3 take place when English pioneers settle down in India and cultivate enormous swampy districts and jungles into fertile fields and pasture grounds. And if Mr. Peers's argument is of any worth, such alterations will " necessitate a corresponding alteration" in the weather of the conti- nent of India and consequently of the whole world. Would Mr. Peers, in consequence of these alterations, place a veto on these improvements ? Such a step would show not merely the " parochial-minded " man, but a man centuries behind the age. In conclusion, I must say I think it is rather unfortu- nate that Mr. Peers should so completely ignore the scientific aspect of the question under discussion' and betake himself to the "mazes" of metaphysics and Bib- lical criticism. In such a retreat, however' he can un- doubtedly do good, and it is to be hoped that he will shine either as a metaphysician or as a Bible critic.— Yours, &c., GNOSTIC. October 19th, 1891.

div.head: LIFE INSURANCE: ITS USE AND ABUSE.
div.p: LIFE INSURANCE: ITS USE AND ABUSE.

bitterly learned the cost of disputing,and so on the large funds permitting them to settle without demur,they are willing dupes to contracts that bring in large premium incomes for the time being, and are of too prolific a source upon which to draw for agents to give them up. Old folks are entered for large premiums, otherwise the sum assured is small. These large premiums build up collecting books quickly, which means large new business fees, often from 10 to 26 first weeks; a large bonus or pocket money every quarter, and large commission, from 17 to 25 per cent., on collections. An uncle, &c., entered for one shilling premium means a week's wages along with commission, &c. Of course, ho will not be content until every uncle and aunt belonging to the household is put on his boak. These two people may have between them from 5 to 20 uncles and aunts, and these are sought out with diligence so long as the income of the householder permits. If a man of some means, every encouragement is held out to speculate on lives where little will be lost, and nearly all is gain at death. In these kind of cases there is aburdance of business to be done, and it is done. Thus mean prac- tises, forgery, deceit, and falsehood, are in our midst to an alarming extent. " s. d. "seems lobe everything; morality is nothing. I cannot denounce in too strong terms the persons who are connected with any contract having for its object and purpose the making of money upon persons in whom they have no assurable interest, and who gamble and traffic in human blood in order to reap where they have no right to gather—where at the death they sustain no loss. The slave trader, who openly barters foe flesh and blood is no worse than the secret traders in white slaves, who are willing dupes, for small considerations.

It is astonishing that so many persons are obtaining a livelihood simply by conspiracy and stratagem, and by the use of will forms (often forged as well as the pro- posals themselves) assignments, and nominations. They are simply cooked ad made palatable for use at the chief offices to ensure payments being made. When disease shall have accomplished its work on their victim, these very forms are instruments in the hands of officials and members—cover up false contracts—and make it easy to carry on this scandalous business. But if the next of kin were taught how to interfere—or interested persons knew their duty, to warn the 1 next of kin, these will forms, assignments, and nominations would fall to the ground, and be of none effect, in the great majority of cases. Ministers of religion would do well to find space in sermons, oppor- tunities in visitation among members,to check this evil of gambling in its worst form. The rising generation should be enlightened as to what is insurance—its uses and abuses. There may then arise some hope of elev- ation above the gambling propensities of the present age. To every householder I would say—enter only those members of your family who depend upon you for sup- port and whom it would be your bounden duty to pro- vide a decent burial—(the only proper use of life assur- ance.) Avoid payment of premium on lives where no assurable interest exists, that is on lives, outside your own immediate family. Beware of men who will assure everybody and anybody ; shun them as you would a viper, and have nothing to do with them. Beware of falsehood, deceit, and forgery. The cross is an emblem of purity ; do not allow others to deface any proposal form on your behalf. But have a genuine signature 9r your own mark. Beware of agents who will bribe and offer every promise not contained on their prospectus and offer to keep up your payments for the first five to twenty weeks. Beware of men who upon entering their cases immediately set to work to evade the law of the land by the use of will forms,assignments. nominations, &c. Endeavour to learn the use of insurance to every member of your family, and make adequate provision against the evil day of affliction and the days of old age. Prevent, as far as you can, any speculation on the lives of ether people, and so protect yourself and those honest paying membersagainst those who plot and scheme to rob and plunder the office in which you have cast your lot. _ _
"Truth is divine, and howsoe'er Her voice disturb the quiet air, He is a craven who for peace Shall bid that ringing voice to cease. I am yours faithfully,
JOHN MOORFIELD. 44, Parker-st., Warrington, October, 1891.

Sir,—Continuing this subject, I wish to say how much better it would be if people were taught how far they should go, and what limit was allowed to them to insure other people to keep within bounds of the law, and above all, the laws of morality and justice, instead of the one-sided: advice and instruction imparted by the vast army of agencies, who can be counted by the tens of thousands employed by the collecting Friendly Societies and companies. The reader may readily imagine, in what direction such agency advice is given when there is borne in mind the very extraordinary pressure em- ployed to force these agents to put in a certain amount of new cases every week, to press so many men and women and children's names on their books. Failing this, and little coming in, the agent must prepare to give up his agency. It does not require any strain or effort to de- monstrate that these men will act in such a manner and offer every facility to make it easy to rush in business, refraining as much as possible from putting obstacles in in the way, by warnings when they must stop. If the public were enlightened more fully upon the fallacies of own life policies upon lives paid upon by another person from the commencement of policy, and only one narne appears on the policy, making a false contract, the vast numbers thus issued would be sent back to the offices which issued them. These very cases, if they had been entered on the proper forms, intended by aw (viz, proposal forms—one on the life of another) to show who was the proposer, and what was the object of the assurance, would have been rejected wholesale by every respectable office. It is a fact that own life poll- ees on uncles and aunts, brothers and sisters, cousins and distant relatives, are not allowed, and cannot La legally passed by any Life Insurance Company or Society under the sun if such policy has only one name, and that person has not entered into the contract or paid the pl miums or signed the proposal. It is shameful to observe the fact that thousands and thousands of invalid own life policies are in existence. But the own life proposal form is a most convenien form for the agents, superintendents, and head offices ,t for with a little" wink "and" Ignorance is bliss "system the thing is done hourly, weekly, and yearly, and it means money and promotion to officials and a grand array of new business at. headquarters at " Reckoning day" when all meet to rejoice over results, not to men- tion quality, so long as every district pays its way, with a few hundreds of pounds as a surplus. The extent to which this uncle and aunt, &c., business is carried is surely alarming, and more trouble, worry, and vexatious law suit 6 are attributable to these Lind of cases than any other. At last the water echtinetfnr Frodsham, suggested by Mr. Timmins, of Runcorn, has been adopted by the Sanitary Authority. Mr. Edwards carried his opposition to the bitter end, but as he had nothing better to propose than the Frodsham Committee recommended, be was entirely alone when the vote was taken. Speaking under the smart of his de- feat, Mr. Edwards declared that he would not attend at Dutton Workhouse again, but I hope on calmer reflection that he will see the folly of this course. Better to have fought and lost in a cause that one considers just, than not to have fought at all.

The discussion that has taken place will do good. It has shown many of the farming community how unjust is what is termed the incidence of taxation, and if they will study the subject closely, the com- munity will benefit if they have the courage of their opinions. At the meeting, on Tuesday, Mr. Stokes urged that the provision of a water supply was a landlords' question, and all present appeared to heartily agree with him, but as the law stands the occupier has to bear this burden and many others which of right belong to the landlord. But what can be expected when the law has been made for so many centuries by the landlords for the land- lords. I suppose, however, that the farmers will go on voting for the land-owning class as usual.

The Liberal demonstration on Tuesday, was a complete and most gratifying success. It was a happy idea on the part of Mr. Ockleston,the popular and respected Chairman of the Club to open the pro- ceedings with a reception and there was only one drawback to the pleasure of the large number who partook of his hospitality. That was that the host was not in his usual health, and it was the general wish that he may soon be completely restored. Mr. Brunner, accompanied by his wife, was present looking as jovial and genial as ever, and he took full advantage of the opportunity offered to have a chat with a few of his numerous supporters, on various matters of mutual interest. The hour and a half spent in the Club was most pleasant and profitable.

Then came the public meeting which Mr. Ockleston was not allowed to attend by the orders of his medical adviser, a fact univer- sally regretted, and his place as chairman was ably filled by Mr. Alfred Norman who takes an active interest in our local political organisations. The speeches wore bright and interesting and the applause at the sentiments expressed was spontane- ous and hearty. Alluding to local matters Mr. Brunner gave our Free Library a powerful adver- tisement, and it is to be hoped that his appeal for subscribers, of however small an amount,so that the usefulness of the institution may be extended, will have a response from those who can afford out of their abundance to give a little over what they con- tribute through the penny rate. At present the Committee have to cut their coat according to the cloth, and vary careful management is needed to carry on the Library and reading room as efficiently as it is at the present time. The only one subscri- ber at the present time is Mr. Brunner, who annu- ally contributes £5.

To a well known and skilful Runcorn pilot be- longs the honour of haviiig steered the first foreign vessel up the Ship Canal. Last week the Norwegian steamer Hertha, 319 tons register carrying over 500 tons of flints, arrived in the Mersey consigned to Messrs. J. F. Walsh and Co. Captain Harry Hill, of Runcorn, was engaged to pilot her up the river and through the canal to Ellesmere Port, and he suc- cessfully performed his task. The master of the vessel is Captain Nygaard, of Bergen.

Failing to prevail upon Mr. Charles Rey- nolds J.P., to contest the Frodsham County Coun- cil Division against Mr. Slater Lewis, the Tory party have sought a candidate from amongst their own party and it is now announced that Dr. Weaver, of Frodsham,will enter the lists. He is the son-in- law of the late Mr. E. Abbot, Wright.of Castle Park. It seems likely that Mr. Lewis will remain C.C. for Frodsh am.

Mr. F. H. Gossage.J.P.,Chairman of Widnes Local Board, has applied for a patent for use in the mak- ing of boots and shoes. Mr. W. T. Husband, the cloputy coroner, and Mr. Gibbings have applied for a patent for a regulating tap for liquids or gases. The latter patent has been sold to the Widnes In- ventions Syndicate, Limited.

The new Victoria-road now wears quite a finished appearance at the Greenway-road end, and when the whole length is completed it will be the finest roadway in the town. The Ship Canal Company have accomplished their part of the agreement, and the viaduct they have constructed across is a monument of solidity and good workmanship and must have cos", the Company a very large sum of money in material alone. If the granolithic pave- ment, of which the footpath is to he constructed, and is now partially laid, is as durable as it is claimed to be, the Commissioners have done a good thing in introducing it because of its immense advantage over tiles both in appearance and comfort in walk- ing.

I am glad to announce that the University Exten- sion Lectures have not succumbed to the" Runcorn disease "—apathy and indifference. We are to have a course of lectures from the Rev. W. Hudson Shaw, M.A., that prince of extension lecturers, who will, in his own graphic, cultured, and convincing style, give us a sketch of the history of Florence.
HEARTLESS CONDUCT AT ST. HELENS.
"DYING LIKE A DOG."

On Tuesday, Mr. S. Brighouse held an inquest at St. Helens Town Hall, touching the death of Bridget 111‘Manus, 48 years of age, wife of Andrew M‘Manus, labourer, 12, Bold-st., who was found dead on Sun- day morning. From the evidence given by the husband, and a married daughter named Ellen Smith, it appeared that the deceased had been addicted to drink, the husband's statement being that "she was never sober." On Saturday night she was intoxicated, and was noticed to be bleeding from the body. She was removed upstairs, and was placed at the foot of a bed, in which her husband who had been unwell for some time, was lying. She was supplied with a drink of water, but she continued to bleed profusely. The married daugh- ter left her, and no other attention was paid to her. The husband fell asleep, and next morning he found his wife lying deal in a pool of blood in a corner of the room.—Police Inspector Goodall stated thac he was cal'ed in about noon, and at that time the woman was lying in a corner near the bed. The room floor was covered with blood, as well as the stairs and the floor of the kitchen downstairs. He could not find any marks of violence about the pody, and Dr. Al‘Nicoll attributed the death to natural causes. The people in the house told him (Inspector Goodall) that the body had remained in the same position as when it was found in tho morning. Dr. Challenor, assistant to Dr. M`Nicoll, who had seen the body, had informed him that if medi- cal aid had been called in the bleeding would most likely have been stopped, and the woman's life saved. Dr. Challenor examined the body, and he could not find any marks of violence.

The Coroner, in summing up the evidence, remarked that neither he nor the police had any suspicion of foul play, but they thought it was a case for inquiry, inas- much as both the husband and the daughter knew the woman was bleeding, but did nothing except put her across the bed. To him it seemed a very cruel thing. The jury retired, and, on their return, the Foreman said they had found a verdict of "Death from natural causes.' They thought the father and daughter ought to be censured for their neglect, and further, that in future cases of a similar kind medical evidence ought to be called.

The Coroner said he was much obliged to them for their recommendation, but that in reference to medical evidence that was not within their jurisdiction. 'rhat was a question for him, and if they would decide on that case alone he should decide on what medical evidence ought to be called in future. In that particular case he had told the jury before they retired that if they required medical evidence he should be glad to adjourn. He did not want any misapprehension or misunderstand- ing. If they had wanted medical testimony he could adjourn and order a post mortem examination.— A Juror: We thought that as there is a medical officer of health for the borough he ought to be called in. He is paid for it, and Nye think the police ought to have power to call upon him.—The Coroner said that under the present condition of things the medical officer would want his fee if he was called, and he could not have given them any more information than that they had received from the inspector. The husband and the daughter were then called. The Coroner strongly censured them, and asked the husband what he would think if he was neglected in such a manner as his wife had been. He must have known by the bleeding that there was some- thing wrong, and he must consider himself well off that he had not been committed for trial in connection with her death. He had no right at all to let his wife lie as he had done. In regard to the daughter, he (the coroner) considered she was very much to blame. She was a married woman, and must have known it was extremely dangerous to leave her mother bleeding as she was. She ought to have sent for a doctor, and not have allowed j her to die like a dog.

div.head: PEN R ETII.
div.p: PEN R ETII.
SCHOLARSHIP.
We are pleased to learn that Miss Mainley, of the Penketh Wesleyan Day School, hag gained a first class scholarship at the July Examination, South- lands College.

div.head: PENKETH WESLEYAN CHAPEL,
div.p: PENKETH WESLEYAN CHAPEL,
RE-OPENINO SLUICES.

For several years past it has been found that the Wesleyan Chapel, at Penketh, was too small for the requirements of the neighbourhood. About two years ago a meeting was held, and the matter dis- cussed, but, owing to the existence of certain diffi- culties, _nothing could be done. At the beginning of the present year, however, the need for some altera- tion had become so urgent that immediate action be- came necessary. In February last a meeting of the con- gregation and other persons interested in the matter was held in the schoolroom. There it was decided to enlarge and beautify the chapel, at a cost of about £1,200. Promises were given in on the same night which covered about £BOO of the sum required. A building committee was formed, plans, &c., got out and approved, and the work was eventually let to Mr. R. W. Collin. During the past four months the work has been steadily pro- gressing, and its successful completion and re-opening was witnessed on Sunday. The alterations executed have provided accommodation for seating about 100 persons. The front of the chapel has been taken down and built out up to the roadside. At the back new ves- tries have been made on each side of the main building, and the old vestry has been rebuilt, and the organ and choir placed therein. It was at first proposed to build transepts out on each side of the chapel in front of the vestries, but, owing to difficulties about the land,and the inability to raise the money required, this part of the scheme had to be abandoned. On the north side of the ' chapel a vestry and lavatory have been fitted up for the preacher's use, and on the south side a larger vestry capable of seating 50 to 60 persons has been built and furnished. It is proposed to hold classes and various meetings incidental to the chapel in this-, room. The pulpit has been removed from the old position at the north side of the chapel, and placed in the centre with the communion table in front ot it. Where the pulpit and organ formerly were, pews have been put, which will scat 24 persons. At the front of the chapel a gallery has been erected which will accommodate 60 people. At the front an additioaal line or pews has been made all across the chapel. Under the gallery a vestibule with a coil of pipes for heating purposes has been made. This can be used as a waiting room for late corners, and in case of necessity could be utilized for other purposes. The pulpit, communion, vestries, &c., are being furnished in red, and it is requested that pew owners who intend putting down new carpets and cushions should Pave them of such a colour as will harmonise with the surroundings in the chapel. The stained glass window in the front of the chapel had been placed in its old position again and a stained glass window, circular in form has been put in over the organ at the back. The heating arrangements for the chapel have been carried out on a more improved plan. The chapel is now lighted with gas, which is a great improvement on the lamps formerly used. The work of beautifying, &c., has been deferred till next year. Now it is finished, the building presents a very pleasant and comfortable appearance, and it is hoped the improvements effected will commend themselves to everyone. The first of a series of re-opening services was held in the Wesleyan Chapel, yesterday afternoon, and was largely attended. The preacher was the Rev. F. L. Wiseman, 8.A., from the Birmingham Central Mis- sion, and took for his text Galatians v., 22-23., " But the fruit of the Spirit is love, joy, peace, long-suffer- ing, gentleness, goodness, faith, meekness, temperance." The sermon was one of more than usual ability and originality. The rev, gentleman attacked the philoso- phy of Alexander Bain and others which supposed, he said, that freedom was to follow the desires of the flesh. To be led captive by these impulses was not freedom, but to destroy our menhood and to reduce us to machines. The preacher believed that there could be no real morality apart from the spirit of God. The morality of the pre-Christian philosophers was not equal to that of the gospels. As to that manifested in ancient times, by Plato, for instance, there was no proof that it was not due to Divine guidance. The law of heredity was often cited as an argument that man could not help his character being what it was, as he was a compound of the characteristics of his ancestors. Now,it was said many men showed good fruit who rejected Christianit,y,but the law of heredity applied here,for they had got 2,000 years of Christianity behind them in their ancesters,and their morality was the result of this. The rev, gentleman congratulated the congregation on the alterations in the chapel, which he considered great im- provments, and presumed that they were not made for mere excitement or artistic effect. What the Christian churches had more and more to do was to make charac- ter, and it was, he hoped, what that chapel was being re-opened for. Tea was partaken of,after the service,in the schoolroom. To-morrow (Sundae) the services will be continued, the Rev. C. T. Newton being the preacher. After tea there was another service. We bold over our report under pressure on oar space.

The death is announced of Admiral the Hon. George Disney Keane, C. 11., of Mere Hall, Knutsford. Such enormous damage has been caused in parts of Portugal by the renewed storms and floods that many landowners ore completely ruined.

div.head: IN THE COMMONS.
div.p: IN THE COMMONS.

The Right Hon. Arthur James Balfour, who has succeeded the late Mr. W. H. Smith in the leader- ship of the House of Commons, is, it is pretty well known, a nephew of Lord Salisbury, his mother be- ing a sister of the Premier. Ile was born in 1848, and was educated at Eton and Trinity College,Cam- bridge. He entered Parliament in 1874 as M.P. for Hertford, and this constituency he continued to represent until 1885, when he was elected for East Manchester for which he still sits. By his work entitled "A Defence of Philosophic Doubt," Mr. Balfour gave promise of abilities which could hardly have failed to win recognition by the Con- servative party, even had he not been connected by family ties with Lord Salisbury. He acted as priv- ate secretary to his uncle at the Foreign Office dur- ing the critical period 1878-80, when the Berlin Treaty was negotiated. In the early portion of his parliamentary career, he acted fora time with the "Fourth Party," but did not come into pro- minent notice until 1885,when he became president of the Local Government Board in Inrd Salisbury's first administration, and on the return of his Lordship to power in 1886. after serving for a short time as secretary for Scotland, was appointed chief secretary to the Lord Lieutenant of Ireland. Mr. Balfour introduced the Crimes—alias Coercion —Act of 1886, and after its adoption he set himself very energetically to the work of its provisions. His reputation as a Parliamentary debater rose considerably during the animated debates which preceded and followed the enactment of that mea‘ure. lie was elected Lord Rector of the Uni- versity of St. Andrews, and is also an hon. L.L.D..of Edinburgh and of Cambridge. The hon. gentleman has long since been known for his interest in golf, and on this subject he has written for the Badmin- ton series of books on British Sports. It is not so well known that he has written able cyelopcedic articles on musical subjects. Mr. Balfour's pro- motion to the position of Conseiwative leader of the House of Commons has been cordially approved by Conservatives, who anticipate great things from him. As a Liberal organ has very well put it, " he possesses a larger share of the necessary qualities than anybody else on the Treasury benches. He can combine a conciliatory manner with a firm grasp of control. He can preserve an even temper under the stimulus of a supreme responsibility. That acridness towards the Irish members which characterised him in his first years of the Chief Secretaryship has passed away. He went to the Irish Office with the spirit of acombat- ant, and di 3med it incumbent upon him to return as hard blows as he received. But experience has had a beneficial effect upon him. During the passage of the Land Purchase Act his tone and temper were admirable, and he discovered that more could be achieved in this may than by the tactics of the belligerent. An indispensahlequality in a leader of the House is courtesy under all [ circumstances. Mr. Smith possessed it to an unusual extent, and won an amount of esteem such as was due and given to Sir Stafford Northcote and Sir Michael Hicks-Beach. Mr. Balfour has a great opportunity afforded to him, and all parties will watch with interest the manner in which he utilises it."

div.head: MR. BALFOUR IN MANCHESTER.
div.p: MR. BALFOUR IN MANCHESTER.

Mr.A.J.Balfour spoke at Manchester,on Wednesday, in defence of the Free Education Act,saying that over by far the largest area of England the Act would be of enorm- ous assistance to the voluntary and denominational achoal._ where the measure bore hardly upon church schools churchmen, ho thought would not be behind- hand in meeting any eentan.A-tnat nugut occur- in

consequence of the operation of the Act. Mr. Balfour attended the Convocation dinner of the Victoria University in Manchester on Wednesday night, and, replying to the toast of his health, said it was practically a new phenomenon that science and industry should be brought so closely together as they were now. It was perfectly impossible-for any nation to keep in the van of industrial progress if it ignored the teaching of theoretical science, and theoretical science could not advance without learning much from practical men of business. He trusted that in that University they would do their best to make every theoretical advance subserve its corresponding purpose for the ordinary wants of man, and for the encouragement of our great industries.

On Thursday Mr. Balfour. accompanied by Messrs. G. Wyrdham, M.P., J. W. Maclure, M.P., and Alderman Chesters-Thompson, with whom he is staying, visited several important works in his constituency in East Manchester. At Messrs. Moseley's a number of em- ployes offered Mr. Balfour congratulations on his recent appointment.

div.head: RIOUNG AT EASTBOURNE.
div.p: RIOUNG AT EASTBOURNE.

Serious rioting took place at Eastbourne on Wednes- day night. The Salvationists marched out as usual with their band. Several thousand people assembled, and accompanied them on the march to their headquarters. The Salvationists were hustled, their instruments smashed, and several free fights occurred, many people being knocked down and hurt. The crowd afterwards smashed the windows of the barracks.

div.head: HALTON COURT LEET.
div.p: HALTON COURT LEET.

The annual Court leet for the Manor and fee of Halton took place in the Court-room of Halton Castle Hotel, on Saturday afternoon. Mr. Robert Davies, of Warrington, the High Steward, opened the Court in the ancient fashion. There were pre- sent Messrs. Thomas Wright, William Stokes, Joseph Astbury, Harry Whitlow, Joseph Pritchard, Hugh Rowe, John Davies, Joseph Acton, John Clayton, Beswick, William Weir, Joseph Whitfield, Sydney E. Stokes, T, Lowe, George Turley, and the Rev. G. D. Wray. Mr. Thomas Wright was elected foreman of the jury, and took the usual oath, and then the jury were sworn in. The jury having no presentment to make, Messrs. J. Astbury and W. Nickson were elected constables and burleymen. Mr. Davies then gave an historical sketch of the Court, which we hold over until our next issue.

After the Court had been closed, those present sat down to dinner, served by the landlady of the hotel. The High Steward occupied the chair, and the Foreman the vice-chair. On the removal of the cloth, the high Steward proposed the health of the Queen, as Lady Paramount of the Manor; and afterwards the Prince of Wales, and the rest of the Royal Family. Both toasts were duly honoured. He then submitted the toast of the Bishop and Clergy, and Ministers of all denominations of the Diocese. In reply, the Rev. G. D. Wray expressed the pleasure he derived from attending the court as chaplain. The vice-chairman then proposed the health of the High Steward in complimentary terms, and the toast was drunk with musical honours. The High Steward in response,dilated upon the antiquity of the court and the opportunity it now afforded for social intercourse amongst those who perhaps sel- dom met, and he said the court should be continued as long as he lived, and whoever happened to be steward after him he hoped would uphold the in- stitution.—Mr. Pritchard then proposed the health of the Foreman, and the Vice Chairman, ieplying to tho toast, which was drunk with musi- cal honours, said it afforded him much pleasure to do what he could for the court. In the course of the proceedings Mr. Turley sang "The British Lion, in capital style, and Mr. W. Stokes sang an Irish air appropriately. The proceedings concluded with the singing of the National Anthem.

A Manchester organist, named Charles Nicholson Darlington Pickett, was on Wednesday bound over at the Old Bailey in £5OO to appear when called upon to answer to a charge of threatening to murder Miss Mac Intvre, the well-known vocalist. John Johnson, a Lichfield baker, attempted to murder his wife at Walsall, on Wednesday, by cutting her throat. The woman is in a critical condition.
Lord Bute, it is announced, intends to present a gold cup, of the value of £2,000, to the Cardiff Corporation on the termination of his year's Mayoralty.

div.head: ST. HELENS CHEMICAL WORKERS.
div.p: ST. HELENS CHEMICAL WORKERS.

A meeting of chemical ard copper workers was held in the Town Hall, on Sunday afternoon. There was a large attendance, and Mr. J. P. King, presi- sit-Ent of the Chemical and Copper Workers' Union, who pres'ded, was supp 3. ,d by Mr. G. Moon, Mr. J. Smit ), Mr. J. Mather, &c.—Tne Chairman stated that they were met for ti e purpose of spreading Trade Union principles among the working-men of S. Helens. Referring to the question of technical education, he said he understood that a sum of £1,200 was available in St. Helens, and he wanted to know if it was being expended for the benefit of the working- classes. He asserted that it was not, and instanced the high charges for the chemistry classes. He said the ex- cessive fees debarred the workers from attending the classes, and the fees had been fixed so high because the committee—employers of labour—were afraid of their workmen learning the details of their occupations, such as the cost and composition of the raw materials. They were afraid of the workers demanding a fair share of the wealth and profits they created. For every pound pro- duced by the workmen 15s. went to the capitalist and the professional men. That was not a fair division,and an improvement rested with the working-classes them- selves. It was for the workmen of the country to bind themselves together firmly,and stand shoulder to shoulder until they obtained their rights. (Applause.) No other addresses were given, but a Meeting of the committee of the Union followed.

IMPENDING ELECTIONS. The Speaker notifies in last night's " Gazette " that it is his intention six days hence to issue his warrant for the election of members for the South Moulton Division of Devonshire, and the City of Cork, Mr. Martin Flavin Butler, Manchester, has cnsented to stand as Anti-Par- nellite candidate for Cork against Mr. John Redmond. The polling for the Strand takes place on Tuesday next, and the result will be declared the same evening. THE FLOODS.—A PILE DAM BURST IN SOMER. SETSHIRE. A pile darn in course of construction in front of the gap in t:le Aller Moor embankment of the river Parrett. in Somersetshire, was carried away yesterday and a tremendous quantity of water is now pouring through the gap spreading destruction far and wide. TERRIBLE TRAGEDY AT CHESTER. MURDER AND SUICIDE. The citizens of Chester were startled at an early hour yesterday morning by the news of a horrible murder and suicide. About half-past five o'clock John James Jugger murdered Harriet Butterwarth, a woman with whom he lived, by stabbing her under the left ear. He then jumped through the bedroom window and hanged him- self to a post in the back yard. Jugger was formerly a keeper at the Cheshire County Asylum at Upton-by- Chester, but latterly he had followed the employment of a stevedore. He was between forty and fifty years of age, and unmarried. Mrs. Butterworth,who was about 45, hal been a widow for a couple of years, and kept a lodging-house at 28, Leadworks-lane. For more than a year Jugger had cohabited with Mrs. Butterworth. 'The suicide's body was removed to the mortuary. The mur- dered woman's corpse lies at the house in charge of the eldest daughter. There are no signs of drinking in the house, and no motive for the crime can yet be assigned.

COLLIERY ACCIDENTS AT HAYDOCK. Yesterday week a singular accident occurred at the Haydock collieries, belonging to Messrs. Richard Evans and Co., Limited. The company are sinking a new shaft known as the "Princess," tome few hundred yards from the King pit, where in June last fovr men were killed by the upsetting of a hoppet. This new shaft had been sunk to a depth of 300 yards, and had passed the mouth of the Queen pit some thirty yards. About eight o'clock on Friday morning some twelve men were engrged in excavating, and had just filled one of the hop- pets with dirt and rock. The hoppet was drawn up from the men, and at the top a tran s ,00d ready ;o take it off. By some singular mi ',hap the dashing over the headgear, fell with a loud crash upon the pfatrorm which pardy covered the mouth of the shaft. It is stated by some of the men that a quantity of the rock fell among the twelve men below,but the manager of the colliery stated that this was not the case. As soon as possible one of the under managers went by way of the Queen pit and shouted down to the men. He found them in a terribly I excited state, and wanting to be taken up. As soon as possible this was done, when it was found that a man named Patrick Stanton, of Stubshaw Cross, Ashton, had had his ankle injured. It was not stated how the hoppet came to be over-wound,as the indicator appeared to work all right. Work in the shaft was stopped for the day. On Monday afternoon an accident happened in the Wood Pit, Haydock. Job Harrison,a ccllier, aged 33 years, residing at 2, Lyme-st., Haydock, was following his em- ployment when a large piece of coal fell and knocked the point of his pick, which he had in his hand, nearly through his leg, just above the knee. He was conveyed to the Cottage Hospital and attended by Dr. Hayward, Isurgeon to the collery company.
